The inapplicability of protection never implies that action is justified. Normative choice still requires a separate judgment.

The person responsible for the action specifies only who is responsible for carrying out or stopping it. Having such a person provides no basis for inferring that the mode of claim is intervention conversion, nor does it establish that the action is effective or justified. Every external action must correspond to a normative choice record (see Part 14) and disclose its value premises and the normative premises actually adopted this time. The normative premise “Explanation Does Not Confer Authority to Act” (§14.3) can by itself only block actions that exceed authorization. It cannot generate an affirmative option. The feasible options in the choice record are not a list of names but options whose content is set down. For each option, its kind, action type, target object, geographic area, validity period, reversibility, expected impacts, and distributional impacts are fixed in advance, and the options explicitly include one no-action option. The selected action must correspond to one of the external-action options and must match it item by item on action, object, geographic area, and validity period. All three of the following must be rejected: pointing in fact to the no-action option while using it as the basis for an external action; matching only the name in words while the content does not match item by item; and rewriting both the action and the authorization while the approved option remains unchanged. There must also be at least one currently valid, independently reviewed itemized authorization that covers this subject, object, action, geographic area, and period together and agrees with the stated source of authorization. An authorization unrelated to this action cannot back the proposed action, even if it is formally valid. The record must also have the following: the ten components that “Normative Bridging” requires, all of them passed; the records of each step of the four-step operational procedure; the person responsible for the action; prohibited actions; and the arrangements for stopping, protection, appeal, review, and restoration. If any item is missing, the action ceiling can only be taking no action or continuing deliberation. Whether an intervention conversion has occurred empirically is judged separately by the relevant formal test.

Joining several transformation steps one after another only sets the order of composition. Support gained at one step does not automatically carry to the next. Checking such a chain must ensure that each step has its own separate record, not confused with other steps; that each step contains only one transformation; that the objects and identity criteria referred to by adjacent steps are compatible; and that the target scale of each step matches the source scale of the next. If any step is unresolved, becomes invalid, or exceeds its loss limit, this must be retained in the conclusion for the whole chain. Success at the final step cannot override it.

Evaluation of the whole chain must also state whether the final task is consistent with the tasks at the individual steps and whether shared resources have been committed more than once. Two tasks can each be feasible with one unit of capacity and yet be impossible to complete together if they share that unit in the same period. If time limits, resources, or permitted strategies are legitimately changed, the new joint option should be evaluated. Representational sufficiency, joint causal response, and joint resource feasibility each have their own criteria. Passing one cannot substitute for passing the other two.

## 5.8 Consistency Checks and the Protection Floor

A consistency check deals only with formal matters: whether the items, references, versions, and outcome statuses are consistent with one another, and whether the recorded axis relations have been combined correctly. It cannot replace the judgments that substantive comparisons in each domain make about geometry, organizational graphs, causal abstraction, network embedding, object identity, or authorization validity. Without substantive comparisons and independent materials about the objects, a complete record or algorithmic output cannot justify determining scale elevation. A record may take any form, but it must meet the same requirements for traceability and review.

The four missingness statuses form a closed set, to which nothing else is added. “Unknown” means that it is not yet known. “Not applicable” means that it genuinely does not apply under the definition. “Unobservable” means that materials cannot be obtained under current conditions (§2.9). “Withheld for protection” means that it is not disclosed in order to protect. None of the four means “absent,” and deleting the item cannot substitute for marking its status.

Uptake carriers and responsible parties must be written down separately. Taking something up, being visible, being affected, or having greater capability does not by itself create responsibility. Whenever there is an effect on the rights of humans or sentient subjects, on the allocation of their scarce resources, on their exposure to risk, or on how they are treated in practice, the protection floor (§14.8) must identify low-power positions and local exclusion zones. It must provide arrangements for safe submission, anti-retaliation, stopping, appeal, review, and restoration. In these cases, it must not be marked “not applicable.” Insufficient protection lowers both the judgment ceiling and the action ceiling. A purely descriptive record may, under certain conditions, mark protection “not applicable,” but downstream actions cannot carry over that inapplicability. Once the use changes, the protection review must be reopened.

## 5.9 Evidence Boundaries and Independent Support

The names, numbers, summaries of meaning, and classifications of the nine scale transformations specify only how a transformation should be described and tested. They provide no empirical support that the transformation occurred, the mapping is valid, or the target property holds. Concept labels internal to the framework, examples, how completely the items are filled in, and results reported by the algorithm itself must not serve as evidence at the source end or the target end in place of materials about the objects.

Every actual transformation must obtain independent, verifiable materials separately for the source object and the target object. It must state the mapping, what is preserved, changed, or lost, the error, and the competing explanations, and it is judged in the same way by the four outcome statuses, the positive criterion, and the null-conclusion criterion. Source-domain materials can only propose candidates for the target end. Without independent support at the target end, the conclusion remains “a mapping awaiting testing” or “unknown.”

## 5.10 Cross-Circle Relation Transformation

Scale transformation and cross-circle relation transformation must be kept separate. Scale transformation asks which variables are preserved, changed, or lost for the same question between the source scale and the target scale. Cross-circle relation transformation asks how two or more candidate circles[^tn-circle-06] stand in parallel, contain one another, overlap, bridge, compete, or form temporarily at the same or different scales. A change in relations may accompany a change in scale. Neither term can stand in for the account of the other.

An account of a cross-circle relation needs to set out, at minimum, the source of the relation, its target, the type of static relation, whether membership or interfaces serve as the basis, direction, channel, delay, threshold, time window, evidence, and counterexamples. It also sets out before-and-after snapshots. “Transformed” is used only for the outcome of a relation update. A formerly parallel relation may become bridged when a bridging party appears. An overlapping relation may become nested through institutional integration, and a temporary circle may become institutionalized or undergo dissolution. Each such transformation needs a check of whether the identity criterion is preserved. If the identity criterion no longer holds, record an object conversion or a dissolution (§6.10). A new name must not be used to carry the old object forward.

| Question to Answer | What to Use | Distinctions to Preserve |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Can an individual’s state represent a team? | Aggregation (§5.5.1), the account of the scale transformation, and distributional loss | Team membership alone does not make a member’s state representative of the team |
| Is a team contained within an organization? | Nesting (§5.5.2) and a specific basis for containment | Having a superior in common does not imply membership containment |
| Are two circles associated because they share members? | The overlap relation, membership mappings, and the common environment | Overlap does not by itself produce effective feedback |
| Does a bridging party change another circle? | Network propagation (§5.5.3), a channel, and a counterfactual | Contact does not amount to transmission. Transmission does not amount to representation |
| Does a temporary group form a durable object? | The identity criterion, longitudinal material about the object, and institutionalization (§5.5.5). A claim of grouping gain takes a separate grouping-gain test, and a claim of a historical conditional increment takes a separate historical-increment test | Traces do not amount to institutionalization. The fact of durability need not depend on an additional historical residual |

When the same actor belongs to several circles, the actor’s distinct roles, visible information, responsibilities, risks, and ability to exit in each circle need to be retained. An actor must not first be merged into a single state that is then copied to every circle. Cross-circle projection should start from local states, propagate through stated membership or interface channels, and record the loss caused by aggregation at each step.

Translation involves both tasks and permissions. Accurately relaying what someone said, helping both sides understand each other, having permission to publish that person’s exact words, and signing an agreement on their behalf are four distinct capabilities or qualifications. The same translation can suffice to book an appointment and may still be insufficient to preserve poetic rhythm or distinctions in legal status. Insufficiency for the latter task does not justify saying retroactively that the former was never completed. The limited translation that succeeds should be retained, and the meanings and rights that did not transfer with it should be stated. 〔Studies 12.10, 26.08–26.09〕

### 5.10.1 Three Kinds of Transformation Must Be Kept Separate

Scale transformation asks which variables are preserved, changed, or lost for the same question between one scale profile and another. Cross-circle relation transformation asks how parallelism, containment, overlap, bridging, competition, or temporary relations among candidate circles are updated. Representational or discursive recasting (§3.4.1) asks how content with an identified source enters the vocabulary, variables, or expressions of the target task. All three can occur together, but they must be split apart and accounted for separately, in order.

Recasting needs its own account of what it preserves, changes, and loses. It can use the scale transformations “Network Propagation,” “Compression or Abstraction,” and “Horizontal Transfer,” or others (§5.5). Each of these operations has its own account, and they are linked according to their respective inputs, outputs, criteria, and failure conditions. A further transformation must not be counted merely because a name differs, and failures of different operations must not be merged into a single overall status.

### 5.10.2 Reviewing Recasting Loss

If two source states that can be distinguished in the source task cannot be distinguished in the target representation, record a task-relevant loss for that distinction. An identity mapping, reversible encoding, or mapping sufficient for the target task may yield no detected relevant loss. The rule is therefore “do not assume losslessness in advance.” It does not say that a mapping is “necessarily lossy.”

| Review Item | Minimum Question | Distinctions to Preserve |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Preservation | Which facts, relations, modalities, rights, or uncertainties must stay the same? | Preserving a title does not amount to preserving its semantics |
| Change | Which formats, units, levels of granularity, or expressions may change? | Permitting change does not permit arbitrary changes in meaning |
| Collapse | Which differences at the source end are merged at the target end? | Collapsing a difference does not imply that it is absent at the source end |
| Omission | What was left out of the target representation, and why? | Withholding for protection does not amount to absence |
| Addition | Which explanations, inferences, or target variables does the conversion produce? | Adding a variable does not amount to discovering a real-world entity |
| Return | When an anomaly occurs, which parent record (the record one level up from which it directly comes) or which arrangement is revisited? | Returning only reopens review. It does not patch what has already been done |

Round-trip reconstruction, from the target representation back to the source representation, can serve as a test but is insufficient by itself. A conversion may appear to round-trip by using hidden source records while failing to preserve the semantics of the target task. A one-way summary, by contrast, may be sufficient for the specified task. Review must return to the items to preserve that were stated in advance, the tolerances for loss, and the results at the target end.

Whether the target representation retains a needed distinction and whether the actual rule uses it correctly are two separate judgments. An error in acting on the representation does not by itself establish a recasting loss. If the distinction is still discernible but used incorrectly, record the gap in the rule or its execution. Representational loss and execution errors can also coexist. Their grounds should then be stated separately, and other local results that have already been established should be retained.

When both kinds of failure occur, the same unavoidable error should not be counted again as an additional failure of the rule. If the target answer is nonunique within a preimage (the source states mapped to the same target representation), no deterministic rule using only the current representation can answer correctly for all of its source states. This by itself establishes that the representation is insufficient. If the target answer is unique in another nonempty preimage but the actual rule gives the wrong answer, that case alone suffices to show, independently, that the rule is in error. When it is unclear what representation is actually used internally, the original material’s continued public availability does not establish that those implementing the rule had grasped the distinction at the time. The existence of material, timely access to it, and actual use must be checked separately.

### 5.10.3 Effective Variables, Closure, and Returning in Response to Residuals

An effective variable is a candidate variable proposed for a target scale or task in order to compress the state and improve an explanation, foresight[^tn-foresight-06], or comparison of options fixed in advance. Proposing an effective variable must at the same time state the object, scale, time window, and task it addresses, how it is measured, the simple baseline it is compared with, how large its error is, when it fails, and when it is retired. “Effective” does not mean that the variable is a real entity, a root cause, a universally applicable variable, or a basis for authorization.

The target representation carries no presumption of dynamic closure. For static descriptions or questions at the same scale, first check sources, conversion rules, and answers to the task, using the conditional formal propositions “Task Recovery” (§4.18.1) and “Task Preservation through Successive Conversions” (§4.18.4) when necessary. Check formal dynamical models for closure under the conditional formal proposition “Closure under Dynamics and Admissible Interventions” (§4.18.2), and obtain separate evidence for their correspondence to reality. For a descriptive mapping, the items that belong only to empirical tests do not apply and may be marked “not applicable” with reasons. A corresponding scale-closure test, with its positive criterion and null-conclusion criterion, is needed only when seeking formal empirical support under §4.6 for scale closure, object conversion, or intervention conversion. A scale change must not be fabricated to fill in every item. Failure to find a significant increment does not by itself establish closure. When an increment occurs, record the corresponding impact as a candidate for memory, noise, hysteresis, an unresolved term, or a residual. The shape alone must not be used to name a new entity.

The scale transformation record (§5.7) must state the target task under the two aspects “Identity and purpose” and “Semantics.” Under the three aspects “Transformation,” “Evidence,” and “Loss,” it must state which parent representation (the representation one level up from which the new representation directly comes) is used, which differences were collapsed, where to return when an anomaly occurs, the result of the reconstruction test, and the candidate effective variables at the target end. If the relevant information is missing, retain an explicit missingness status. A completely filled-in table must not be taken to establish that all of the source semantics have been preserved.

## 5.11 Representing Parallelism and Nesting Together

Real-world structures cannot be reduced to a single hierarchical tree. Local containment relations can coexist with lateral networks, membership overlap, competition for resources, and bridging through platforms. They are represented by a directed multigraph of relations. Each node keeps the definition of its own object, and each edge keeps the definition of its own relation. “Higher layer” denotes only a particular relation of containment, jurisdiction, or aggregation. It carries no implication of greater reality, correctness, or authority.

When several circles share an environment but have no direct channel, the model retains a node for the common conditions and must not invent a direct edge between the circles. When a channel is open only within the time window of an event, its edge has a start time and an end time. When different relations run in opposite directions, draw separate edges. This makes it possible to determine after an event which relation actually changed, without redrawing the whole structure as a story told after the fact.

[^tn-circle-06]: Translator's note: Circles may be parallel, nested, overlapping, or bridged.

[^tn-foresight-06]: Translator's note: Foresight in this book requires a registered target, horizon, and baseline, along with calibration.

<a id="part_6"></a>

# Part 6 Operation and Evolution

This Part develops the definitions of objects into explanations of processes. Operation, feedback, learning, maintenance, load, phase, and systemic selection are not narrative terms that can be used interchangeably. They are conditional mechanisms with distinct inferential premises and enabling conditions. The mechanisms also differ in their counterfactuals and stopping points. Naming a mechanism does not supply sufficient conditions. Only when the premises it depends on, its conditions, minimum evidence, and competing explanations all pass can the mechanism be determined to hold in a case, within the specified scale, time window, and identity criterion.

## 6.1 Describing an Operation

An account of an operation needs to set out at least the inputs, a specified carrier or channel, state transitions, outputs, environmental conditions, a time window, and any traces that may be left. If the output returns, also set out the return channel, the receiving position, and the item that changes. For a claim about intertemporal effects, first distinguish three things under §4.5: how history formed the current state, how current carriers transmit it, and whether there is any additional historical increment beyond the current representation. Check the materials on timing and mechanism for each. Of these, only the claim of an additional historical increment requires a comparison between a model that takes history into account and a model in which “the current state is already sufficient.” If the operation crosses scales, also complete a mapping that meets the definition of scale transformation (§3.4) and the epistemic constraint “Testing Cross-Scale Transfer” (§4.8.5). Accounting item by item in this way is not meant to force a complex process into a linear chain. It makes it possible to test each delay, loss, alternative channel, gap in evidence, and limit of extrapolation.

## 6.2 Effective Feedback (CM-FEEDBACK)

Grounds: the definition “Effective Feedback” (§3.3); channel effect (§4.4). Must also meet: the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and the conditions for evidence (§2.5). These three are method requirements, not additional empirical causes. The “Effective Feedback” mechanism does not presuppose a historical increment (§4.5).

The enabling conditions are as follows. A prior state or output enters a later process through a specified return channel that a channel-effect test has identified. Compared with the case of no return or a blocked channel, at least one subsequent state, transition probability, or constraint differs by more than the threshold. The temporal order and which item is changed have been stated before the results are seen. The mechanism chain is:

Prior state or output → return signal → transmission through the specified channel → signal uptake at the receiving position → change in a subsequent state, probability, or constraint → review against a blocking counterfactual

Minimum evidence includes a channel-effect test that has met its pre-registered criteria; the return channel and receiving position; temporal order; the item that changed; the subsequent difference; and a comparison with the case of no return or a blocked channel. Effective feedback is not determined in any of three cases: the signal arrives but the subsequent transition is unchanged; an independent common input can explain the change; or the difference is unchanged after the return channel is cut. Effective feedback establishes only that the return caused a subsequent change on that occasion. It does not amount to learning, repair, or a positive outcome, and it requires no durable historical trace.

### 6.2.1 Feedback Delay and the Stability Interval

A local model that can be analyzed on its own is x\_{t+1}=x\_t−k x\_{t−d}. Here x\_t is the signed, dimensionless deviation from the target, k is a fixed real-valued gain, and d is a fixed nonnegative integer delay. The sampling interval is fixed. The model excludes external shocks, measurement noise, saturation in execution, and state bounds. For every finite initial history, the zero solution is asymptotically stable if and only if 0<k<2sin[π/(4d+2)]. Equality at the bounds is outside the stability interval. The proof is in Appendix C.10.

For example, let k=0.8 and set every entry in the initial history to 1. The model is asymptotically stable at delays of 0 or 1 step and unstable at delays of 2 or 3 steps. In all four cases the first step takes the value from 1 to 0.2. With the channel blocked at k=0, the value stays at 1. The model thus exhibits both effective feedback and failure of stability. Crossing the stability boundary means that a nondecaying or growing mode exists. It does not imply that every trajectory, including the one with zero initial history, grows.

Stability does not guarantee that the deviation shrinks at every step, that transient peaks are acceptable, or that execution costs are affordable. A negative x\_t indicates only that the target has been overshot. It does not represent a negative number of tasks. The equation does not model nonnegativity, demand, heterogeneous service, strategic responses, or permissions in real queues. Independent measurement and model validation are needed before applying this criterion to a real process. The criterion must not be used to set a real-world corrective gain that has not been identified.

## 6.3 Feedback-Mediated Learning (CM-LEARNING)

Basic grounds: the “Effective Feedback” mechanism (§6.2). Must also meet three method requirements: the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and the conditions for evidence (§2.5). Feedback-mediated learning requires a return to cause an update that can be retained and is actually used in a subsequent task. It has two branches, each requiring its own evidence: the carrier branch, transmitted through a current carrier, and the historical-increment branch, which claims a historical increment beyond the current representation. They correspond respectively to the carrier-transmission route and the historical-increment route of §4.5.

The carrier branch. Its enabling conditions begin with effective feedback changing an internal state, parameter, rule, memory, or structure that can be located. A specified carrier retains the update or sustains continued updating, and the update is actually used in repeated rounds. The later task, fixed in advance, shows a reviewable difference relative to a baseline or an alternative process stated in advance. A causal claim must have interruption, replacement, recovery, or a comparison that meets the conditions for identification, and must address common inputs, continued training, selection, attrition, and changes in measurement. A claim about transfer or predictive gain also requires evaluation suited to that claim, using an independent task or out-of-sample data. The mechanism chain is:

Effective feedback → locatable internal update → retention or continued updating through the update carrier → actual use in later rounds → change in the outcome of the prespecified task

A single parameter change, a single success, a single write-back, or the archiving of materials is insufficient to establish this learning mechanism. Write-back means that feedback changes rules, records, resources, or roles, and the change is actually carried out. The corresponding mechanism claim is not supported if the update is not retained, if it is not used later, if a common input alone can explain the task outcome, or if only a proxy measure changes while the task fixed in advance is unaffected. Effective feedback, learning in general, transfer across contexts, and net benefit need to be judged separately. Established learning does not imply improvement, a unified goal, or authorization to act.

When the goal itself changes, the reasons for forming the new goal and the decision procedure should be stated. The results, failures, and costs under the old goal should be preserved before a comparison is established for the new task. A goal reconstructed later must not be used to rewrite failure on the old task as success (see §2.14).

Learning in general can be supported by evidence from the relevant domain, such as new tasks that can be completed repeatedly, skills that are retained and used, or traceable teaching or organizational processes. It need not first be formally determined, under this framework, to be a case of this mechanism. A report may state together that “the practice has changed,” “the subsequent net effect remains undetermined,” and “the feedback-mediated mechanism has yet to be identified,” without collapsing these judgments into a single “pass” or “fail.” 〔Studies 16.02, 25.01–25.08, 31.08〕

Learning evaluation should also distinguish task completion with support, independent transfer after support is withdrawn, and subsequent outcomes in everyday life. Necessary support can form part of an expressive or collaborative task. In that case, failure without support does not negate an earlier success. If independent transfer was the original goal, testing it requires a comparison suited to that goal with support withdrawn. Responsibilities for choosing the goal, confirming retention of the update, measuring task performance, and judging net benefit are separate. Continuing support must not be used to deny a functional gain, and performance with assistance must not stand in for independent skill.

The historical-increment branch. In addition to carrier updates, repeated use, and a task comparison, there must be a historical-increment test that supports an additional historical conditional increment relative to an explicitly stated current representation. When the current carrier has sufficiently retained what has been learned, this increment can disappear while learning in the carrier branch still holds. Known current carriers must not be omitted to manufacture an increment. Branches must not be switched after the results are seen to rescue the original test. The two routes each state their own comparisons, counterexamples, and failure conditions.

## 6.4 A Hypothetical Appeal Illustrating Feedback, Institutional Write-Back, and Learning

Suppose a hypothetical institution receives an appeal. This example illustrates the method of classification only. It draws on no real-world material and provides no external empirical proof.

The appeal is received and a receipt is generated. Records, rules, resources, roles, responsibilities, memory, and stopping conditions all remain unchanged. This is signal arrival alone, with neither effective feedback nor institutional write-back.

The appeal changes the case-status item through a specified channel, but the change is not put into effect. This can be effective feedback in the sense of the definition (§3.3) while still falling short of complete institutional write-back in the sense of the human-domain clause “Institutional Write-Back” (§7.1).

The change in that item is put into effect, and intake, the change, execution, and duration are all recorded. This is an institutional write-back. The fact of write-back does not establish that the institution is justified, nor does it amount to long-term repair.

When the write-back produces an update to a rule or state that can be retained, the update enters several later rounds of similar cases, and a corresponding task comparison and causal basis are available, a candidate for carrier feedback-mediated learning may be proposed, that is, a candidate in the carrier branch. If a historical conditional increment beyond the current representation is also claimed, a historical-increment test tests it independently.

Thus, neither feedback nor write-back amounts to learning. The evidence requirements increase from one of the three to the next. Having an appeal entry point or making a public response cannot satisfy them all at once.

## 6.5 Maintenance and Preservation–Dissipation (CM-MAINTENANCE)

Basic grounds: structural object (§3.1); channel effect (§4.4). Must also meet three method requirements: the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and the conditions for evidence (§2.5). Basic state terms (§3.2) supply its domain restriction in state terms. Maintenance has three requirements. The current identity criterion or functional criterion is stated in advance, together with the maintenance time window. A channel-effect test must identify replenishment, replacement, correction, or removal as the specified channel that changes how identity or function continues to hold. The comparison also needs to cover maintenance, reduced maintenance, mismatched maintenance, and cessation of maintenance.

The mechanism chain is:

Wear, drift, loss, or component exit → specified maintenance channel → replenishment/replacement/correction/removal → change in how long identity or function holds or in the probability of failure

The maintenance mechanism has three branches. The current branch checks what effect maintenance inputs have on how the current identity or function continues to hold. The carrier-accumulation branch also uses §4.5 to check the current carrier of wear or capability, how previous inputs formed that carrier, how it is retained or replenished across time windows, and longitudinal and causal evidence that maintenance changes how identity or function holds later. The historical-increment branch is of the historical-increment kind. A historical-increment test is added only when a historical conditional increment beyond the current representation is claimed. The maintenance claim should be narrowed or withdrawn in the following cases: the object continues to satisfy the identity criterion or functional criterion in the target time window without ongoing maintenance; a change in maintenance input makes no difference to the relevant outcome; or an independent shock can explain the supposed wear. The definition also fails if the old maintenance criteria are still used after the original identity criterion has changed.

A need for maintenance does not imply that an object should persist indefinitely. The existence of a maintenance channel cannot directly designate a specific party to take up the work, assign responsibility, or impose a duty to make sacrifices. Mismatched maintenance can prolong the period during which the old identity criterion holds while undermining the target functional criterion. An orderly stop, object conversion, or dissolution may also be outcomes the definition permits.

Maintenance analysis also needs to distinguish tasks during normal operation, migration, failure, and recovery. Interface standards specify conditions under which interoperability is possible. Actual compatibility still depends on implementation versions, business semantics, environment and load, testing, and on-site adaptation. The existence of parts does not imply that their specifications fit, their quality can be verified, personnel can reach the site, or personnel are authorized to shut the system down. Additional maintenance work can take place outside the original object and be supplied by users, households, outsourced workers, or other institutions. Central work orders and operational outputs alone cannot account for the total amount of maintenance.

Test redundancy against failure conditions. A count of backups alone is insufficient. Two paths may share a power source, software state, transport channel, supplier, operator, or approval node. They can substitute for each other in normal operation and still fail together during a fault. Spare capacity, exposure to common causes, the time needed to switch, on-site skills, and the actual authority to switch should be verified separately. The communications, roads, fuel, spare parts, and personnel on which recovery depends should be included in the same time window. Adding backups, reducing coupling, and retaining independent local operation are only candidates. Their net effects depend on the specific failure and the cost of maintenance.

## 6.6 Load, Capacity, and Recovery (CM-LOAD)

Basic grounds: structural object (§3.1); channel effect (§4.4). Must also meet three method requirements: the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and the conditions for evidence (§2.5). Demand and capacity must be quantities of the same type or have explicit units and a conversion mapping. Demand, available capacity, replenishment, and spillover need to be measured in the same time window and at the same position. A channel-effect test supports only the measured channel and its relevant dimensions.

The mechanism chain is:

Demand of a matching type enters the specified channel → occupies available capacity → produces an immediate gap or cross-boundary spillover → load reduction/replenishment/capacity expansion changes the gap

To explain subsequent accumulation or delayed recovery, separately check the carriers of damage, capacity, or recovery and their effects across time windows.

The load mechanism has three branches. The instantaneous branch determines only the demand–capacity relation of the same type and the immediate gap within the same time window. The carrier-accumulation branch checks under §4.5 how historical exposure formed the current damage or capacity state, how that state is retained or recovers across time windows, and the subsequent outcomes and comparison conditions. A causal claim must have grounds for identification appropriate to the claim. The historical-increment branch is of the historical-increment kind. A historical-increment test separately tests the conditional increment beyond the current representation. Capacity that expands at the same time can absorb demand. An instantaneous gap may leave no lasting difference once it closes. Load therefore need not accumulate monotonically, and an instantaneous overload need not cause damage or collapse. Conversely, expanding capacity, buffering, or protection may also change demand and exposure themselves: needs previously shut out are met, new use is induced, or the threshold for drawing on the capacity falls and exposure rises with it. An estimate of the gap after an expansion must check whether these responses occur and what share each takes, and must re-estimate under §11.9 together with the affected downstream positions; it cannot carry over the demand from before the expansion. A claim that the expansion has induced new demand must have the corresponding channel evidence. The meeting of needs that were previously unmet is not recorded as a failure of the expansion (§2.5.1).

Load must be stated by position and distribution. A mean alone is insufficient. For capacity, distinguish peak and sustained levels, alternative channels, and replenishment. For recovery, distinguish recovery of visible output, recovery of identity or function, and recovery of the internal margin. Quantities of different types cannot be directly subtracted. A need for recovery does not by itself impose a duty to make sacrifices on any subject or grant any subject authorization.

A recovery judgment should state at the same time what recovered, for whom, under what support conditions, and through what point in time. The following are evidenced separately: the quantity, quality, continuity, and accessibility of actual output; staff recuperation, spare parts, maintenance backlogs, and continuity of funding; the added burdens outside the boundary from care, commuting, borrowing money, or substitute services; and subsequent disruptions and near misses. The pre-disaster population, current population, eligible people, and actual users must not be silently substituted for one another when calculating recovery rates. Confirming that a particular limited function has recovered does not require all other outcomes to recover at the same time.

Temporary facilities, continuing outside support, or assistive equipment can provide real functional repair. Dependence on support does not by itself indicate failed recovery. The sustainability and expiration of support should be verified, along with whether alternative uptake is already in operation. Any demand peaks, maintenance cycles, or seasonal exposures that have yet to be experienced should also be stated. The term “false recovery” should be reserved for a claim that extends beyond what the evidence supports about the object, population, function, or conditions for continuation. That alone provides no basis for inferring deception. If destabilization recurs after recovery, several possibilities must be compared separately: the persistence of earlier damage, unreplenished reserves, interruption of support, new shocks, and changes in measurement definitions. A new failure must not erase an earlier result stated within its proper limits. Necessary support must not be withdrawn to validate recovery.

## 6.7 Phase and Threshold Transition (CM-PHASE)

Basic grounds: structural object (§3.1); basic state terms (§3.2). The epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4) and the conditions for evidence (§2.5) are the shared method requirements for the phase-pattern branch. Add the conditions for causal claims (§2.4) when making a causal claim about a trigger, persistence through a carrier, or historical-increment hysteresis. They are not a prerequisite for basic pattern classification, and a purely predictive historical increment does not thereby become causal. Basic phase identification does not require a historical-increment test. Under the same definition of the candidate object and the same identity criterion, it is possible to test whether there are at least two reproducibly distinguishable ranges of operation once the state variables, candidate parameters or trigger conditions, threshold, and robustness to noise and binning have been stated in advance.

The mechanism judgments have the following branches.

The phase-pattern branch. It requires “the same identity criterion, two reviewable intervals, and a threshold pattern fixed in advance.” It determines only the relation between the intervals and the threshold and makes no causal claim about the trigger.

The causal-triggering branch. It requires “a specified trigger channel and either an intervention on the channel or natural variation suitable for identification.” A channel-effect test is also required to locate the effect of the trigger.

The carrier-persistence branch checks how, under the same identity criterion, the current carrier maintains a phase, sustains it across time windows, or gives rise to delayed recovery. Use §4.5 to document the carrier and temporal order, make longitudinal comparisons, and obtain causal evidence appropriate to the claim. The hysteresis branch of the “Phase and Threshold Transition” mechanism is limited to the historical-increment kind. A historical-increment test separately tests the conditional increment beyond the current representation. An identical curve shape cannot stand in for evidence under any route.

The phase conclusion should be withdrawn in three cases: a continuous trend already fully explains the change within the same state distribution; the threshold shifts arbitrarily with the way of binning; or the identity criterion had already ceased to hold before the transition. These are recorded instead as continuous change, an effect of how the measurements were partitioned, and object conversion or dissolution, respectively. A reversible phase need not have a historical path. Only the historical-increment hysteresis branch adds a historical-increment test. Phases do not form a mandatory sequence of maturation through the seven state prototypes (§8.3). A new phase does not thereby rank higher, become better, or carry greater authorization.

## 6.8 Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction (CM-SELECTION)

Basic grounds: basic state terms (§3.2). Must also meet three method requirements: the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and the conditions for evidence (§2.5). This mechanism is set out on its own as conditions that can be tested. It does not follow automatically from the definition of “evolution has occurred,” and a conceptual explanation or the framework’s own account cannot establish it directly.

The three outputs must be kept separate.

The selection pattern. It requires “variation, difference, retention, entry into the next round, repeated rounds, and random drift as a competing explanation.” Before the results are seen, define distinguishable variations (written V) and their sources. In comparable environments, observe differential outcomes (written D) that exceed the threshold. The differences carry forward into the next round through retention (written R) and can be reviewed across repeated rounds. Test random drift, common external causes, and sampling bias at the same time. Its basic grounds are the basic state terms alone.

The specific mechanism. It requires “a specified channel of retention or reproduction and either a perturbation of the channel or natural variation suitable for identification.” Beyond an established selection pattern, a channel-effect test is also required to locate the mechanism that carries the process.

The path across rounds. It requires “a conditional increment from historical terms across rounds and control for the current state.” Beyond an established selection pattern, a historical-increment test is also required.

Change without a differential outcome amounts to change alone. A one-off difference with no retention, no entry into the next round, and no repeated rounds is a one-off outcome. If the random-drift model is already sufficient, no selection pattern is determined. If retention remains unchanged after the candidate reproduction channel is perturbed, that specific mechanism is not determined. A single case of persistence does not amount to differential retention. What is retained does not thereby become better, more advanced, or more justified. Systemic selection is distinct from choice by an acting subject, and still more from collective governance choice (§14.2). A choice by an acting subject requires a subject, options, and evidence of a decision. Collective governance choice requires normative premises, authorization within the scope of authorization, and operational procedures.

## 6.9 Conditions for Coevolution

A candidate for coevolution may be proposed when two candidate objects change each other’s environments, feasible paths, specified channels, or retention conditions and the effects in both directions are traceable within their respective time windows. The following must be stated separately: each object’s definition and identity criterion, their respective scales and time windows, the channel in each direction identified by a channel-effect test, temporal order, differences in speed, and the shared environment outside the two objects. Obtain separate evidence under §4.5 for carrier effects across rounds. Add the corresponding historical-increment tests separately only for claims of historical conditional increments beyond the current representation.

Joint change, synchronized fluctuations, and long-term correlation cannot substitute for bidirectional mechanisms. One-way dependence, common shocks, and synchronization of measurement protocols are all necessary competing explanations. Coevolution does not imply symmetry, mutual benefit, shared values, or a duty to maintain the relationship.

A shared final state does not establish a shared mechanism. Two processes can converge on the same fixed point while having different update rules, speeds of return, transients, and responses to intervention. A simpler representation may suffice if the only question concerns the long-run terminal value. The original conclusion does not automatically extend to questions about whether the target can be reached by a deadline or about targeted operations. Analyses of recovery, coevolution, and cross-circle continuation must retain these differences as required by the question. Converging curves are not taken as a substitute for identifying the mechanism.

## 6.10 Dissolution, Object Conversion, and the Limits of Repair

The criterion for dissolution is that the original identity criterion no longer holds. If the original identity criterion fails but another object’s definition can hold, object conversion should be distinguished from termination. A phase change is distinguished from dissolution only if the original identity criterion continues to hold. Dissolution does not automatically count as failure, and persistence does not automatically count as success. What this section and other places call “recording an object conversion” is a descriptive record made after the distinction in the second sentence of this paragraph has been drawn: the original identity criterion no longer holds, another object’s definition can hold, the two stretches of record are thereafter no longer treated as the same object, and the new object does not cover over the old object’s failures, responsibilities, and traces (§10.9). Determining the identity classification as “object converted” in a scale-transformation record, or putting forward an object conversion as an empirical claim, additionally requires meeting the conditions of §5.7, including a supported scale-closure test of the subtype for object or intervention conversion.

The criterion for repair is a target identity criterion or target functional criterion made public before the results are seen (§3.2). Repair can make use of old traces, and it can change components, boundaries, relations, interfaces, carriers, and scale positions. It does not turn back time to an earlier state. A claim that a repair window exists requires, besides the target identity criterion or target functional criterion, a comparison of how intervening at different times affects whether the target can be reached and at what cost. Use the carrier route to obtain evidence about current constraints formed through history (§4.5). A historical-increment test is additionally required only for a claim of a historical conditional increment beyond the current representation. Even if these empirical conditions all hold, whether the goal is justified, who chooses it, who is responsible, and who may implement it must still be reviewed under the normative premises (§14.3), the scope of authorization, and the four-step operational procedure (§14.6).

### 6.10.1 Formation, Maintenance, Recovery, and Replication

That an arrangement forms, that it can then be maintained, that it can recover after a disturbance, and that it can be replicated elsewhere are four outcomes, each with its own conditions and evidence. Formation usually requires start-up conditions and a path of transition from the original state. Whether maintenance depends on continuing replenishment, replacement, and correction is tested under §6.5. Recovery depends on the carriers and margins still available after the disturbance, the external replenishment that can be reached, and the time remaining; whether what recovers is output, identity or function, or internal margins is specified separately under §6.6. Aiming at a target identity criterion or target functional criterion made public in advance rather than seeking a return to the original state is called repair and is judged under §6.10. When the arrangement is replicated in a new location, the results in the original location provide only a candidate; the new location must itself have the corresponding personnel, equipment, time, and conditions for error correction, and must have its own materials.

The four are judged separately, and none can vouch for another. All four are also descriptive judgments and do not mean that the arrangement should be maintained, recovered, or replicated. Operating well in the current period can coexist with no one taking it up in the next round; that longer-term or wider-scope results have not yet been demonstrated also does not cancel local results already achieved under criteria fixed in advance. When replication or scaling up fails, distinguish at least four situations: the scheme itself fails, including cases where the results in the original location were not caused by the scheme; the scheme was not implemented as written in advance; the new location lacks enabling conditions the mechanism requires; or scaling up itself changed the treatment or the object (§2.4.1). Both what was implemented and the enabling conditions must be written down before the results are seen and be verifiable independently of the results. An implementation deviation or a missing condition raised only after failure can only be recorded as a candidate to be tested in the next round and does not change the present record.

## 6.11 Final Gate for Mechanism Outputs

For each of the six conditional mechanisms, the following must be set out clearly, in this order: the statement of object and scale, inferential premises, enabling conditions, mechanism chain, minimum evidence, competing explanations, counterexamples, and failure boundary. If any item is missing, retain only a candidate mechanism or a question to check. A determination of feedback does not carry with it a determination of learning. Likewise, instantaneous load does not carry accumulation with it, a basic phase does not carry hysteresis, a selection pattern does not carry a specific mechanism or a value, and maintenance and repair do not carry a duty to persist. Conceptual explanations and teaching examples only illustrate how to use these conditions. They supply no external empirical support.

## 6.12 Operation with Multiple Asynchronous Clocks

A multi-circle joint state includes at least five clocks: immediate, interactive, organizational, institutional, and long-term (§10.7). An event can first change fast variables, then change expectations about relationships through repeated interaction, then change resources through organizational decisions, and only then potentially lead to institutional write-back. If these changes are compressed into one moment, a delay can be misread as a lack of effect, or a short-term fluctuation as long-term evolution.

Changes in fast variables do not automatically indicate long-term institutional outcomes or outcomes in everyday life. Industrial expansion, a signed agreement, the end of overt violence, the completion of facilities, or public cooperation still calls for checking execution, distribution, rights, relations, and continuity. If the material is insufficient, retain the local results that are known and stop extrapolating over longer ranges.

Each mechanism should state which clock it updates on and what its bridges across clocks are. The arrival of a feedback signal does not establish that organizational rules have changed. An organizational decision does not amount to institutional execution. A change in institutional text does not imply actual write-back at every local position. A bridge across clocks must specify the carrier, execution, confirmation, and failure conditions.

| Clock Transition | Minimum Evidence for the Bridge | Common Failures |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Immediate→Interaction | A difference in state persists over multiple rounds and changes the other party’s response | A one-off emotional reaction fades |
| Interaction→Organization | Changes in relations or strategies are incorporated into roles, processes, resources, or records | Verbal consensus is not put into practice |
| Organization→Institution | Verifiable changes in rules or procedures, arrangements for responsibility, and actual execution. Authorization, legal validity, and normative justification are stated separately | A document is issued without implementation, or an institutional change that actually occurred is omitted because it lacked legal validity |
| Institution→Long Term | Continued execution, maintenance, learning, and alternative paths | Rebound after short-term compliance |

The table records how changes actually follow one another step by step. Legal validity, normative justification, and authorization do not serve as criteria for establishing that “an event occurred.” Rule changes and their execution must enter the process record if there is corresponding factual evidence, even when they violate rules, exceed authorization, or are contested. Their authorization and legal status are noted separately. Explaining how they formed and what consequences they had does not amount to permitting their implementation. Conversely, authorization, issuance of a rule, or an institution’s announcement of completion cannot substitute for evidence of actual execution.

## 6.13 Cross-Circle Cascades and Coevolution

A cascade occurs when a local change in one circle[^tn-circle-07] triggers changes in other circles through overlapping membership, bridging interfaces, shared resources, network propagation, or top-down institutional transmission. The object, channel, scale, and evidence need to be checked again at each step. The first step holding does not warrant assuming that all later steps hold. Capacity limits, filtering, delays, offsetting effects, and local exclusion zones can cut a cascade short.

A discussion of cross-circle propagation must first identify what propagates and what conditions the target needs in order to change. A message can arrive through a single bridge. An action that requires actual cooperation from several people, confirmation from different sources, or adequate support for acting safely can stall in that same network. A count of relays from one source cannot stand in for a count of independent confirmers, and a count of confirmers cannot stand in for actual collaboration. A bridge’s effect depends on how the sources are related, where the transmission arrives, the order of arrival, the duration of action, and the conditions of feasibility. It cannot be determined directly from the shortest path, the number of connections, or any one model threshold.

Three situations must also be distinguished: one failure triggers the next; multiple failures jointly obstruct recovery; or a common external cause damages multiple locations at the same time. The first requires evidence of transmission at each hop. The other two require checks on the conditions on which recovery depends and on exposure to common causes, respectively. A mechanism by which people adopt something only after confirmation from multiple sources can coexist with supply dependencies among facilities, but their state variables and thresholds cannot be interchanged. Complex contagion does not guarantee that higher clustering is more beneficial. The gains it brings from reinforcement can be offset by reduced reach across groups.

Coevolution requires at least two objects to change one another’s selection environments, transition probabilities, or constraints over a period of time while retaining their own independent identity criteria. If one object is simply absorbed by another, it should be recorded as nesting or object conversion. Synchronized changes due solely to a common external environment are not called coevolution. If a return signal changes no subsequent state, the relationship is called only coupling or shared exposure.

Multi-circle cascades and coevolution carry no inherent direction of value. Tighter coupling can improve coordination or increase vulnerability and diffuse responsibility. Decoupling can reduce efficiency or protect local autonomy and the ability to limit losses. Evaluation and action still belong to the normative layer (Part 14).

## 6.14 The Search Order for Mechanisms and Paths

For a specific question, first screen for potentially applicable mechanisms according to the object, scale, time window, and requested output. Then look for paths based on observed differences in state. The state prototypes for human collectives (Part 8) apply only to objects that meet the corresponding conditions. Actors, technical systems, and natural processes must not be assigned the same set of states merely because their names are similar.

Start the search with four kinds of material. These are the object’s current state that can be confirmed, direct changes that can be confirmed after the event, channels, capacities, and clocks that can carry later changes, and mechanisms and external disturbances not yet distinguished. Use a state’s exit conditions to propose candidate paths and observed changes to propose candidate mechanisms. Then check the enabling conditions, stages of propagation, and minimum evidence item by item. The order serves only to locate candidates. Finding one earlier does not make it more likely to be true.

When using a candidate, retain competing candidates and simple baselines that can explain the same phenomenon. Return signals should be distinguished from learning. Local overload should be distinguished from temporary rises in demand, declining capacity, and common external causes. Cross-circle cascades should be distinguished from synchronized exposure. Counterexamples and exclusions specified in the full conditions of the relevant mechanism must not be omitted merely because the search has found the corresponding mechanism.

For each candidate path, state separately the conditions under which it continues to hold, the observable changes the mechanism should produce first, signals to the contrary, and the stopping point. Without evidence of enabling conditions, a candidate can still guide observations designed to distinguish the alternatives. It cannot be promoted to an identified mechanism. An early signal must not be just a scaled-down restatement of the outcome. When paths share evidence, citing it again does not add independent support.

The search order may be adjusted in light of missed cases, misclassifications, and the cost of use. Adjustments must preserve the original limits of applicability for the mechanisms and be compared with simpler search methods. Ease of search, a complete set of cards, or the use of the same order by several analysts does not establish that a real-world mechanism holds.

[^tn-circle-07]: Translator's note: Circles may be parallel, nested, overlapping, or bridged.

<a id="part_7"></a>

# Part 7 The Human Structured World

Rather than pushing human experience directly into the universal core, this Part adds over the universal structural grammar (Part 3) a further layer of concepts designed specifically for the human world, referred to below as the human adaptation layer. The eleven basic structural concepts describe broadly conceived empirical structures. The human adaptation layer alone handles intent, meaning, power, institutions, authorization, responsibility, and value. The eleven human variables and the eleven basic structural concepts are managed separately. Similar names or functions, or an equal number of terms, do not establish one-to-one equivalence between the two. Judgments made specifically for the human world must not be applied back to nature as general rules.

The eleven human variables all come under the human-domain proposition role (§2.2), but they are variables, not the six human-domain clauses. The eight categories of generative condition, generative subject, generative event, uptake carrier, responsible party, source of destabilization, mechanism of destabilization, and behavior of destabilization (§7.2) are category definitions. The variables and the category definitions carry no empirical truth on their own. Formal support under this framework for empirical questions and human empirical hypotheses must come from one of two kinds of test. One is a formal test of one of the four empirical questions, which needs to meet the requirements for the pre-registration of formal tests (§4.1). The other is a specific test of one of the three human empirical hypotheses (“Meaning and Coordination”; “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity”; “Historical Trace Carriers”), which needs to meet the corresponding requirements for such tests (§4.2). Existing domain research still supports limited conclusions according to its own objects, designs, and evidence. That support must not be revoked wholesale merely because the research has not obtained eligibility for a formal test under this framework. The other three clauses (“Action Uptake and Classification of Responsibility”; “Institutional Write-Back”; “Open-Ended Undertaking”), the variables, and the category definitions must not be presented as empirical support on the strength of fully completed items or a successful classification.

Applying this Part requires first defining the object clearly by the seven elements of a structural object (§3.1) and stating its scale profile. Any judgment about the human world must specify the effective object, comparison conditions, time window, and observation position. It must also specify evidence coverage, affected positions, and the scope of authorization. Technologies, crises, resources, institutional conditions, and statistical trends do not acquire intent by having impacts. Visibility, disagreement, or proximity to a disturbance does not automatically make a person, group, or dissenter a mechanism, source, or responsible party.

## 7.1 Role Boundaries of the Six Human-Domain Clauses (H1–H6)

The six human-domain clauses have different roles. Three are empirical hypotheses that await specific tests, two are operational or classification rules, and one is a normative boundary. How each clause can hold depends on its role.

| Clause | Role | What May Be Determined | Limits That Cannot Be Crossed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Meaning and Coordination | Empirical hypothesis | If a candidate meaning arrangement specified in advance produces a difference beyond the threshold in resource, action, or coordination outcomes relative to the comparison condition, determine it to be a conditional orientation anchor | Do not infer a unified inner state, genuine consent, or a common will from slogans, shared language, or an interpreter’s projections |
| Action Uptake and Classification of Responsibility | Operational rule | State the uptake carrier, bearers of costs of the same type, beneficiaries, the right to stop, and the responsible party separately | Classification alone does not establish intertemporal reproduction. The ability to take up the work does not become an obligation to do so |
| Institutional Write-Back | Classification rule | If an appeal, a check, or feedback changes records, rules, resources, roles, responsibilities, memory, or stopping conditions and actual execution is documented, determine it to be institutional write-back | Intake does not amount to write-back. A single write-back does not establish learning, and a single update does not establish long-term repair |
| Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity | Empirical hypothesis | If position, mediation, disclosure conditions, outcome measure, comparison conditions, and threshold are all specified in advance, determine the channels of masking, amplification, or reflexivity that the evidence supports | Labels such as “power,” “platform,” “metric,” or “AI” must not substitute for a mechanism chain and a counterfactual. Silence does not amount to consent |
| Historical Trace Carriers | Empirical hypothesis | If the historical event, candidate carrier, baseline, trace measure, threshold, and durability window are all specified in advance and a durable difference exceeds the threshold, determine only a candidate trace | Traces do not establish path effects. Obtain separate evidence under §4.5 for the subsequent effects of the current carrier. Only a claim about an additional historical increment requires a historical-increment test. Repair or protective action needs to pass the conclusion rule “Normative Bridging” (§4.14.1) separately, with the normative premises stated explicitly on this occasion, the corresponding authorization, and the operational procedures |
| Open-Ended Undertaking | Normative boundary | Describe actual costs, voluntariness, direction, alternative explanations, structural consequences, and the right to stop | Do not diagnose whether a person “has love,” treat sacrifice as proof of love, or coerce one party into continuing to bear the burden |

The outputs of the six clauses are limited to empirical descriptions, classification results, gaps in evidence, or normative requirements. These outputs do not themselves authorize any real-world adjustment. Classification under “Action Uptake and Classification of Responsibility” does not authorize redistribution or attribution of responsibility. Classification under “Institutional Write-Back” does not authorize changing records or rules. The normative boundary of “Open-Ended Undertaking” does not itself implement protection or stopping measures. Any real-world action must in every case separately pass the conclusion rule “Normative Bridging” (§4.14.1), with the normative premises stated explicitly on this occasion, the corresponding authorization within the scope of jurisdiction and authorization, and the operational procedures.

The evidence status of all three empirical hypotheses is “awaiting evidence from a specific test.” Their specific tests follow the same procedure as the formal tests of the four empirical questions (§4.1). They have two stages, pre-registration and results: the target, criteria, and rules are set down before the results are seen, and the results are appended after the test is carried out. They use the same four outcome statuses. They likewise have a positive criterion and a null-conclusion criterion. Any deviation is disclosed. The same discipline applies to evidence references and analysis materials. The only difference is that such a test can test only one of these three hypotheses.

A “Meaning and Coordination” test must select in advance exactly one outcome criterion among resource allocation, action choice, and coordination outcomes. A “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” test must select in advance exactly one criterion among evidence coverage, safety of expression, object behavior, and reflexive response. A “Historical Trace Carriers” test must select in advance exactly one carrier family, one specific carrier belonging to that family, and one durability criterion. A list of multiple carriers, or a specific carrier that does not match the selected family, makes the test ineligible. Criteria that were not selected must not be used to rescue a test after the results. Failure on the positive criterion does not automatically mean that the null model (a comparison model without the claimed factor) is supported. A “Historical Trace Carriers” test establishes only a trace within the specified carrier and time window. Obtain separate evidence under §4.5 for future effects of the current carrier. A historical increment beyond the current representation requires a separate, independent historical-increment test. Internal definitions, concept labels, and the framework’s own statements do not count as external empirical support.

## 7.2 Three Sets of Categories That Must Be Kept Distinct

The eight categories fall into three sets: generative condition, generative subject, and generative event; uptake carrier and responsible party; and source, mechanism, and behavior of destabilization. Separating the categories keeps the subsequent questions, evidence requirements, and limits on responsibility distinct. The categories specify what materials a case must supply. They do not assert that the corresponding facts about the world already hold. Each category requires grounds directly relevant to the claim in question. A single record can support several distinct facts among them, but their dependence on that same source must be retained, and the record must not be counted repeatedly as independent validation. A single case can be placed in several categories at once. Establishing one category cannot settle the others on its own. When stating formally that categories hold independently of one another, identify each category exactly, one by one. A collective name for the set must not be used in their place, and a short name that could coincide with a name used elsewhere once taken out of context must not be given on its own.

### 7.2.1 Generative Condition (GC)

The generative condition asks “What conditions make generation possible or more likely?” Resources, technologies, institutions, relationships, trauma, crises, and windows of opportunity can all be candidate conditions. Conditions have no intent. When compiling the condition inventory, first record when the conditions arose, changed, or were removed, and what the actual exposure was. A claim that a condition makes generation more likely also requires a comparison suited to that claim, a difference in outcomes, a candidate channel, and competing explanations. Generative conditions, generative subjects, and generative events are tested separately. Observing a condition neither identifies the generative subject nor establishes that a generative event has occurred.

### 7.2.2 Generative Subject (GS)

The generative subject asks “Who can understand and carry out acts of initiation, translation, or handover?” The identity of the subject, capability, resources, actual actions, and authorization status must be verified separately. Technologies, crises, platforms, metrics, and resource windows must not be counted as subjects. Evidence of subject status cannot be inferred merely from the occurrence of an event. The generative subject does not automatically correspond to the full set of responsible parties.

### 7.2.3 Generative Event (GE)

The generative event asks “What state transition took shape, and when?” First use the same measurement conventions to record the state before generation, the time of the event, the state afterward, and the criteria used. Competing events during the same period and a bridge to the mechanism are used to explain further how the event formed. The absence of an identified mechanism must not be written up as nonoccurrence of an observed event. A generative event can result from action by a subject or from emergence without a subject. A generative subject must not be invented for emergence without a subject. The event itself must not be personified.

### 7.2.4 Uptake Carrier (CV)

The uptake carrier asks “Who or what actually executes, transmits, maintains, records, provides care, or repairs?” Personnel, positions, procedures, facilities, and technical systems can all be carriers. Evidence comes from task logs, flows of resources and capacity, costs, rights to stop, and changes in function after carrier replacement. An uptake carrier is not a responsible party. Facilities and procedures perform functions. Doing so does not by itself make them morally or legally responsible parties. Whether an organization can bear institutional or legal responsibility must be judged separately according to its standing as a subject and the specific rules. An organization must not be put in the same category as equipment.

### 7.2.5 Responsible Party (RS)

The responsible party asks “Who bears which kind of responsibility for what, and on what basis?” Responsibilities arising from conduct, decisions, authorization, oversight, benefit, and remedy must be stated separately. Specify knowledge, control, scope, period, appeal, and remedy. Evidence for determining the responsible party must be independent of who is most visible, who actually takes up the work, and who bears the consequences. Someone carrying out the work with limited authority must not become the default primary responsible party merely because they are the most visible.

### 7.2.6 Source of Destabilization (IS)

The source of destabilization asks “Where does a disturbance enter, or where does it accumulate?” The record must include where the disturbance first appeared or accumulated, its point of entry, temporal order, differences in exposure, and alternative sources. Finding a source does not establish malice, a mechanism, or full responsibility. A dissenter’s status must not be counted directly as a source.

### 7.2.7 Mechanism of Destabilization (IM)

The mechanism of destabilization asks “Through what causal path does a disturbance change a state, boundary, feedback, rhythm, or orientation?” The evidence must show, at each step, the mediating links, temporal order, evidence for the bridge, conditions under which the claim can fail, and competing mechanisms. People, groups, and dissenters must not be directly labeled as mechanisms. A story about a mechanism must not substitute for causal evidence.

### 7.2.8 Behavior of Destabilization (IB)

The behavior of destabilization asks “What actions, failures to act, or outputs were actually observed?” Original records, logs, or observations from multiple sources must retain the subject or carrier, context, scale, and time window. Observed behavior does not establish its source or mechanism and does not by itself establish malice or full responsibility. For silence and absence, also distinguish nonoccurrence, unobservability, and concealment for protection.

The source, mechanism, and behavior of destabilization are not attachments belonging only to the variable “Structural Load.” They are a classification of destabilization that cuts across several variables. They all apply to six human variables (§7.3): “Boundaries and Interfaces,” “Drive–Uptake Chain,” “Feedback Write-Back,” “Conditional Potential Field,” “Structural Load,” and “Evolutionary Phase.” A case may state source, mechanism, and behavior separately under these variables, but independent evidence must be submitted for each of the three. The source must not be inferred from visible behavior. A person or dissenter must not be labeled a mechanism. Malice and full responsibility must not be inferred directly from the location of a source.

## 7.3 A Unified Description of the Eleven Human Variables

All eleven variables belong to the human adaptation layer; they are not a universal ontology. Every variable is described by the same set of items, and the complete detailed descriptions are in Appendix A. The items, in order, are: name; proposition; scope of application; the proposition role it belongs to; conditions for suspension; what can be inferred; what cannot be inferred; inferential premises; method requirements; domain restriction; objects of application; support routes; nine-axis scale profile; effective object; states; observables; evidence requirements; input dependencies; output effects; uptake carriers; responsible parties; time window and lag; uncertainty; local exclusion zone; affected positions; normative status; items kept unchanged across scales; items that must be added on scale elevation; items that change with scale; objects to which it does not apply; elevations that are prohibited; judgment ceiling; action ceiling; counterexamples; appeal; restoration. For a specific application, fill in the required material according to the selected support route. Mark the remaining items under §2.9 as unknown, not applicable, unobservable, or withheld for protection, and give the reasons. Completing the items does not require unlimited collection of personal information. Nor is it a prerequisite for ordinary understanding, seeking help, or accessing lawful services.

The four kinds of formal dependency must be written separately (§2.3). Inferential premises list only the formal premises indispensable at every conclusion level. Method requirements list only the epistemic, normative, or procedural requirements that every level must pass. Domain restriction states which definitions, classification rules, or normative boundaries restrict the variable. Objects of application state only the objects to which the variable applies.

Conditions needed at only one particular level go in the support routes.
