| Functional transfer | A core function moves to another object. The function can continue while the original identity, relationships, or memory disappear | Outsourcing one task does not amount to functional transfer. Functional continuity does not establish continuity of responsibility or memory |
| Paradigm replacement | A new object with a different identity criterion, interfaces, or rules bypasses the old object without repairing it | An upgrade within the same object or a change of brand name need not constitute paradigm replacement. Outstanding obligations remain |
| Trauma-built development | Boundaries, identity, rules, or ways of taking up work form under harm, deprivation, failure, or threat | A narrative of trauma does not automatically establish future effects. Whether the arrangement provides protection and whether it reproduces the original harm must be tested separately |
| Pseudo-steady state | Surface indicators are stable while actual uptake is being exhausted, weak signals disappear, feedback fails to write back, or debts increase | Keep two ledgers, one for appearances and one for actual conditions. Return to costs, recovery, the right to stop, and feedback from the downstream end |
| Forced rewrite | A subject with greater power rewrites the object when consent that can be reviewed and corrected, exit, and protection of memory are lacking | Distinguish this from authorized, negotiated revision that can be withdrawn and appealed. Check for irreversible erasure of identity |
| External carrier migration | When the path to repair is closed off, personnel, capabilities, resources, relationships, evidence, or memory move to a safer system for taking them up | A move with no capability to take up what is transferred is not safe migration. Romanticizing departure or privatizing harm does not establish safety either |
| Collapse | The original identity criterion ceases to hold, and functions, uptake, relationships, or boundaries break down without a plan | Distinguish collapse from “Orderly Exit and Benign Demise,” functional transfer, protective dormancy, and object reorganization. Releasing resources does not justify harm |

Path names likewise generate no value or responsibility. For example, “regression” does not amount to moral decline, “split” need not be failure, “merge” need not be progress, “takeover” is not automatically unlawful, and “external carrier migration” does not require individuals to flee on their own. Paths only allow competing explanations into the record. Mechanisms, justification, and action still each have their own conditions to meet.

## 8.5 Orderly Exit and Benign Demise (X0)

“Orderly Exit and Benign Demise” is not an eighth state. Its number does not follow on from the seven state prototypes, and it is not counted as an eighth stage. It is an independent path in the life cycle of human collectives. It applies when maintaining the original object no longer serves the stated anchor, its core functions can be completed, terminated, or taken up by a safer party, and personnel, relationships, resources, memory, debts, and appeals can all be dealt with explicitly. The path then records how the object closes out its mission, transfers functions, releases resources, preserves memory, settles outstanding responsibilities, and retains limited weak ties.

This path does not require first reaching the prototype of efficient coordination and flexible expansion or the prototype of adaptive dynamic balance. A temporary initiative in the prototype of coalescence around an anchor can close in an orderly way when it finds that the problem is already being taken up elsewhere. An expansion project in the prototype of initial expansion and differentiated uptake can wind down if continuing to expand would only create harm. An institution stuck in the prototype of development under interconnected constraints may also enter exit if repair is infeasible and external uptake is adequate. Conversely, a collective in the prototype of adaptive dynamic balance cannot claim eligibility to disband on the strength of a “higher-stage” label. Capabilities at a stage, normative justification, and operational conditions are three distinct matters. No state number can become a prerequisite for eligibility for self-initiated exit.

This boundary is fixed. The path can be entered from any stated starting position. There is no minimum state requirement, no requirement to be in any particular prototype first, and still less a requirement of the prototype of efficient coordination and flexible expansion or the prototype of adaptive dynamic balance. Its entry and completion conditions must not treat any of the seven state prototypes as an eligibility requirement. The numbers of the prototypes may only describe the starting position and must not become a threshold for exit.

### 8.5.1 Candidate Entry for Orderly Exit

First, the anchor has been fulfilled, ceased to apply, or been taken up by a safer object, or continuing to maintain the object chiefly serves the organization’s own persistence. This judgment must be independently reviewable. The center must not certify completion for itself after rewriting the goal. Second, personnel, functions, resources, relationships, records, debts, and irreplaceable values have been inventoried, and there are verifiable receiving parties or protective arrangements. Short-term setbacks, tight funding, leadership fatigue, or evasion of responsibility can create similar appearances. A narrative alone therefore cannot justify a finding of “benign completion.”

### 8.5.2 Completion Conditions for Orderly Exit

| Aspect of Completion | What Must Be Preserved | Signs of Failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anchor and object | Independent verification of completion, termination, or invalidity. The time when the identity criterion ends and matters still open | Redefining the goal, deleting failures, or the center unilaterally declaring completion |
| Core functions | Mark each as completed, terminated, transferred, or unresolved. Record the receiving party’s capability, permissions, resources, and arrangements for restoration | A declaration alone, with no continuity for maintainers or users |
| Personnel and relationships | Safety, basic rights and interests, the right to stop, protection against retaliation, and arrangements for continuing care and relationships of dependence | Privatizing organizational obligations by leaving members to bear them on their own |
| Resources | Traceable objects, boundaries, sequence, timing, and destinations to prevent capture by those with greater power | Dividing resources internally first, then leaving the losses to low-power positions |
| Memory and evidence | Preserve successes, failures, repairs, and memory attached to positions. Specify access, privacy, correction, and protection against retaliation | Keeping only a record of victories while deleting or exposing materials from vulnerable positions |
| Debts and responsibility | Continuing responsible parties for contracts, labor, data, maintenance, environmental matters, appeals, and future risks | Responsibility, review, and maintenance all disappear when the object is deregistered |
| Weak ties | Limited to advice, shared experience, and buffering, with clear boundaries and duration | Reviving the original power structure without new authorization |

The outcomes of this path should at least distinguish “candidate,” “in progress,” “partially complete,” “complete,” and “unknown.” As long as the affected groups, outstanding obligations, the capability to receive, appeals, or the safety of memory remain “unknown,” the result must not be recorded as “benign completion.” A transfer of functions without continuity of memory and responsibility may be only “functional transfer.” Unilateral closure and rewriting of identity by an external power may be “takeover” or “forced rewrite.” A breakdown with no uptake is “collapse” and must not be dressed up as “orderly exit.”

Classification under “Orderly Exit and Benign Demise” grants no authority to dissolve the object, abolish posts or units, transfer assets, publish archives, waive debts, or consent on members’ behalf. It can tell us only which objects, obligations, evidence, protections, and unknowns must be entered in the same ledger to judge whether an exit is orderly.

## 8.6 How Regulation, Early Warning, and Uptake Enter State Judgments

A static snapshot alone cannot establish a state classification. The regulation layer requires observing the target, sensing, comparison, execution, feedback, and time lag. The early-warning layer requires checking whether slower recovery, larger fluctuations, more severe consequences of similar disturbances, and local flickering form a cluster. The repayment layer requires tracing who makes commitments, who bears the costs, to whom returns flow, and whose costs or claims are deferred to the future. If the apparent stability of the prototype of efficient coordination and flexible expansion or the prototype of adaptive dynamic balance rests on off-ledger labor, silence, and future debt, the case should be treated as a candidate for a “pseudo-steady state” (§8.4).

Clues generated by the same sequence or shared channel of change do not become independent pieces of evidence merely because they cluster. Dependent clues can still be used jointly. Their value for early warning must be evaluated under compatible dynamics, noise, sampling, and observation time windows, against fixed targets, horizons, real-time baselines, and signals in the opposite direction (Scheffer et al., 2009). See D.31 and §12.6.

Clustering is not a universal prerequisite for early warning. A single domain-specific signal can be sufficient for a limited judgment. The absence of critical slowing down or a second signal does not prove safety or invalidate an existing specialist forecast. A rule that uses several clues jointly requires a joint distribution or corresponding validation. An increase in its positive predictive value does not guarantee a reduction in total loss given false alarms, missed detections, and action costs.

Uptake cannot be assessed merely by asking whether there is a successor. Check whether a pool of potential successors, shadow roles, memory attached to positions, authorization paths, handover windows, translation of legitimacy, and protective conditions are actually in place. A clean departure by generative actors leaves a vacuum of authority if those taking up the work cannot enter. Frequent changes in personnel do not amount to adaptive renewal if key knowledge and permissions remain locked in the original center. Four human-domain clauses (§7.1) come in here. Use “Action Uptake and Classification of Responsibility” to distinguish uptake carriers, cost bearers, beneficiaries, rights to stop, and responsible parties. Use “Institutional Write-Back” to determine whether feedback actually changes the relevant content and whether the change is executed. Use “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity” to examine power and observation channels, and “Historical Trace Carriers” to verify traces. Whether carriers actually continue is tested under §4.5. If a historical increment beyond the current representation is also claimed, add a historical-increment test. For the candidate mechanism by which this kind of dependence strengthens across rounds, see §7.6.1.

## 8.7 Limits and Exclusions of the Current Prototypes

The seven state prototypes are prototypes of human collective states. A proposed classification can be refuted, can lack necessary data, can apply in parallel, and can be withdrawn. Each candidate must be checked item by item for entry, exit, observations, counterexamples, falsification, scale, evidence, missing data, and the boundary that no action is authorized. If these conditions are missing, it can only be kept as an impression or recorded as “unknown.” The numbers do not represent a universal evolutionary path from 0 to 6. States allow regression, parallelism, mixing, jumps, dormancy, splits, mergers, takeover, functional transfer, and collapse.

“Orderly Exit and Benign Demise” (§8.5) is an independent life-cycle path and does not depend on the prototype of efficient coordination and flexible expansion, the prototype of adaptive dynamic balance, or any minimum state. Capabilities at a stage, normative justification, and the operating conditions for exit must be judged separately. A match to any prototype cannot itself authorize dissolution, advancement, elimination, or forced conversion.

A physical metaphor must supply a formal mapping, the dimensions of the quantities involved, falsifiable predictions, and conditions for ending the analogy to enter the formal mechanism library. For example, “quantum tunneling” cannot explain why a human collective jumps to another configuration. In this framework, determining that failed attempts are a historical conditional increment beyond the current representation still requires support from a corresponding historical-increment test (see §4.5). No necessary coordination is presumed between biological death and social renewal, or between love and intergenerational transmission. Intergenerational uptake is recorded only in terms of roles, memory, authorization, and handover.

The seven prototypes make no claim to exhaust the states of human collectives. If cases consistently fall outside them, first preserve the unexplained residuals. Then use independent materials to test whether prototypes need to be added, merged, or split. Cases must not be forced into the numbered categories.

Prototype fit, interobserver agreement, stability across time windows, and practical gains over using variables directly are distinct questions. Clear diagnostic cards can make a classification easier to review but cannot establish that it is reliable or more effective than a specialist description. Without actual comparisons, do not report accuracy, predictive gains, or savings in reading time. If the task calls only for direct description of members, channels, and load, the prototypes may be skipped.

## 8.8 Boundary With Actor States and Multi-Circle Projection

The seven state prototypes describe candidate states of human intentional collectives under a specified definition of the object. They do not describe individual personality, psychological maturity, or moral rank. Part 9 covers actors’ slow, intermediate-timescale, and fast variables. Part 10 covers parallel, nested, overlapping, bridging, competitive, and temporary relations among multiple collectives. Classifying a circle[^tn-circle-09] to which a person belongs under the prototype of initial expansion and differentiated uptake does not imply that the person’s personality is in that prototype. A person displaying stable capability likewise does not imply that their circle is in the prototype of efficient coordination and flexible expansion or the prototype of adaptive dynamic balance.

Multi-circle projection can represent different circles as fitting different prototypes at the same time. It can also represent the same circle as having a mixed state on different scale axes. State changes must be tied to specific events, channels, and time windows. An institutional change in an outer layer does not automatically update inner relations, and individual exit does not automatically cause the collective to dissolve. If prototype classification adds no value beyond using the variables directly, the prototypes should be skipped in favor of a simpler joint state.

[^tn-diagnosis-09]: Translator's note: Diagnosis here denotes a nonclinical assessment of a collective configuration against the stated criteria.

[^tn-circle-09]: Translator's note: Circles may be parallel, nested, overlapping, or bridged.

# Part 9 Actor States and Personality Hypotheses

This Part brings people into multi-circle projection without reducing anyone to a fixed label. An actor in an event brings long-term tendencies that change relatively slowly. They occupy roles and positions in relationships and access to resources that are specific to a period. Immediate emotions, bodily states, information, and opportunities also affect them. The same person may act differently in different circles[^tn-circle-10]. These differences need not be explained by hypocrisy, a split in personality, or a change in essence. They may also arise from changes in role activation, risk structure, visible information, rewards and penalties, ability to exit, and affected positions.

## 9.1 An Actor Is Not a Single Variable

The minimum form of a description of an actor’s state is:

`A* = <所指的行动者，观察窗，圈层成员关系，角色，慢变量，中变量，快变量，物质条件，体验—意义条件，未知项，证据状态，隐私与允许用途>`.[^tn-actor-tuple-10]

The asterisk indicates that this remains a candidate state description. An actor’s name, occupation, social status, or a single action cannot automatically fill in their state. Information that is unobservable, has no source, is withheld because those concerned decline to disclose it, or conflicts with other information must be retained as distinct kinds of unknown. The model must not fill the gaps with “common sense.”

Each of the following aspects answers a question, has content that needs to be set out at a minimum, and has things that cannot be inferred from it.

The actor referred to: this answers the question of whom, or which unit of action, the current analysis addresses. At a minimum it needs to set out a stable reference, the time window, and the limits of identity. No authority to represent the actor’s entire life can be inferred from it.

Circle memberships: these answer the question of which relational and institutional positions the actor occupies now. At a minimum they need to set out which circles are involved, the actor’s entry and exit, and on what basis the actor counts as a member. It cannot be inferred from them that the actor identifies with the circle’s goals.

Role: this answers the question of what the actor is expected, permitted, or compelled to do. At a minimum it needs to set out the source of the role, rights, responsibilities, and conflicts. The actor’s actual capabilities and genuine willingness cannot be inferred from it.

State variables: these answer the question of which observable or candidate states there are at present. For each, at a minimum, the time band, source, status, and counterevidence need to be set out. A stable essence of personality cannot be inferred from them.

Conditions: these answer the question of what makes a particular behavior more feasible or riskier. Material conditions and experience–meaning conditions need to be recorded separately. It cannot be inferred from them that a single cause determines behavior.

Unknowns: these answer the question of which key information is unavailable for now. At a minimum they need to set out the kind of missingness, its impact, and the limits on obtaining the information. It cannot be inferred from them that the model may freely fill in values.

## 9.2 Slow, Intermediate-Timescale, and Fast Variables

The three time bands are neither personality types nor independent compartments. They are distinguished in order to constrain the rate of updates. Some states can change after one event, others take multiple rounds to change, and still others should be updated only after more time has passed, evidence across contexts is available, or the person’s life has been substantially reorganized.

### 9.2.1 Slow Variables

Candidate slow variables include long-term value priorities, habitual ways of interpreting, long-term capabilities and resource positions, identity commitments, and tendencies of trust and attachment. Calling them “slow” means only that they change relatively slowly within the current research window. It implies neither that they are innate or fixed nor that they express a true self or hold across all contexts.

Calling a variable slow must rest on evidence across time sufficient for the persistence claimed. A further claim of stability across contexts also requires materials covering different contexts. The validity of a measurement scale cited for a single measurement does not establish that the person has been observed in every setting. If a tendency appears in only one high-pressure circle and does not appear in others, the competing explanation that it is “activated by that circle” must be retained. If resource positions, trauma, major changes in relationships, long-term learning, or moves between institutional settings change patterns of action, slow variables should also be updated, split into conditional variables, or retired.

Learned tendencies can develop through repeated practices in families, schools, workplaces, and peer groups. Who has time to practice, who receives correction or encouragement, and which kinds of speech, posture, qualifications, and judgment are rewarded can affect which actions later feel natural, possible, or worth trying. This process of historical formation differs both from a single strategic choice and from an essence of personality. Connect opportunities for training, repeated practice, institutional responses, and differences across contexts. One action cannot be used to infer family background or an entire life history.

The same actor may carry different tendencies from several experiences of socialization. An old tendency may fit poorly in a new environment. A resource recognized in one domain may bring no return in another, and repeated new practices may change earlier tendencies. Slow variables should be open to splitting by context, revision, or retirement. An average association at the group level does not fill in an individual’s state. Deviation from what is typical in the group does not automatically make the individual abnormal.

### 9.2.2 Intermediate-Timescale Variables

Intermediate-timescale variables include role identity, goals for the current period, expectations in relationships, positions in alliances, accumulated fatigue, recent reputation, and trust specific to the period. They generally span several rounds of interaction but may change with the end of a project, organizational restructuring, repair of a relationship, a public event, or a change in resources.

Intermediate-timescale variables are the main junction in the mutual constitution of individuals and circles. Circles shape them through roles, metrics, reputation, rewards and penalties, and a sense of belonging. Actors in turn change circles through the fulfillment of responsibilities, resistance, exit, alliance formation, interpretation, and institutional write-back (§7.1). Observing only one side can lead to treating structural pressure as a personality defect or reducing individual choice entirely to determination by the environment.

### 9.2.3 Fast Variables

Fast variables include immediate emotions, arousal, attention, fear, impulses, current beliefs, short-term bodily states, perceptions of opportunity, and current strategies. They must be tied to a specific time and event. A single state of a fast variable must not be used to infer long-term personality.

Although short-lived, fast variables may feed into intermediate-timescale and slow variables through thresholds, public traces, irreversible actions, or feedback from others. For example, a brief fear does not by itself amount to lasting distrust. But if the fear leads to a public exit, punishment by the organization, rupture in relationships, and repeated avoidance, it can form a more durable path through multi-circle feedback. A projection must spell out that channel. The result must not be read backward to conclude that “they were distrustful to begin with.”

| Time Band | Typical Rate of Change | Evidence Required | Permitted Updates After an Event | Common Misuses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slow variables | Slow relative to the current window, possibly spanning months, years, or major periods | Assess persistence using materials across time. A claim of stability across contexts also requires coverage of the corresponding contexts. Record dependence among sources and counterexamples separately | New evidence may change the level of support or the variable’s value. Check separately whether the change persists | Treating a label as innate or prescribing the same update rate for everyone |
| Intermediate-timescale variables | Several rounds of interaction to one period | Repeated observations within the same period, and role and circle conditions | May be updated as relationships, projects, organizations, or resources change | Treating a response to a role as personality |
| Fast variables | Minutes, hours, or several days | Tie to the time, event, bodily state, and information state | May be updated after each event | Using one emotion to predict the entire future |

## 9.3 Personality Only as a Conditional Hypothesis About Slow Variables

This framework uses the term “personality” in a limited sense. It treats personality as a set of hypotheses about slow variables that seek to compress variation in behavior across time and contexts. At minimum, a personality hypothesis must state what behavior was observed, in which contexts it was or was not observed, how long it lasted, what sources and counterexamples exist, what simpler explanations are available, and what the hypothesis may be used for.

What enters the analysis falls into two layers. One layer is specific, verifiable behavior, recorded as an “observation record”; it is not a conclusion about personality, nor is it a status of a personality hypothesis. The other layer is the personality hypothesis, whose status can only be supported hypothesis, candidate, disputed, unknown, or retired. A “supported hypothesis” is still qualified by its time window, context, and error. A “candidate” is only awaiting testing. “Disputed” means the evidence or explanations conflict. “Unknown” means no judgment can currently be made. “Retired” means the hypothesis no longer offers a gain or has proved unacceptably misleading.

A personality hypothesis must set out each of the following.

Hypothesis description: describe the tendency in terms that can be distinguished and refuted, without insulting or pathologizing labels.

Behavioral indicators: specific behaviors, choices, or expressions, without substituting the analyst’s impressions.

Observed contexts: circles, roles, pressures, resources, information, and time windows.

Contexts without observations of the tendency: settings that have not been covered, or where contrary behavior has appeared.

Competing explanations: role demands, short-term emotions, material constraints, strategies, cultural norms, measurement bias, and others.

Counterevidence: facts, testimony, and results inconsistent with the hypothesis.

Current status: candidate, supported hypothesis, disputed, unknown, or retired.

Permitted uses: research, communication, scenario projection, or other limited uses.

Prohibited uses: clinical diagnosis, judgments about the essence of personality, discriminatory screening, automatic authorization, or automatic punishment.

This framework does not perform clinical diagnosis, psychiatric diagnosis, or unauthorized psychological assessment. Even if a professional diagnosis exists outside the framework, it can enter only as material with a source, authorization, and limits of applicability. The framework must not generate or expand diagnoses itself or use them to take action incompatible with their original purpose.

## 9.4 Role Activation and Circle Conditions

At least six conditions can change when an actor enters different circles. These are visible information, available resources, rewards and penalties, responsibility, identity activation, and the ability to exit. In explaining differences in behavior, these conditions, independently measured individual differences, and the interaction between the two should be considered together as competing explanations. Looking first at contexts that are easier to change does not mean assigning in advance, in the model, all of the part explained jointly by context and individual differences to context.

For example, a person may be silent in their family circle, assertive at work, and open among friends. At least the following competing explanations are possible. Past conflicts in the family may raise the cost of speaking. The role at work may grant formal authority. Friendships may entail lower penalties and greater trust. The three settings may activate different identities. Observers may have access to different information in each circle. The behavior samples may cover different time windows. Comparisons should hold the target, data split, available information, complexity, and measurement budget fixed and test models of individual differences, context, and their interaction separately. If a personality indicator improves prediction of behavior in a new window, it can support a limited prediction. This still does not establish that the indicator is the main causal mechanism, an innate essence, or a priority for intervention. If the same person is always paired with just one setting, repeated observations cannot by themselves separate the contributions of the two.

A claim that a role has been activated should answer these questions: which event activated which role; whether the role comes from formal rules, informal expectations, a commitment by the actor, or a threat; whether the actor identifies with it; whether it conflicts with other roles; what it permits, what it prohibits, and what costs it requires the actor to bear; and what conditions are needed to exit the role.

A claim of stability across contexts must also specify whether it concerns rank order, mean level, the distribution of state fluctuations, or a profile of “how the person responds under specified conditions.” Changes in the proportions of different contexts a person encounters can change their overall mean behavior even if their conditional responses are unchanged. Long-term resources and capabilities are also slow variables. A person-specific random intercept in a statistical model represents only individual differences that have yet to be decomposed. It cannot be directly labeled personality.

## 9.5 How Individuals and Circles Affect One Another

Effects in both directions must be separated into two testable chains.

The circle-to-individual chain can be described as follows. A circle’s rule or an event changes information, resources, risk, roles, or conditions of meaning. Through the actor’s perceptions and capabilities, this changes fast variables. The change then reaches intermediate-timescale or slow variables through repeated feedback, public traces, or the reconfiguration of relationships.

The individual-to-circle chain can be described as follows. The actor’s expression, labor, refusal, exit, bridging, alliance formation, or innovation changes the circle’s resource flows, role allocation, shared interpretations, membership boundaries, institutional records, or external interfaces. This in turn changes the states of other members and of the circle.

| Direction | Starting Point | Channel That Must Be Found | Observable Outcome | Main Counterexample |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Circle→Individual | Change in rules, events, resources, or meaning | Information, rewards and penalties, physical load, roles, reputation, and belonging | Changes in states, behavior, or probabilities of choices | No change under the same exposure, or an external event explains the change |
| Individual→Circle | Expression, action, refusal, exit, or bridging | Resource flows, imitation by members, institutional write-back, network propagation, and a mechanism of representation | Changes in rules, boundaries, allocation, relationships, or collective states | The action is not received, or the change in the circle precedes the individual action |
| Circle↔Individual Feedback | The two chains above form a continuing closed loop | Return channel, delay, thresholds, and traces | Changes in transition probabilities in subsequent rounds | Only a signal arrives, without changing any subsequent state |

Saying “affect one another” does not complete an explanation. It requires the analyst to go on looking for direction, channels, delays, thresholds, losses, and counterfactuals.

## 9.6 Evidence Levels and Upgrading Variable Status

Actor variables are upgraded in a conservative order. A model can propose candidates from residuals. It must not promote a candidate directly to a fact. A single account by the person themselves, a single account from another person, a single behavioral observation, and a single measurement scale result each carry different biases. Agreement across sources does not automatically rule out a common environment, a shared narrative, or the same measurement bias.

| Current Status | Permitted Use | Requirements for Upgrading | What Must Be Retained |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unknown | Raise questions and flag impacts | Lawful and appropriate new observations | The kind of unknown and the reason for leaving the information uncollected |
| Candidate | Use in scenario projection and design a minimal test | Indicators, time window, and counterexample criterion stated in advance | Competing candidates, privacy, and risks |
| Supported hypothesis | Use for explanation or foresight in limited contexts | Out-of-sample review, tests across contexts, or independent sources | Limits of applicability, counterevidence, and error |
| Observation record | Describe behavior or a state at a specific time | Complete sources and a stated account of the conditions of observation | Do not promote behavior to personality |
| Disputed | Present conflicting materials side by side and lower the strength of the output | Independent review or new discriminating evidence | The positions and interests of all parties |
| Retired | Preserve the history and exclude it from the current projection | Later revisions may append only the reasons for retirement | Impacts caused by the earlier judgment and remedies |

If a variable is proposed only after results are known, it can help explain those results and generate a test for the next round. It cannot retroactively support the original prediction. If the definition, time band, or indicators of the same variable change, a new version should be created. Earlier failures must not be overwritten with it.

## 9.7 Material and Experience–Meaning Conditions in Actor States

An actor’s material conditions include physical load, observable aspects of health and sleep, time, space, money, tools, transportation, care responsibilities, standing under the law, and the actual ability to exit. Experience–meaning conditions include feelings, expectations, memory, identity, trust, shame, hope, fear, commitments, perceived legitimacy, and conflicts of value.

Record the two groups separately according to their relevance to the current question. If the task only needs an adequate technical or quantitative indicator, collection of irrelevant private experiences must not be compelled. If the conclusion concerns life opportunities, meaning, or autonomy, material totals cannot substitute for the corresponding experiences. Material deprivation can increase pressure without automatically determining how the actor interprets meaning. Positive beliefs can increase persistence but cannot remove constraints imposed by resources, the body, or institutions. An inference across channels must specify which material change affects behavior through which experiential mechanism, or which change in meaning alters material conditions through which action.

Status also has an institutional dimension that cannot be reduced to personal experience. Self-identification, classification by others, administrative registration, legal eligibility, and actual treatment must be recorded separately. A designation can alter access to hiring, services, the submission of evidence, or appeals, even if the person does not accept it. Institutional standing and the experience of dignity can affect one another without either establishing the other. The categories and comparison groups used by researchers must be open to challenge by those concerned. Their successive revisions must also be open to review.

A person can still act under constraints. A person signing under a credible threat and a device moving their body to produce the same handwriting involve different processes. The first can still be the person’s own action, even though there is no safe way to refuse and valid consent is absent. Attribution of the action, knowledge, control, feasible alternatives, blame, and remedy each require their own grounds. A causal explanation does not automatically exempt anyone from responsibility or establish that blame is warranted.

## 9.8 Privacy, Absence, and Refusal to Disclose

The closer the analysis gets to an individual, the higher the cost of misuse. Actor records must distinguish information that is public, limited to a particular context, sensitive, or highly sensitive, as well as information a person declines to disclose. Permitted uses must be consistent with the purpose of collection, authorization, and protections for those affected. Using material for communication does not by itself qualify it for use in hiring, insurance, law enforcement, medical care, punishment, or public evaluation.

Refusal to disclose is not evidence of hostility, deception, ignorance, or risk. Silence can stem from safety concerns, trauma, privacy, language, trust, differences in power, or reasonable noncooperation. The analyst can only record under §2.9 that no material was obtained (unobservable) and how this limits projection. Personality inferences must not be used to fill the gap.

## 9.9 Actor State Snapshots

A snapshot that can be checked needs to set out at least the following aspects. The last sentence of each gives the ceiling it sets on the output.

Observation boundaries: the actor, time window, observation position, and data cutoff. The output is limited to the current sample.

Circles and roles: memberships, roles, conflicts, and the ability to enter and exit. Identification with the circle and common goals are not presumed.

Slow, intermediate-timescale, and fast variables: the status, source, time, and counterevidence of each. No judgment is made about the essence of personality.

Conditions in both channels: material conditions and experience–meaning conditions. Neither substitutes for the other.

Competing explanations: structural factors, roles, strategies, measurement, and chance. Explanations that cannot be distinguished all need to be retained.

Privacy and uses: privacy level, authorization, and prohibited uses. The limits on use are not crossed.

Update conditions: which variables a new event reaches and when to review them. Not every state is refreshed at once.

The snapshot needs to retain its observation cutoff and the time at which information was obtained. When a new event occurs, first determine which channels and time bands it reaches and then update the corresponding variables. Calculate autonomous changes caused by the passage of time itself separately under the stated rules for dynamics. When neither a new observation nor a reliable rule for advancing the state is available, the last observed value and its time can be retained, or the state can be changed to “unknown,” but the old observed value must not be treated as the actual current state. Having the model compute again is likewise no evidence that all variables changed at once.

## 9.10 Example of Actor Analysis in an Event

Suppose a project lead suddenly vetoes the team’s proposal in a public meeting. The observation record can establish only the veto, the context of the meeting, what was said, and the visible consequences. Candidate fast variables might include time pressure, physical fatigue, perceived threat, and immediate anger. Candidate intermediate-timescale variables might include project goals, responsibilities of the role, a recent decline in trust, and reputational risk. A candidate slow variable might be long-term tolerance of uncertainty, which would require evidence across contexts.

The circles must also be examined. Has management just changed the metrics? Is the team short on resources? Has public opinion on a platform raised the cost of failing publicly? Do care responsibilities at home reduce the time available? Does organizational culture reward forceful decisions? The lead’s veto may change trust and subsequent expression in the team. The team’s silence may reinforce the lead’s belief that “only coercion works,” creating feedback. Writing only “controlling personality” would obscure multiple channels open to intervention. Writing only “determined by structure” would erase the actor’s choices, responsibilities, and capability to bridge circles.

A reasonable output should be layered. It should separate confirmed facts about behavior from the support each hypothesis about states has received. It should also specify circle conditions and channels in both directions, the next observation that would best distinguish the alternatives, and what remains unknown when evidence is insufficient. Such an output can enter path projection in Part 11. It cannot itself produce a diagnosis of the person, punishment, or authority to compel.

## 9.11 Where This Part Stops

The actor state layer can describe which observable states and candidate variables are currently available. It can identify changes that roles and circles may activate and the channels through which individuals and circles constitute one another. It can also describe which time bands a new event may reach first and which information remains unknown or protected by privacy.

This framework does not adjudicate the essence of a person. No professional assessment amounts to an ontological definition of a person. The clinical significance and scope of application of personality descriptions should be assessed by qualified professionals on the basis of relevant evidence, valid authorization, and participation by the people concerned. This framework cannot supply that assessment on its own. Future paths enter conditional foresight. Value and action enter the layer of normative choice and authorization. Prediction, professional status, and labels do not automatically confer authority to act.

[^tn-actor-tuple-10]: Translator's note: The full tuple in English is `A* = <the actor referred to, observation window, circle memberships, roles, slow variables, intermediate-timescale variables, fast variables, material conditions, experience–meaning conditions, unknowns, evidential status, privacy and permitted uses>`.

[^tn-circle-10]: Translator's note: Circles may be parallel, nested, overlapping, or bridged.

<a id="part_10"></a>

# Part 10 Multi-Circle Objects and Joint States

Analyzing a single object or circle[^tn-circle-11] often compresses other conditions into a black box called “environment.” Multi-circle analysis brings into one joint state the structural units that can change the path of an event and that can be distinguished by boundaries, relations, channels, and time windows. The aim does not require adding background without limit. Families, teams, institutions, platforms, markets, cultural communities, bodily systems, and geographic spaces can all matter in the same event. Naming them does not automatically supply grounds for object facts about them or support for a grouping gain (§4.3).

## 10.1 Treating a Circle as a Candidate Object

As a candidate object, a circle can be represented as follows.

`C* = <所指的圈层，候选边界，成员资格，角色规则，进入与退出，内部状态，外部接口，物质通道，体验—意义通道，约束，时间窗，尺度剖面，同一性判据，证据状态，反例>`.[^tn-circle-tuple-11]

“Several similar people” does not suffice to define a circle. A circle need not have shared consciousness or a unified goal. Members may not know that the analyst has grouped them into the same circle. They may disagree about goals, and a candidate structure may form solely through shared exposure to the same platform, rule, space, or risk. Documents, memberships, sustained interactions, or shared exposure can support the corresponding facts about the object. A further claim that adopting this grouping improves explanation or foresight requires testing for a gain within the stated scope against a complexity-matched alternative grouping or no-grouping baseline. Support from a grouping-gain test concerns eligibility for this latter, task-specific claim. It does not decide whether the organization, relationships, or people affected exist.

| Admission Question | Evidence Required | If the Check Does Not Pass |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Can the boundary be distinguished? | Membership rules, interfaces, shared exposure, or sustained interaction | Retain it as the analyst’s grouping and do not call it an objective circle |
| Is there differentiated structure within it? | Roles, relations, channels, or constraints | Reclassify it as a population category or an environmental variable |
| If a grouping gain is claimed, does the grouping improve explanation or foresight? | Out-of-sample comparison with a simple baseline | Do not claim that a gain has been established. Retain facts about the object that have independent grounds. Depending on the task, fall back to a single focus, continuous variables, or a candidate grouping |
| Does identity hold within the time window? | The identity criterion, entry and exit, and conditions for conversion and dissolution | Record separate segments, or record an object conversion |
| Have counterexamples been retained? | Boundary perturbation or review across time or locations | Report the sensitivity and narrow the related conclusions; a grouping gain already claimed is handled under §4.3 |

## 10.2 Defining the Joint Object

The multi-circle joint object is written as follows.

`MC* = <行动者集合 A，圈层集合 C，圈层关系 Rcc，成员与角色映射 Rac，物质状态 M，体验—意义状态 Ψ，通道与约束 Q，事件流 E，多时钟 T，尺度剖面 SP，证据状态 W，同一性判据 K>`.[^tn-joint-tuple-11]

The value of a joint object lies in preserving local differences and cross-boundary channels. It does not put all related objects into one large circle or assert that a higher-level subject exists. Circles with no identifiable relation may only be observed side by side. If they share only an environment, a direct effect should not be invented. If the relation appears only during an event, it should be recorded as temporary, and the conditions under which it ends should be stated.

Each component of the joint state has something to safeguard and a typical error of its own.

Actor set A: Preserve the states, roles, and privacy boundaries of each actor. The typical error is substituting a circle average for the individual.

Circle set C: Maintain the boundaries, states, and identity of each circle separately. The typical error is merging all background conditions into one overarching circle.

Circle relations Rcc: Record direction, type, delay, threshold, and evidence. The typical error is substituting “interrelated” for a mechanism.

Membership and role mapping Rac: Allow multiple affiliations, role conflicts, and differences in ability to exit. The typical error is assuming that each person belongs to only one circle.

Material state M and experience–meaning state Ψ: Material conditions and experience–meaning conditions are represented side by side. The typical error is material determinism, or reduction to narrative alone.

Channels and constraints Q: Specify the extent and capacity of propagation. The typical error is assuming that impacts are lossless, instantaneous, and reach every position.

Event stream E and multiple clocks T: Record the event stream and the several clocks that are not synchronized. The typical error is updating every state synchronously after each event.

Evidential status W and identity criterion K: Record evidence, unknowns, residuals, and object identity. The typical error is mistaking a complete model for a complete account of reality.

## 10.3 Six Kinds of Circle Relation

The six kinds of relation are six starting points for description, used to distinguish different questions. They are nonexclusive, address different dimensions, and do not exhaust real-world relations. Parallelism, nesting, and overlap describe positions along a specified dimension. Bridging and competition describe connections or constraints. Temporariness describes duration and conditions for ending. These descriptions can be combined. For each actual circle relation, state separately the source circle, target circle, direction, shared members or interfaces, channel, extent, time window, and relevant evidence. Do not force a value for a delay or threshold that does not apply.

### 10.3.1 Parallelism

Parallelism means that, under the current definition, the circles have no relation of containment in either membership or operating arrangements. Parallel circles may still be related. Two parallel teams may share a budget, a platform, and higher-level institutional arrangements. They may also be triggered simultaneously by the same event. If only shared exposure can be confirmed, record a shared environment. Record cross-circle propagation only when a channel for information, resources, personnel, or institutional write-back (§7.1) has been found.

### 10.3.2 Nesting

Nesting means that one object’s extent is actually contained within another along an explicitly specified relational dimension. The basis of containment must be stated. Membership, roles, resource accounting, institutional jurisdiction, and space are distinct dimensions. If the claim concerns containment of only a part, first identify the contained subobject and its boundary. If two sets intersect but neither contains the other, record overlap on that dimension. Describing the intersection as “partial containment” does not also justify classifying it as nesting. A subcircle’s state cannot directly represent the higher-level circle, and the outer circle’s rules need not take effect in the same way at every position inside it.

### 10.3.3 Overlap

Overlap means that circles share some members, roles, resources, or interfaces without fully containing one another. Positions of overlap may take on bridging, translation, and coordination. They may also face role conflict, conflicting loyalties, duplicated work, and risks of information leakage. The proportion of overlap cannot substitute for a record of what is actually shared.

### 10.3.4 Bridging

Bridging means that an actor, institution, interface, text, platform, or event connects previously separate circles. A bridging party need not have authority to represent others or be loyal to either side. For any bridge, transmission capability, translation losses, selective filtering, responsibility, substitutability, overload, and exit conditions must be stated separately.

### 10.3.5 Competition

Competition means that circles create identifiable exclusionary constraints on scarce resources, attention, legitimacy, member commitments, interpretive authority, or room for action. Different goals do not automatically amount to competition. Record competition only when one circle’s use of what is available, its rules, or its actions changes the set available to another circle. Cooperation and competition can coexist through different channels.

### 10.3.6 Temporariness

Temporary circles form around events, tasks, crises, shared exposure, or short-term goals. They may dissolve rapidly or become more durable through traces, stabilization of roles, and institutionalization. Calling a circle “temporary” may follow from a task deadline set in advance or be a provisional judgment based on the short time window observed so far. The two cases should be distinguished. A temporary relation can be important, carry responsibilities, and already be real. A temporary alliance can still overlap in membership, compete for resources, and be bridged through particular interfaces.

| Relation | Minimum Criterion | What to Check in Particular | Failure or Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Parallelism | No containment relation at present | Shared environment and indirect coupling | Containment, overlap, or bridging emerges |
| Nesting | Explicit containment in membership, operating arrangements, jurisdiction, or space | Downward constraints and loss from upward aggregation | The identity criterion changes, exit occurs, or jurisdiction is reconfigured |
| Overlap | Some members, roles, resources, or interfaces are shared | Role conflict and double counting | Shared items disappear or the relation becomes containment |
| Bridging | Identifiable interface for cross-circle transmission | Translation, filtering, overload, and authority to represent | The channel closes, is replaced, or becomes institutionalized |
| Competition | An exclusionary constraint on the available set | Scarce items, time window, and channels for cooperation | Resources expand, rules are coordinated, or a party exits |
| Temporariness | A clearly finite duration, or support so far limited to a short time window. Distinguish the two | Ending, traces, and who takes up responsibility. Temporariness can be combined with other dimensions of relation | The temporary relation ends, is extended, or becomes institutionalized. Its positions and channel relations are recorded separately |

“Change” in the table records a shift in a relation’s type or defining conditions between the states before and after an event. Referring back to the relation by the same name does not by itself establish that it has changed. Relations can persist, strengthen, weaken, change direction, change type, or dissolve. Every such judgment must be tied to snapshots before and after, the dimension that changed, and object identity.

## 10.4 Relations Do Not Form a Single Tree

Actual multi-circle structures typically form a directed multigraph of relations with local containment. The same family can be nested within a community and within a legal system. A person can belong at the same time to overlapping family, work, platform, and interest circles. Platforms may bridge parallel groups. Different organizations can compete for funding, cooperate on safety, and overlap in personnel.

The framework therefore does not require each node to have only one parent node. Nor does “higher level” automatically mean greater importance, reality, or authority. Each edge expresses just one stated relation. If a pair of circles has multiple edges, the channel and time window for each edge should be recorded separately. If edges at different scales are incomparable, keep them side by side without forcing an order.

The graph representation must pass at least four checks. Has the analyst’s classification been mistaken for an object? Has a shared environment been mistaken for a direct relation? Has membership overlap been mistaken for organizational containment? Has contact with information been mistaken for effective feedback? Record feedback (§3.3) only when a signal returns and changes a subsequent state, transition probability, or constraint.

## 10.5 Multiple Memberships and Role Conflicts

Membership cannot be reduced to a binary, permanent status. Records should include the basis for membership, start and end times, roles, strength of commitment, actual participation, ability to exit, and disputes. Formal members may lack the capability to act. Informal participants may bear key costs. People drawn in involuntarily may be unable to leave. Representatives may lack authorization from the people they represent.

| Membership Dimension | Example States | Implication for Projection |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basis for entry | Voluntary, employment, kinship, law, platform rules, shared exposure, or coercion | Determines the limits of responsibility and exit |
| Extent of participation | Core, intermittent, peripheral, nominal, or passively bearing the consequences | Determines visible information and channels of impact |
| Role | Decision-making, execution, care, bridging, oversight, affected party, or dissent | Determines rights, obligations, and conflicts |
| Commitment | High, medium, low, disputed, or unknown | Affects paths without amounting to personality |
| Ability to exit | Free, costly, subject to approval, or impossible in practice | Triggers the protection floor (§14.8) and the action ceiling |

An actor’s multiple memberships do not automatically establish actual bridging. Potential bridging capability, actual transmission across boundaries, and outcomes caused by transmission are recorded separately. An identifiable interface supports a description of capability. Records of actual transmission support a description of the process. A causal effect on state requires a corresponding comparison. If recipients do not change their choices, this does not negate the limited transmission of information that already occurred. Authority to represent, transmission capability, and responsible parties must be kept distinct.

## 10.6 Material Conditions and Experience–Meaning Conditions

The joint state maintains both the material state (M) and the experience–meaning state (Ψ). The material state includes the body, time, space, money, energy, equipment, infrastructure, property rights, supply, care, and actual capability to act. The experience–meaning state includes feelings, expectations, memory, identity, trust, shame, hope, fear, commitments, conflicts of value, and perceived legitimacy.

The two channels can affect one another. For example, a platform’s rules for traffic change visibility and income, affecting material and informational conditions. Members interpret the decline as exclusion or failure, a change in experience and meaning. This interpretation may affect exit, protest, or cooperation and thereby feed back into platform metrics and resource allocation. Each step must specify a carrier, direction, delay, and counterexamples.

| Bridge Between Channels | Starting Point | Mediating Factors | Outcome | Counterfactual Question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Material→experience–meaning | A change in income, space, the body, or time | Sense of safety, sense of control, or interpretation of identity | Changes in trust, fear, or commitment | Do interpretations differ under the same material change? |
| Experience–meaning→material | Legitimacy, hope, shame, or conflicts of value | Cooperation, refusal, migration, care, or protest | Changes in resource flows, labor, property rights, or use of facilities | Would the action occur without the change in meaning? |
| Closed loop between the two | Effects in both directions occur in succession | Feedback and traces | Path dependence or phase transition | Does the return signal actually change a subsequent state? |

Analyzing material and experience–meaning conditions side by side requires neither equal weights nor full collection on both sides for every narrow task. If the objective concerns members’ control, well-being, or relationships, relevant differences on both sides should be retained. For a question such as the total amount of equipment, for which an adequate summary is already available, the analysis may stop within that scope.

### 10.6.1 Resource Conversion and Multiple Positions

Resources create usable opportunities only under specific conditions for conversion. Income pays current expenses. Wealth provides a buffer or collateral. Qualifications and skills need recognition from the relevant institutions. Relationships must be possible to mobilize, and the other party must actually have resources and be willing to help. Transportation, time, care, standing under the law, information, and the cost of refusal may cause equal amounts of resources to yield different practical options. These quantities cannot be added into a single capital or power score without specifying units, conversion rules, double counting, weights, and purpose. A well-grounded monetary valuation or an index for a specific task can answer the question within its limits. A total cannot fill in each person’s control, qualifications, or well-being. A nominal allocation cannot substitute for resources actually at the recipient’s disposal.

The combined effects of multiple positions need not take the form of simple overlap among several circles. Rules of admission, accumulation of seniority, evaluation, and redress within the same institutional arrangement may change a group’s opportunities in succession. For example, later entry into a position where seniority accrues can continue to produce differences when opportunities are subsequently allocated uniformly by seniority. The sequence of rules, the denominators for entry at each stage, comparison groups, and positions that are absent should be traced. The number of categories, an interaction term, or a group average does not by itself establish the cause of harm to an individual.

Different statuses must not be put in a fixed order of disadvantage in advance. The same cue may receive different responses in different jobs, locations, relationships, or periods. Retain differences within categories, those who did not enter, and those who succeeded. Adding sensitive classifications is warranted only if it can answer a clear question, the material is sufficient to support it, and the privacy cost is tolerable. Do not compel disclosure to fill a cross-tabulation or treat the positions as nonexistent because the material cannot be obtained.

### 10.6.2 Assets, Liabilities, Contracts, and Transmission Through Credit

In financial relations, the material state must at least distinguish stocks at a point in time from flows over a period, asset valuations from funds that can be converted into cash, principal payable from interest, and net worth from the ability to refinance. Assets in excess of liabilities do not guarantee that cash will be available when payments are due. A new loan does not by itself repair a shortfall in asset value. The market price of collateral, the contractual borrowing limit, the actual outstanding loan balance, and recovery on default are distinct quantities. Each must be tied to the currency, maturity, contract, repayment priority, and observation window.

One testable path of amplification starts with changes in assets or cash flow that alter net worth and the amount that can be pledged as collateral. Through loan quotes, credit limits, loan extensions, or margin calls, these changes affect net financing. Changes in financing then affect consumption, investment, hiring, and subsequent income and feed back into demand for assets. A candidate for self-reinforcement may be proposed only when the relevant constraints are binding and cash, equity, alternative loans, or arrangements for bearing risk have not cut the chain. Earnings expectations, interest rates, or policy may also drive prices and spending jointly. Changes in the same direction are insufficient to identify a financial accelerator mechanism.

In a financial network, common exposure, defaults on direct claims, calls on contractual guarantees, price spillovers from fire sales, and withdrawals of funds prompted by information must be recorded separately. Risk transfer changes who holds the risk and what they can bear. Whether it reduces overall risk still depends on the receiving party’s capital, contingent obligations, and who ultimately bears losses. The face values of mutual claims and liabilities across multiple layers must not be added up as net wealth for the system. Resumption of payments, restoration of capital, recovery of borrowers’ cash flow, and recovery of living conditions are different outcomes.

## 10.7 Five Kinds of Clock and Asynchronous Updating

A joint state needs to distinguish at least five kinds of clock: immediate, interactive, organizational, institutional, and long-term. Immediate reactions may be measured in minutes, trust in interaction in rounds, organizational budgets in quarters, institutional write-back in deliberation cycles, and long-term learning or generational change in years. The timing of the same event’s effects varies by variable.

| Clock | Typical Objects | Update Trigger | Common Error |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Immediate | Emotion, attention, bodily arousal, local prices | Arrival of a signal or a direct shock | Recording short-term fluctuations as long-term change |
| Interactive | Trust, strategies, expectations in relationships, local norms | Several rounds of action and feedback | Ignoring the order of rounds and memory |
| Organizational | Roles, budgets, processes, metrics | Cycles of decision, execution, and review | Assuming a decision amounts to implementation |
| Institutional | Rules, rights, responsibilities, appeals, records | Actual change in rules or procedures, actual write-back, and execution. Record authorization and legal validity separately | Treating a verbal commitment as institutional change |
| Long-term | Capabilities, identity, infrastructure, culture, and relations across generations | Accumulation, learning, maintenance, and replacement | Extrapolating to the long term from short-term data |

External events directly update only variables reached through their channels and for which the conditions hold. Endogenous processes, expiration, accumulation, and recovery proceed on their own clocks and under the stated rules for dynamics. A variable untouched by the current event is not necessarily unchanged in reality. Without reliable grounds for an update, retain the last observed value, its time, and uncertainty, or mark it “unknown.” Do not refresh all variables at once just to make the joint snapshot “complete.”

Asynchrony can also change the direction of effects. Asset prices can change immediately, while loan contracts adjust only upon revaluation or renewal. The timing of payments differs between fixed-rate and floating-rate debt. Public guarantees may provide cash first and distribute losses later. A joint projection should check when each constraint actually binds, when alternative financing is possible, and whether the recovery window precedes irreversible harm. Extending a short-term backstop must not be treated as restoration of the long-term ability to repay.

## 10.8 Joint State Snapshots

A snapshot is a fixed starting point for projection. It does not permanently reproduce reality. It must state the point in time at which the snapshot is taken, when the evidence cutoff falls, the actors and circles referred to, relation and membership mappings, the material state and the experience–meaning state, channels, constraints, the five kinds of clock, the scale profile, unknowns, residuals, and the identity criterion.

Each value in a snapshot should be marked with its status: observed, supported hypothesis, candidate, disputed, or one of the four missing-data states of §2.9. An observed value that cannot be settled because qualifying sources conflict with one another about the same object is recorded as “unknown,” with conflicting sources noted; “disputed” is used for inferred values and means that the evidence or explanations supporting the value conflict (§9.3). When sources conflict, first retain the respective values, how each was produced, and which version each came from. A combined estimate and its uncertainty may be listed separately only if there are grounds for both the measured object and the model used to combine results. An arithmetic mean cannot resolve the original conflict by itself. If a circle is internally differentiated, do not represent all positions with a single mean. If necessary, establish subcircles or use a distributional representation, but this requires going through object admission (§10.1) again.

## 10.9 Boundary Perturbation and Object Conversion

Multi-circle models can easily mistake chosen boundaries for natural boundaries. At least three kinds of perturbation must be tested. Change the membership threshold and check whether the conclusion is stable. Move the time window and check whether the relation still holds. Replace or remove a circle and check whether the joint model’s gain disappears. If small changes in the boundary reverse the conclusion, narrow the conclusions that depend on that boundary and report the sensitivity; a grouping gain already claimed is recorded under §4.3 as “not supported or unresolved.”

If a circle’s identity criterion no longer holds after an event, object conversion or dissolution should be recorded. For example, a temporary rescue group may become a formal institution, a project team may split into competing alliances, a platform community may migrate to a new platform, or a household’s care arrangements may be reorganized after a member exits. A new object cannot overwrite the old object’s failures, responsibilities, or historical traces.

## 10.10 The Complexity Check for Joint States

Adding circles increases the ability to fit the data and also increases error, data requirements, and degrees of freedom in explanation. Each added circle or relation must be assessed on which residual in the original model it explains, whether it has an independently observable channel, and whether it improves out-of-sample explanation or foresight. Its measurement costs and privacy risks must also be specified, and the conclusion checked with that circle or relation removed.

Multi-circle models must be compared with a simple single-focus or single-circle baseline. If a gain in prediction or explanation is claimed but the complex model only tells a fuller story about the materials already observed, without stable comparative support, downgrade the claim of gain and prefer an adequate simpler model. Keeping an object to describe established responsibilities, differences among members, or lawful permissions need not first establish a predictive gain. The independent question it answers should still be stated, recording costs should be controlled, and more data should not be treated as better explanation. Complexity does not amount to maturity. Using one fewer circle is usually better if no important distinction is lost.

## 10.11 An Example of a Joint Object

An analysis of an employee’s public departure from a job can identify the actor, project team, company management, family care circle, professional community, and public opinion on a platform at the same time. The team is nested within the company. The employee belongs to the overlapping team, family, and professional circles. The platform bridges the employee and the public outside the company. The team and management may compete over resource allocation but cooperate in maintaining reputation. A group that forms around the departure to express support may be a temporary circle.

Material conditions include pay, working hours, care, contracts, job positions, and platform traffic. Experience–meaning conditions include dignity, a sense of betrayal, professional identity, trust in coworkers, and perceived legitimacy among the public. The departure immediately changes attention and emotion, then affects trust and handover in the team. Organizational processes may change weeks later, and institutional rules may be written back later still. Any single-track explanation that the person “left because of their personality” or that the departure was “entirely determined by company structure” must be compared with the joint state.

The snapshot makes different paths visible. If the company responds only through public relations without changing working hours or appeal channels, emotions on the platform may subside while internal distrust persists. If resources are adjusted but repair of meaning fails, people may stay while their commitments continue to weaken. If the pressure of family care is lifted, the actor’s available options change. If the professional community provides resources through a bridge, the cost of exit decreases and others may follow the example. The next Part uses event-driven projection to examine which path the evidence supports.

## 10.12 Where This Part Stops

The layer for multi-circle joint states can identify which circles need to be represented together and whether their relations are parallel, nested, overlapping, bridged, competitive, or temporary. It can also describe how memberships and roles are distributed across circles, how material and experience–meaning conditions are represented side by side, and which clocks are out of sync. It can assess whether the complex model offers a gain relative to a simple baseline.

A structural graph alone cannot establish what must happen in the future. Nor can it decide which circle most warrants protection, who should bear the costs, or who has authority to act. Event propagation, branching, and cascades belong to Part 11. Conditional foresight and bounded choice belong to Part 12. Normative judgments, authorization, and protection remain the responsibility of later layers.

If an event involves only one actor and one stable circle, and neighboring circles, membership overlap, bridging, and cross-boundary spillovers provide no additional information, do not use the full joint model. Multi-circle modeling makes it possible to preserve distinctions where interactions actually occur. An analysis need not bear that complexity every time. When fewer objects, fewer variables, and clearer evidence suffice to answer the question, the framework should scale back.

[^tn-circle-tuple-11]: Translator's note: The full tuple in English is `C* = <the circle referred to, candidate boundary, membership eligibility, role rules, entry and exit, internal state, external interfaces, material channels, experience–meaning channels, constraints, time window, scale profile, identity criterion, evidential status, counterexamples>`.

[^tn-joint-tuple-11]: Translator's note: The full tuple in English is `MC* = <actor set A, circle set C, circle relations Rcc, membership and role mapping Rac, material state M, experience–meaning state Ψ, channels and constraints Q, event stream E, multiple clocks T, scale profile SP, evidential status W, identity criterion K>`.

[^tn-circle-11]: Translator's note: Circles may be parallel, nested, overlapping, or bridged.

<a id="part_11"></a>

# Part 11 Event-Driven Dynamic Projection

Dynamic projection starts from a joint state with evidential statuses recorded. It analyzes state differences, transmission, feedback, and branching after an event, which may be observed, reported, planned, hypothetical, or simulated. Actions that actually occur can change reality with or without authorization. They must all be recorded according to the evidence. Whether an action occurred, how it is evaluated normatively, whether there is legal or institutional authority for it, and whether its execution on this occasion has been permitted must each be judged separately. Projection must specify which changes can be established directly, which are only conditional consequences, and which signals would support or weaken the corresponding paths.

## 11.1 The Difference Between Projection and Narrative Continuation

Narrative continuation can pick what comes next by coherence alone. Structural projection must preserve conditions, channels, and competing paths, and state what failure means. If key variables are missing, the projection should stop at “unknown” or propose variable candidates, rather than fill the gap with the smoothest story. If several continuations are consistent with existing evidence, keep them as separate branches. If paths are incomparable, do not force an ordering.

The minimum inputs to a projection are a fixed snapshot, event records, mechanism hypotheses, parameter ranges, clock rules, propagation rules, unknowns, and stopping conditions. The minimum outputs are a path graph, state differences at each step, support status, early signals, contrary signals, residuals, variable candidates, and write-back requirements.

| Input | What Must Be Fixed in Advance | Consequence If It Is Not Fixed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Joint snapshot | Actors, circles[^tn-circle-12], relations, material state and experience–meaning state, clocks, and evidence cutoff | The starting point is rewritten after the results are seen |
| Event | Type, time, source, objects reached, and channels | Rumors, plans, and facts are conflated |
| Mechanism | Direction, carrier, delay, threshold, and failure conditions | Each outcome can be explained arbitrarily |
| Parameter | Value, interval, level, or explicit unknown | False precision masks uncertainty |
| Stopping | Conditions involving information, risk, exceeding bounds, and resources | The story continues indefinitely |

## 11.2 Defining an Event

There are five kinds of event: observed, reported, planned, hypothetical, and simulated. Which kind each event belongs to must be stated. A reported event can affect people who believe it but must not automatically be treated as having occurred. A plan may change expectations without amounting to execution. A hypothetical event serves conditional analysis. A simulated event belongs only to projection within the model and must not be written back as a fact about reality.

An account of an event must give at least which event is meant, the time or time window of its occurrence, the time it was observed, the source, affected actors, affected circles, channels, direct changes, evidential status, disputes, competing explanations, reversibility, duration, and subsequent observations.

| Event Type | Permitted Uses in Projection | Factual Status | Required Limits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Observed | Explanation, replay, and forward projection | Holds within the stated conditions of observation | Sources, omissions, and measurement error |
| Reported | Propagation of belief and conditional projection | That a report was made does not establish that its contents are true | The reporting party’s position, verification, and disputes |
| Planned | Expectations, preparations, and strategic interaction | Existence of the plan does not establish execution | Authorization, resources, and conditions for cancellation |
| Hypothetical | Counterfactuals and scenario comparison | No factual status in reality | Conditions, purpose, and feasibility |
| Simulated | Unfolding paths within the model | Model state only | Which version of the model and which parameters are used, and the prohibition on extrapolation |

## 11.3 The Joint State Update Formula

The joint state can be written as follows.

`Ω(t) = <A(t), C(t), Rcc(t), Rac(t), M(t), Ψ(t), Q(t), E≤t, T(t), SP(t), W(t), K(t)>`.

The items correspond in order to the twelve items of the joint object (§10.2); `E≤t` is the event stream up to t, and `T(t)` records the round or cycle in which each kind of clock (§10.7) stands at t, together with the expiries already scheduled.

An update can be written as follows.

`Ω(t+Δ) = F[Ω(t), e(t), u(t), ξ(t) | θ, h]`.

Here `e(t)` is the event, `u(t)` is an externally authorized action that actually occurred, `ξ(t)` is an exogenous disturbance or unmodeled residual, `θ` denotes the hypotheses about mechanisms and parameters fixed in advance, and `h` is the historical term. The formula specifies only what each update must record and account for. It does not assert that there is a unique true F, and the function symbol must not be used in place of specific mechanisms.

Observed violations, actions beyond authorization, refusals to carry out orders, and unauthorized acts in another’s stead enter the event term `e(t)` with their evidence, as “observed” or “reported” events.
