The actor, consequences, and status of their authority must be listed separately. The actor’s lack of authority must not be grounds for deleting the event from the facts. Violations that have not occurred enter only “hypothetical” or “simulated” branches. The action term `u(t)` still follows the definition in this section and refers only to actions that have been authorized and have actually occurred. Feasibility in a scenario does not amount to permission in reality. 〔Studies 15.08, 21.03, 21.08, 28.06, 32.08〕

Each update must distinguish four things: directly observed state differences; inferences supported by a mechanism whose conditions have been stated; scenario values set to explore a path; and residuals still unexplained. Each of the four keeps its own provenance in subsequent paths. Appearing together in one snapshot does not give them the same evidential status.

### 11.3.1 States, Observations, and Identified Sets

A joint snapshot is a structured representation of the material currently available. It does not directly read every state of the world. Let `z(t)` denote the actual state yet to be inferred for the current task, and `o(t)` the record produced by observation rule H, sampling positions, and conditions of data collection. It can be written as `o(t)=H[z(t),m(t),ε(t)]`. `m(t)` includes who can enter the record, when they are measured, and which items are withheld from disclosure for protection. `ε(t)` is used only when there is a corresponding error model. Unknowns must not all be called random noise. When conditions allow, numerical measurements can use additive error. Text and categorical records use their corresponding generation rules. The joint state Ω should preserve the distinction between the records and the judgments, so that a change in observation rule is not mistaken for a change in the object.

The same set of records can correspond to several different states or mechanisms. Let `Z(o)` denote the set of states still compatible with the record under the stated model and error bounds. If the answer to question q is the same in every state in `Z(o)`, the current material is sufficient for the question. A limited answer can be given without recovering every latent variable. If the values differ, the output should retain the range of answers, any direction that can be identified, or the parts that genuinely remain unknown. Failure to detect a difference in a finite sample does not automatically establish that only one answer remains over the entire set.

The set also helps plan the next observation. First identify state distinctions that would change the current answer or the comparison of actions. Then check which feasible observations could distinguish them. More precision that leaves the answer unchanged need not help. A low-cost observation that narrows an important branch may be more valuable than expanding the whole variable table. Data collection remains subject to purpose, necessity, and protection. A need for identification does not confer permission to collect data.

### 11.3.2 Event Processing and State Continuation

Each input retains the time of the event, the time the record was obtained, and the time it entered the model. Material that arrives late can change what is now known about the past, but it cannot rewrite the information available at the time. When correcting a source, keep the original record, add a separate record of the correction, and recompute the states and paths that depend on that source. Retain local results that do not depend on it. When multiple sources recount one event, retain each of those sources and count them as a single candidate event, to avoid applying the same shock more than once. Events with similar descriptions must not be merged without verification.

State updating consists of two operations. An evidence update revises the judgment about the actual state `z(t)`. Advancing the mechanism estimates the change from `z(t)` to a subsequent state. Receiving a credible record today that “work stopped yesterday” is an evidence update today, while the stoppage itself belongs to yesterday’s real events. Having the model work it out again and obtaining another answer that work “may have stopped” adds only simulated material. Both kinds of update can change the joint state Ω together, but their reasons and evidential statuses must be kept separate.

Concurrent events may be combined in any order only if the operations commute, shared resources are not in conflict, and neither changes the other’s conditions. If two actions compete for the same resource, overwrite the same record, or change each other’s available action set, retain the branches that unfold in the different orders, or state explicitly the rule for handling concurrency. Close recorded times do not establish that two events occurred at the same time. The order in which execution calls return does not by itself reveal the causal order of real events.

## 11.4 The Nine-Step Projection Loop

### 11.4.1 Step One. Fix the Current State

State the point in time of the evidence cutoff, the objects, variables, unknowns, and disputes, and which version of the model is used. Information obtained after the cutoff must not be fed back into the starting point. If it is to be used, set up a new projection.

### 11.4.2 Step Two. Identify Actors and Circles

Carry out this step under Parts 9 and 10. If a circle has no grounds for object facts and the grouping gain (§4.3) claimed for it is not supported, retain it as a candidate grouping. If a personality hypothesis has insufficient support, retain it as a variable candidate. Do not turn candidates into entities merely to complete the graph.

### 11.4.3 Step Three. Separate Conditions in the Two Channels

List the relevant material conditions separately for the task. Also list the relevant experience–meaning conditions and state which bridges between channels are needed. If material from the other channel is missing and this affects the current judgment, retain it as “unknown.” Do not fill the gap by assuming symmetry. If a channel is genuinely irrelevant to the current task, it may be marked “not applicable” once the reason is stated. Do not collect experiential material for the sake of formal completeness. Suspend only propagation that depends on the missing channel. Independently established states and paths can still be carried forward.

### 11.4.4 Step Four. State Clocks, Thresholds, Capacity, and Delay

Mark each variable’s update clock. If a channel has capacity limits, delay, loss, saturation, reversal, or a recovery window, these should be stated before propagation.

### 11.4.5 Step Five. Introduce an Event or Action

A projection may include multiple events and actions. They are ordered by time, and each retains its own independent sources. First determine whether an action occurred, then record the actor, object, consequences, and authorization status separately. Lack of authorization cannot justify deleting a fact about what actually occurred. Plans, proposals, and simulated actions that have yet to occur retain their conditional status and must not be recorded as executed. If the model is to initiate or carry out a real-world action, valid authorization must be obtained separately. If it only forms a recommendation for people to deliberate on, it is required only to state clearly the recommendation’s evidence, normative premises, costs, gaps in authority, and conditions for revising the judgment.

### 11.4.6 Step Six. Propagate Along Stated Channels

First record directly confirmable state differences, then analyze return signals, indirect effects, and cross-circle cascades. An identified total effect of an intervention may enter a bounded judgment about the outcome. Parts of the internal mechanism that are still unclear remain unknown. The total effect must not be used to fill in missing edges of propagation. Explaining how propagation specifically occurs requires corresponding material about channels and temporal order. Where there is only co-occurrence or correlation, retain common background, selection effects, and other competing explanations. Store state differences derived conditionally from the model separately from those observed in reality.

### 11.4.7 Step Seven. Generate Paths at Branch Points

Conditions, thresholds, actor choices, external disturbances, or uncertainty about mechanisms can all produce branching. Keep mutually exclusive paths separate. Retain parallel paths if they can occur at the same time. Create a merge node only when the conditions for merging are clear.

### 11.4.8 Step Eight. Record Signals, Residuals, and Variable Candidates

List early and contrary signals for each path. State differences that the current variables cannot explain go into the residuals. A residual can give rise to variable candidates, which are entered in the ledger of variable candidates (§11.8), but it cannot automatically supply a value in reality.

### 11.4.9 Step Nine. Write Back the Results

When actual results arrive, append the following: which paths are supported, when results diverged from the projection, whether a simple baseline performed better, how well the projection was calibrated, and which mechanisms or variables should be downgraded, split, given revised boundaries, or retired. Write-back does not overwrite the record of the original projection.

## 11.5 Propagation, Delay, and Thresholds

An account of propagation must at least distinguish two things: the arrival of a signal, and an effective change of state. If information is seen but does not change a subsequent transition, record only arrival. If it changes beliefs without prompting action, record a change in experience–meaning state. Record a corresponding structural change only if the signal changes resources, behavior, rules, or relationships.

| Propagation Factor | Question to Ask | Possible Nonlinearity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Channel | What carrier conveys the impact from the source to the target? | Channel closure, filtering, or substitution |
| Capacity | How much can be carried per unit of time? | Saturation, congestion, and queues |
| Delay | When does it arrive, and when does it take effect? | Delayed feedback or a mistaken finding of no effect |
| Threshold | What conditions must be reached before the state changes? | Abrupt changes, hysteresis, and cascades |
| Loss | What is lost, and what is changed, in propagation? | Drift in meaning or dissipation of resources |
| Direction | Is the impact symmetric? | One-way dependence or offsetting effects in the opposite direction |
| Recovery | How does the object return to its previous state or move to a new one after a shock? | Resilience, cumulative damage, and lock-in |

When the same event reaches different circles through different channels, the effects can be opposite. Additional resources may reduce load in one circle but intensify competition in another. A public statement may repair external legitimacy but activate shame or distrust within the circle. A projection should record each channel separately. Net effects must not hide differences in distribution.

## 11.6 Feedback and Cross-Circle Cascades

A claim of feedback requires that a prior state or output changed a subsequent state, transition probability, or constraint through a return channel (§3.3). A claim of a cascade requires that a local change triggered changes in other circles through membership overlap, bridging, shared resources, top-down institutional transmission, or network propagation. Both require evidence of temporal order and channels.

| Kind of Cascade | Typical Chain | What to Observe | Stopping Condition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Membership | Overlapping members carry behavior, emotions, or information into another circle | Actual transmission as distinct from shared background | Members stop participating or information is not received |
| Resources | One circle takes up, releases, or reallocates resources | Accounting boundaries, conversion, and loss | Resources are isolated or an alternative source is available |
| Meaning | An interpretation of the event changes identity, legitimacy, or trust | Differences in interpretation across positions | The interpretation does not reach other circles or does not change their experience–meaning states. Effects on action or rules are checked separately |
| Institutions | An appeal, audit, or event changes rules that are then implemented at lower levels | Decisions, execution, and actual write-back | The rule is not implemented or is offset locally |
| Platforms | Recommendations, metrics, or public evaluations amplify propagation | Algorithms, selective visibility, and reflexivity | Exposure stops increasing or the audience does not respond |

The importance of a cascade does not automatically increase with scale. A small circle can have a large impact through a crucial bridge, while a large circle may have no effective propagation because its channels are blocked. A projection should focus on positions, channels, and thresholds. Membership counts alone are insufficient.

Two local effects can form a transmission chain only with shared conditions for response. Consider two subgroups of equal weight. In the first, the event changes the mediator, but the mediator does not affect the outcome. In the second, the mediator can affect the outcome, but the event cannot change the mediator. The mean effect on each edge is one-half, yet the effect of the event on the outcome across the entire chain can still be zero. This finite construction shows that the mean edge effects cannot be multiplied unconditionally even if the two studies use the same population. It is also necessary to know whether the successive effects occur in objects, states, and times that allow them to connect.

When determining that a cascade has occurred, one should therefore check together how the output of the preceding segment enters the next one, the scope of support for the joint response, capacity and delay, and offsetting and parallel paths. A limited total effect already identified through an eligible comparison can be retained directly. What is added here is the responsibility to explain the specific process of propagation. It does not require explaining all micromechanisms before acknowledging any effect. When an edge has yet to be identified, retain the independently established upstream changes and terminal effects according to their own evidence.

## 11.7 A Graph of Branching Paths

Each node of the path graph must state at least its parent node, condition set, the event or action that triggers it, state differences, affected clocks, support status, a probability or ordering expression, early signals, contrary signals, the next node, and the reason for termination. The path graph should be a directed acyclic graph. If there is a feedback loop in reality, unfold it over time and represent it with new nodes. A node must not be both its own cause and its own effect within the same projection.

Four kinds of uncertainty can produce branches: uncertainty about facts, uncertainty about mechanisms, actor choices, and exogenous disturbances. Different kinds should not be merged into a single vague probability. Give priority to verifying uncertain facts. Address mechanism uncertainty through observations that distinguish the alternatives. For uncertainty about choices, retain strategies and authorization. For exogenous disturbances, use scenario ranges and resilience checks.

| Source of Branching | Example | Appropriate Output | Inappropriate Output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Facts | Did the event actually occur? | Conditional paths before verification | Picking one account as fact |
| Mechanisms | Does silence come from fear or strategy? | Signals that distinguish the alternatives, and parallel paths | Shutting down inquiry with a personality label |
| Choice | An actor cooperates, resists, or exits | Conditions and consequences of each choice | Claiming that free choices can be predicted precisely |
| Disturbance | Change in policy, prices, disasters, or technology | Stress scenarios and conditions for recovery | Attributing unmodeled residuals to fate |

## 11.8 The Ledger of Variable Candidates

Residuals that the model cannot explain must neither be deleted nor immediately named as real variables. The candidate ledger serves to turn “what might we have missed?” into a testable task. Each candidate must state at least the residual it comes from, its name, possible type, possible channel, observable implications, competing candidates, minimal test, privacy and risk, current status, evidence, and conditions for upgrading or rejecting it.

Candidate statuses include proposed, under test, supported candidate, rejected, and retired. Even a candidate that has gained support remains subject to the definition and conditions of the relevant object or variable. It must not directly become a stable personality, a supported circle, or a causal mechanism. Candidates proposed only after the results are seen can improve the next round of the model but cannot retroactively support the original prediction.

| Candidate Source | Permitted Action | What Must Be Avoided |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Residuals in the system | Propose several competing candidates and observations that distinguish them | Absorbing all errors into one mysterious variable |
| Account by a person concerned | Preserve the person’s position, the meaning of their account, and its verifiable parts; objections it raises to how the question has been fixed are recorded and handled under §2.14 | Automatically downgrading it to subjective noise or elevating it to a complete account of the facts |
| Recurrence across cases | Establish candidate mechanisms and limits of extrapolation | Treating similar narratives as universal laws |
| Model search | Pre-register the next round of testing, that is, set down the target, criteria, and rules before seeing the results | Selecting the best results for reporting after seeing them |
| AI suggestions | Generate and compare candidates. Form judgments and analytical recommendations when the evidence, permitted uses, and explicit normative premises allow | Letting AI output verify facts about reality or authorize action |

On its own initiative, the framework can only identify residuals that the current set of variables cannot explain, propose several variable candidates that can be distinguished from one another, and design for each candidate a minimal test whose risk is acceptable. It cannot decide on its own that a candidate is true in reality.

## 11.9 Scenarios, Counterfactuals, and Simulation

Scenario projection asks, “If these conditions hold, what paths emerge?” A counterfactual asks, “If an event or mechanism had been different, how might the outcome that actually occurred have changed?” Simulation unfolds specified rules and parameters. All three must be kept separate from descriptions of fact.

Counterfactuals especially require comparable conditions. When removing an event, also state which subsequent states, actors’ information, and circle relations change as a result. Do not remove an unwelcome cause while retaining all its consequences. The precision of a simulation cannot exceed what its inputs and evidence of mechanisms support. When parameters are unknown, use ranges, levels, or sensitivity analysis. Do not generate unsupported decimal places.

Counterfactuals must preserve the information boundaries at the time. Replacing an event or choice means reassessing the beliefs, resources, orders, and downstream behavior it affects. Do not remove an announcement while holding fixed the attendance and subsequent execution it brought about. Evidence for a short-range branch does not mean an alternative history decades later is already knowable. The actions of ordinary people, the discretion of frontline personnel, and organizational constraints can all enter the explanation. There is no need to assign causal percentages without a basis for identifying them. 〔Studies 03.03, 32.04, 32.08〕

The strength of a counterfactual conclusion depends on whether mechanisms still compatible with the evidence give the same answer under the altered operation. Two mechanisms can both produce observations of `X=M=Y`. In one, X changes Y through M. In the other, X changes M and Y separately. This co-movement alone cannot establish whether setting M directly would change Y. More observations of the same kind can improve the precision of the record but need not resolve this equivalence between mechanisms. A design that distinguishes the two mechanisms or independently grounded assumptions are needed. If independent materials already identify the total effect of a specified treatment within stated limits, retain that effect even if a particular mediator has yet to be identified.

Counterfactual analysis can therefore produce one answer, a set of feasible answers, or conditional bounds. Treat a direction as robust only when all compatible mechanisms support the same conclusion. If the conclusion reverses across plausible mechanisms, report the conditions under which it reverses and list the evidence needed to choose between the mechanisms as the next observation. Historically, “removing a person from the post they came to occupy” and “that person having never been there” have different starting points and processes of adaptation. They cannot share the same counterfactual answer.

### 11.9.1 Multi-Order Recursive Projection of the Future

Advancing time over multiple steps, re-entry from a simulated state, and anticipatory reflexivity are three orthogonal dimensions. Advancing time over multiple steps carries a state forward in time within one projection. Re-entry from a simulated state uses one of the simulated futures generated in the first round as the starting point for a child projection. Anticipatory reflexivity occurs when actors in the simulation form expectations about the more distant future or other people’s responses and change their current strategies as a result. These three must not be conflated under the single term “recursion.”

Three orders are one default way to organize exploratory projection. The first unfolds direct consequences and competing paths. The second checks how those changes alter the available actions, resources, relationships, and adaptation. The third checks institutionalization, lock-in, reversal, and changes in conditions for generation. Recursion goes no further than the third order (§11.9.4). The orders mark responsibilities in projection. They do not amount to three points in time, natural stages, or levels of capability. Do not force recursion for static questions or tasks without a distinct question at the next order. Stop when conditions are insufficient.

The general principle is this: the layer that generates possibilities may be bold, the state layer must be strict, the evidence layer must not raise its own status, and the action layer must still be authorized separately. Boldness serves to expand the space of plausible mechanisms, competing paths, and branches with low probability and severe consequences. It also serves to produce clear judgments within the limits of the evidence. The strength of a judgment is supported only by evidence, conditions of applicability, and permitted uses. Tone or the number of generated possibilities cannot make it stronger.

### 11.9.2 Recursive Interfaces and Lineage

Before each re-entry, carry out a recasting review (§5.10.2) and state the following: the current order; the projection, path, and node from which this child projection comes; the simulated time; the time window of the current order and the cumulative time window; which version of the model is used; inherited assumptions; new conditions; what is preserved, changed, collapsed, or omitted; new unknowns; effective variables at the target end (§5.10.3); residuals; identity across re-entry; the return path; and the reason for stopping. The simulated starting point must not be rewritten as present reality.

A child projection must inherit the unresolved unknowns, losses, and residuals of its parent projection. Selecting a hypothetical branch only narrows the conditions. It does not mean that material from reality has eliminated the uncertainty. Increasing the number of draws may reduce computational error. It does not increase empirical support about outcomes in reality.

### 11.9.3 Branching, Merging, and Pruning

At each order, check whether there are substantive grounds for these kinds of path: the main path, its strongest competitor, a path with low probability and severe consequences, and a route for residuals. Retain all conditions for paths that have grounds. If a category is inapplicable or a path of that kind cannot be constructed, explain why. Do not invent an event to fill a category. Every branch must correspond to an explainable difference in mechanisms, a choice by actors, an external disturbance, or an unknown of a specified kind. Retaining a path with severe consequences means only that it calls for investigation or preparation. It does not establish that its real-world probability is known.

Branches may be merged only when all of the following hold: object identity is preserved; key states are equivalent within a tolerance fixed in advance; differences in history do not change subsequent transitions; and the available actions and constraints agree going forward. Pruning rules must be stated in advance. Preserve the pruned branches, the reasons for pruning, the probability they may carry, and the level of harm. Low probability alone cannot justify removing a path with severe consequences.

### 11.9.4 Early Stopping

Stop or downgrade if object identity or scale identity fails, key assumptions cannot be inherited, the transition mechanism falls outside its scope of applicability, the recursive interface lacks closure, or branches multiply sharply without signals to distinguish them. Also stop or downgrade if the results reverse across the board under small changes, residuals exceed the threshold that the intended use allows, a deeper order adds nothing relative to a shallower one and a simple baseline, the calibrated time window is exceeded, a boundary of rights or authorization is reached, or the third-order limit is reached. When stopping, the projection must state what can still be said and what cannot.

## 11.10 Stopping Conditions for a Projection

In any of the following situations, the affected propositions and the paths that depend on them should be suspended or downgraded. If what fails is a shared premise or the overall conditions for use, all related projections must stop. The situations are these: a key object lacks grounds for object facts, or a grouping-gain claim on which a path depends is not supported; the event’s factual status is unclear; a propagation channel is missing; a cross-scale mapping fails; the number of paths grows without signals to distinguish them; the model is extremely sensitive to small changes in parameters; privacy or safety risks exceed the value of the information; someone asks the projection to generate a diagnosis, punishment, or authorization directly; or a simple baseline already performs as well or better.

Stopping is part of the output. It must not be used to conceal failure. When stopping, the projection should state where it stopped, what has been obtained, which unknowns prevent it from continuing, which next observation would be most informative, and what risk further projection would add.

## 11.11 An Example of a Cross-Circle Cascade

Continue with the public departure from a job in Part 10 (§10.11). The starting snapshot shows that the employee faces long working hours and the pressure of care work, team trust is declining, company management is concerned with reputation, the professional community provides outside opportunities, and public opinion on the platform has yet to form. The event is the employee publishing an account of their departure. Part of its content can be verified, and part is personal narrative.

Direct effects include the team receiving the information, the platform obtaining a text that can be circulated, and management facing pressure to respond. On the first path, the company makes only a public denial. In the short term, external public opinion may branch toward either fading or amplification. If members inside the company interpret the denial as suppression, team trust declines and further departures occur through bridges in the professional community. On the second path, the company acknowledges the problem and starts verifiable adjustments to resources and appeals. If these are carried out, working hours and processes change on the organizational clock. Trust may recover more slowly on the interactive clock. On the third path, changes in family care conditions ease the employee’s pressure after leaving. This does not directly change the team’s state unless the employee continues to bridge information or resources.

Early signals can include the number of internal appeals, records of hours actually worked, members’ public statements, and changes in hiring and departures. Contrary signals can include no actual change in resources after a policy is announced, increasing internal silence despite declining external exposure, or the professional community failing to form a bridge. Residuals may come from the states of key managers, the platform’s recommendation mechanism, or unobserved legal constraints. These enter only the ledger of variable candidates (§11.8).

The projection still cannot say which path the company “should” take. It provides conditional consequences and signals that distinguish the paths. Forecast registration, comparison of options, normative premises, and authorization are addressed in the next Part.

## 11.12 Outputs of This Part

A qualifying projection output should include a fixed joint snapshot, event type and evidence, mechanism and parameter assumptions, update steps, and a path graph. For every path, it should record conditions, clocks, support status, and early and contrary signals. It should also include residuals and variable candidates, stopping conditions, a plan for writing back results, and an explicit statement that prediction and action are kept separate.

Projection can improve structured preparation for what follows, but it remains conditional. Without registration before results, a simple baseline, calibration, and continuing write-back, it cannot support a claim that foresight capability has improved. Without normative grounds and authorization, it cannot support a claim that an action should be carried out. An analysis based on explicit normative premises can recommend an option, reject it, or recommend deferral. None of these judgments establishes that the option has been authorized for execution. For each such judgment, its grounds, costs, opposing case, and conditions for revision must be stated in full.

## 11.13 Action Choice and Updating Conditions

For dynamic questions involving actors, having a model evaluate a set of static options is insufficient. At each step, first use the current state to identify actions actually available, actions ruled out, and the source of the restrictions. Then analyze how an actor might choose given their information, resources, relationships, habits, and goals. Capability, belief, willingness, and actual action must be kept separate. Being able to act does not mean the actor will act. Stating an intention does not mean it has been carried out. An analyst’s recommendation does not amount to adoption by the actor.

For each choice with a basis in the material, specify which mechanism it triggers, which states change first, who is affected through which interfaces, and how these changes alter the set of actions available at the next step. State differences must be expressed in concrete terms such as resources, rules, relationships, beliefs, or feasible actions. Feeding the same materials to another model and generating another narrative cannot substitute for updating a state. If no material determines how the actor will choose, retain several conditional paths. Do not decide for the actor just to continue the projection.

Later projection starts from explicitly stated conditional state differences and inherits unresolved unknowns and restrictions. When real feedback arrives, first verify its source and which event it refers to. Then compare it with the original path, competing paths, and the simple baseline. Distinguish factual errors, mechanism errors, different choices by the actor, deviations in execution, and external changes. The corrected result should change the states, parameters, scope of mechanisms, or paths used in the next round. Keeping only the text of the feedback while retaining the same choice rule does not warrant claiming that the model has learned.

[^tn-circle-12]: Translator's note: Circles may be parallel, nested, overlapping, or bridged.

<a id="part_12"></a>

# Part 12 Conditional Foresight and Bounded Choice

Projection unfolds conditions and paths. Conditional foresight goes further by making judgments about the future that can fail. Bounded choice compares what can be done, how to do it, when to stop, and when to refrain within the bounds of values, protection, and authorization. This Part places conditional foresight and bounded choice side by side so that the work forms a closed loop. It also keeps the two apart, each with its own conditions, to prevent “a consequence was predicted” from being taken to mean “there is therefore authority to make others take on an action.” Comparing and recommending options are analytical outputs and can be completed once the normative premises and constraints are clear. Real-world adoption and execution must separately undergo the applicable protection, review, and authorization procedures.

## 12.1 Keeping the Four Outputs Separate

Explanation, projection, conditional foresight, and bounded choice are four kinds of output and must be labeled separately.

| Output | Core Question | Required Inputs | Output Ceiling |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Explanation | What has happened, and why might it have happened? | Object, scale, evidence, mechanism, and counterexamples | An account of the mechanism within stated limits |
| Projection | Which paths could unfold after a condition or event? | Fixed snapshot, update rules, clocks, and branches | Conditional paths and signals that distinguish them |
| Conditional foresight | For the stated target and horizon, which path is better supported as an expectation? | Registration before results, a simple baseline, metrics, and write-back | A judgment that can be calibrated and can fail |
| Bounded choice | Compare and recommend options under explicit normative premises. Real-world adoption separately undergoes protection, review, and authorization | Analysis requires normative premises, evidence, options, costs, and the people affected. Real-world adoption also requires normative premises stated under §14.3, the protection floor (§14.8), itemized authorization and the four-step operational procedure (§14.6), and the conclusion rule “Normative Bridging” (§4.14.1) | A refutable analytical recommendation or an authorized record of bounded choice, with their statuses kept separate |

Explanation can propose candidates for projection, but it cannot automatically establish what will happen. Projection can propose candidate forecasts, but it cannot count every path as a success. Foresight can inform comparisons between options, but it cannot automatically produce values or authority. Even a bounded choice that passes its checks does not guarantee successful execution in reality. Stopping, restoration, and outcome write-back are still required.

## 12.2 Conditional Forecast Registration

The registration of a conditional forecast sets the forecast down after the input cutoff and before the results appear. It is not changed afterward. Each registration states at least the following: which version of the model is used; the target; the horizon; the scope of objects and circles[^tn-circle-13]; the baseline time; the input cutoff; the simple baseline; candidate mechanisms; the set of paths; the probability or ranking expression; the calibration plan; the decision threshold (needed when the forecast is used for the corresponding decision, and otherwise marked “not applicable”); early signals; contrary signals; suspension conditions; retirement conditions; outcome write-back; the time of registration; and the evidence cited. Each registration should be a record that can be identified on its own and checked.

The target must be decidable. For example, “the relationship will improve” must be rewritten to specify which observables change within a stated time window, who observes them, what threshold applies, and what outcomes count as “unresolved.” The horizon can be a time window. There is no need to fabricate a precise date. The scope of the objects and circles must be fixed in advance, so that it is not narrowed to the successful subgroup after results appear.

| Registration Item | Minimum Question | Bias It Prevents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Target | When the horizon ends, how will we know whether it occurred, did not occur, or cannot be determined? | Vague success criteria |
| Horizon | When does the window start and end, and when does input collection stop? | Waiting indefinitely |
| Simple baseline | What is the comparison prediction without multi-circle mechanisms? | Letting a complex story win by its own standards |
| Paths | Which paths are mutually exclusive, parallel, or incomparable? | Post hoc selection |
| Expression | Probability, interval, level, or direction alone? | False precision |
| Signals | What would strengthen or weaken support for a path? | Looking only for supporting evidence |
| Write-back | What is the source of the outcome, and when is it appended? | Letting the record of failures disappear |

### 12.2.1 Limits of Local Predictability

Every claim about predictability must be tied to its limits: the object, state region, scale and circles, time window, allowable error, available information, computing and observation resources, which version of the model is used, the baseline, and the abstention and failure conditions. This framework cannot directly answer whether the world as a whole is predictable. It can test only whether a particular task gains a limited increment within explicit bounds.

Classifications, levels, intervals, and probabilities carry different responsibilities for measurement and expression. They do not form a ladder of precision that every task has to climb. The chosen form of expression must be supported by the target, units, generation method, identification conditions, and calibration status. If there is no basis even for a qualitative direction, retain it as unknown. Direction is not the default when probability is unavailable. For known probabilities in formal models and for empirical probabilities, state the assumptions and limits of extrapolation separately. Text patterns and AI must not be used to invent real-world parameters. When citing an existing mathematical or physical theory, also state its original object, assumptions, mathematical limits or scaling laws, error, domain of validity, the mapping between objects, counterexamples, and exit conditions. Borrowing the form of its equations alone is insufficient.

### 12.2.2 Evaluation of Recursive Foresight by Order

The first, second, and third orders of recursive foresight (for multi-order recursive projection, see §11.9.1) are each set down in advance and evaluated separately. They must not be combined into a single overall hit rate. Each order must be compared with three alternatives: state continuation without further recursion; a direct longer-horizon judgment; and a shallower order followed by simple continuation. If going to the third order adds only narrative without stable out-of-sample gains, it may be retained as an exploratory scenario, but it must not be credited with foresight capability.

Without new external material, the source lineage of every child projection still ends at the same fixed starting point. Processing after the fact can add reasoning within the model and reveal sensitivity and hidden consequences. It cannot manufacture evidence about reality. When actual intermediate outcomes arrive, a new projection with a newly fixed starting point should be carried out and compared with the original recursive paths. The outcomes must not be fed back into the old paths.

## 12.3 Simple Baselines and Incremental Capability

A multi-circle model claimed to improve foresight must be compared with simple models suited to the task and with existing methods in the domain under the same information, cutoff, target, and evaluation rules. Make the comparison materials, inference budgets, and opportunities for tuning as comparable as possible. State separately what is contributed by additional information, additional computation, and additional structural assumptions. A simple baseline need not be artificially enlarged to match the size of the complex model. Predictive systems generally require independent testing or out-of-sample review. If neither can be obtained, explicitly retain the status “capability not yet established.”

Common baselines include continuing the current trend, carrying forward the most recent state, using historical frequencies, using only the actor state, using only the primary circle state, and using an existing model in the domain. Comparisons should use the same target, horizon, data cutoff, and evaluation metrics. If a complex model improves explanation but does not improve prediction, record the outcome as “a gain in explanation is present, and a gain in foresight is not supported.”

Model complexity also has costs. More variables increase missing data, measurement error, privacy risk, overfitting, and maintenance debt. If a multi-circle model works in only a few cases, its domain of application should be restricted. If gains disappear over time, it should be downgraded or retired. If the simple baseline performs equally well, it should be preferred.

## 12.4 Probability, Levels, and Time Windows

Where the evidence permits, one may give a probability or probability interval and state the model, prior, data, and grounds for calibration. When there is insufficient basis for a probability, one may give levels or compare paths to the extent supported by evidence. Sample size alone does not determine the type of output. When even the direction or ordering cannot be identified, explicitly retain it as unknown and identify observations that could distinguish the alternatives. Giving only the direction does not waive evidential responsibility. The strength of the expression depends on the evidence and use, independently of how much certainty the user wants.

| Evidential Status | Appropriate Expression | What Must Accompany It |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A probability model or empirical estimate with clear grounds and a decidable target | Probability or probability interval | Method of generation, prior if applicable, data, limits of applicability, and calibration status |
| Insufficient basis for probability, but grounds for path levels or ordering | Levels of support or an ordering | Grounds, incomparable items, and contrary signals |
| The direction can be identified, or it remains unknown | A supported conditional direction, or an explicit unknown | Identification conditions, trigger points, minimal observation, and stopping conditions |
| Target or object is unstable | Withhold the forecast | The definition that needs to be made anew |

Time windows should match mechanism clocks. Immediate reactions can use a short window. Organizational or institutional changes require a longer one. Compressing a long-term mechanism into a short period can lead to a mistaken finding of no effect. Extrapolating a short-term signal indefinitely can lead to a mistaken finding of a trend. When several clocks coexist, the registration may set separate horizons for different intermediate outcomes.

Real-world probabilities, actors’ subjective beliefs, decision weights, a model’s ordering of paths, and the allocation of computation at the next step are distinct quantities. A real-world probability must specify the target event and the basis for estimation or calibration. For a subjective belief, state who is judging, what information they have, and how they reached the judgment. Decision weights are interpreted according to the descriptive model or normative premises in use. Computational priorities specify why further investigation is worthwhile. Frequencies of branches obtained by taking more draws from a model must not be treated directly as real-world probabilities. The path most worth investigating or most hoped for must not be described as the most likely.

When probabilities cannot be determined reliably, a path may be investigated first because its consequences are severe, the response window is short, or it is easy to distinguish. Disclose the reason for the priority and the budget for investigating it, and retain the probability as unknown. Percentages must not be invented to establish an ordering. An action comparison still has to state normative objectives, distributional consequences, and feasible choices separately. An ordering by probability does not directly determine the order of recommendations.

Probabilities and levels have different meanings. A model’s conditional probability under given assumptions, uncertainty in an individual judgment, empirical calibration in a long series of repeated tasks, and normative priority must not use one number as though they referred to the same thing. A posterior can be obtained from a small sample and an explicit prior, but its real-world applicability still depends on the model. A large sample cannot repair an incorrect definition of what is observed. Without evidence, even the direction can remain unknown. Reducing the claim to direction alone does not automatically make it reliable. 〔Studies 03.04, 07.07〕

## 12.5 Calibration and Evaluation

Foresight capability is established by results registered over time. It does not follow from a style that sounds accurate. Where applicable, evaluate probability tasks with the Brier score, log loss, calibration curves, resolution, and interval coverage. Use ranking metrics registered in advance for ranking tasks. Use precision, recall, or domain metrics for event detection. Use window coverage and lead time for predictions of timing.

Every metric must match the actual use. If low-probability events with severe harms call for caution, evaluation cannot rely only on overall accuracy. A false positive costs something different when the output prompts further observation than when it is used to compel action. Good metrics establish neither that the model’s explanation is correct nor that action is justified.

Once early warning is in use, the object of evaluation must be stated together with the response regime. Is the task to predict actual events under an existing regime, or to ask separately what issuing a warning or taking action changed? Retain every record that could affect the evaluation, including reach, execution, the entry and exit of objects, and how the data were produced. When the regime changes, state again which outcomes are still comparable. The absence of an observed event cannot automatically be recorded as a false positive or taken to establish successful protection. A claim that harm was avoided separately requires a causal comparison suited to that claim. Forecasts already defined under the current response regime can still be evaluated against the original target. There is no need to turn every prediction task into a study of intervention effects. The original target, horizon, and success rules must not be rewritten after the fact because a response took place (Perdomo et al., 2020). See also §2.4 and §12.6.

| Evaluation Dimension | Question | Action After Failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calibration | Of events assigned 70%, do roughly 70% occur over the long run? | Adjust the expression or downgrade probability outputs |
| Resolution | Can the model distinguish different risks or paths? | Remove variables that make no contribution and return to the baseline |
| Coverage | Do intervals or time windows cover the actual outcomes? | Widen intervals or revise the clocks |
| Gain over baseline | Does it outperform the simple model? | Stop making foresight claims for the complex model |
| Stability | Does performance hold across times, locations, and boundaries? | Restrict the domain of application or retire the model |
| Distribution of error | At which positions do persistent underestimates or false positives occur? | Review by people affected, remediation, and stronger protection |

Three parallel questions can fix the terms of the evaluation.

| Question | What Sufficient Material Can Answer | What Must Be Retained |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How did the original prediction perform against the target registered in advance? | Compute loss, classification outcomes, or coverage using actual labels defined on the same basis | A single case score does not establish long-run calibration. Do not enter zero for missing labels |
| How much did publication or action change the outcome? | Give a limited effect estimate based on a causal comparison suited to the question | An observed absence of the event cannot by itself distinguish initially low risk from successful prevention |
| Is it appropriate to adopt this prediction and response? | Compare protection, false rejections, delay, distribution, and cost under explicit normative premises | Neither predictive accuracy nor a positive effect by itself confers permission |

For example, suppose a forecast registered in advance assigns an event probability of 0.8 under the current response regime, and the complete label at the end of the horizon is 0. The Brier loss for that case is 0.64. If the threshold for binary classification was set in advance at 0.5, a false positive may also be recorded for that target. This limited calculation establishes neither the risk without action nor that the response was ineffective. If monitoring was offline and no label was obtained, the same calculation cannot be used. Complete labels for people who were approved or received services can directly evaluate only the corresponding population. Extending the evaluation to people who were rejected, were not reached, or exited requires labels for them or well-grounded methods of identification and bounding.

After a change in the response regime, first check whether the original target is still the same question. If the target is retained, report the performance change as observed. If the target shifts to a different response regime or population, create a new registration and retain the old results. Reflexivity must not be used to cancel a score that can be computed. One successful response must not be used to rescue all incorrect predictions after the fact.

## 12.6 Early Signals, Contrary Signals, and Trigger Points

An early signal is an observable change that the path’s mechanism should produce first. A smaller version of the outcome does not suffice. A contrary signal indicates that a key condition of the path is failing or that a competing path is gaining support. Both must enter the registration before results appear, to avoid collecting only supporting material.

Trigger points connect foresight to review. Observing a signal calls for reassessing the object, path, probability, normative grounds, and authorization. It does not automatically trigger action. High-risk cases should also have veto triggers, such as a breach of the protection floor, inability of key affected people to exit, distortion of data sources, or deteriorating model calibration.

Use completion of a feasible action as the endpoint when comparing clocks. Detecting the signal, verifying it, publishing the warning, reaching people, and understanding the warning each involve a delay. Gathering resources takes time, as can carrying out a transfer or waiting for a measure to take effect. Earlier algorithmic detection does not guarantee that the last person affected can receive protection before harm occurs. If no harm follows an alert, use the target and labeling conditions registered in advance to decide whether it may be recorded as an operational false positive. Identify separately whether a successful response prevented harm. Keep the denominators separate for the operational false positive rate, the proportion of false alerts among alerts, and the missed detection rate. 〔Studies 31.05〕

## 12.7 What Forecast Failure Means

When the horizon of a forecast ends, the result can be “supported,” “not supported,” “unresolved,” “target invalid,” or “not evaluable.” “Unresolved” is no compromise between success and failure. It is a state agreed on at registration, indicating that the evidence is insufficient. A result recorded as “not evaluable” must state whether the problem lay with the data, the object, the horizon, or the execution, or whether a premise that was written into the target at registration, and whose continued holding can be determined, has not held, so that under §12.5 the original target is judged to be no longer the same question; for example, the target was limited to an established response regime and that regime itself has changed, not merely a response having been made under it. Where the original target is still the same question, it is evaluated as usual; the standard for judging whether it is still the same question does not differ according to whether the result is a hit or a miss; a premise that was not written into the target at registration cannot be used after the result appears to re-record the result as “not evaluable” (§2.12). “Target invalid” means that the object of the prediction has undergone conversion, or that its identity criterion has failed. Such a result must not be counted as a hit.

Changing the target, horizon, or scope of circles after results, or merging several paths into “it happened to some extent,” cannot preserve the original forecast’s eligibility to count as a success. A new interpretation can be set out in a new version. The old record remains.

## 12.8 The Bridge From Foresight to Bounded Choice

Foresight outputs answer only questions about conditional consequences. Before an analytical recommendation is formed, the following must be made explicit: normative premises, evidence, affected positions, options, costs and benefits, and conditions for revising the judgment, that is, what would change the recommendation. A recommendation does not confer permission to execute. Before real-world adoption, the following must be added: explicit normative premises, the choosing subject, jurisdiction, affected positions, rights floors, options, the distribution of costs and benefits, authorization, stopping, appeal, restoration, and remedy. What applies here is still the normative premises stated under §14.3, the protection floor (§14.8), itemized authorization and the four-step operational procedure (§14.6), and the conclusion rule “Normative Bridging” (§4.14.1). No separate shortcut is opened for prediction.

Prediction cannot automatically confer authorization. Even an extremely probable path does not show that anyone has authority to compel others to bear the cost of avoiding it. Even the highest average benefit does not show that the rights of positions in the minority may be ignored. Even if the model recommends taking no action, continuing harm and responsibility arising from inaction still require review.

## 12.9 The Option Set Must Include Action and No Action

When proposing options, check the applicability of each of six categories: maintaining the status quo, acting proactively, delaying action, taking a small exploratory action, exiting or transferring, and explicitly taking no action. For each applicable category, develop genuine and comparable options. For each category that does not apply, explain why. Do not invent options to meet a quota. If the task calls for a choice, the explicit no-action baseline must not be removed, and maintaining the status quo must not be merged with taking no action. Maintaining the status quo may require ongoing resources and execution. Taking no action may allow existing conditions to change on their own. Specific tasks may add options. Tasks that do not call for a choice need not produce a list of actions.

| Option Type | Main Use | Risks That Must Be Checked |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Maintain the status quo | Protect existing stability and uptake arrangements | Hidden costs, continuing harm, and lock-in |
| Proactive action | Change a path or its conditions quickly | Authority, irreversibility, and cross-circle spillovers |
| Delayed action | Wait for information, procedure, or the right time | Harm and lost opportunities from delay itself |
| Exploratory action | Obtain information through a small reversible step | Who bears the costs of the trial and whether the prior state can actually be restored |
| Exit or transfer | End an unsuitable object or relationship | People unable to exit, responsibilities, and preservation of history |
| No action | Avoid overstepping authority or taking high-risk action | Bias toward the default, continuing consequences, and responsibility for inaction |

Taking no action does not mean that nothing happens. Other actors, circles, resources, and clocks are still changing. The no-action option must also have a baseline time, expected path, observation plan, conditions for reopening the decision, and a responsible party.

## 12.10 A Common Card for Comparing Options

Compare each option against the same baseline. The assumptions each option makes about implementers’ capabilities, information, conflicts of interest, and resources, and about how the people affected will respond, should be equally close to reality; the ideal operation of one option must not be compared with the actual performance of another. Where some options have a record of implementation and others have only a design, the level of evidence each rests on must be stated; for an option that has only a design, the part of its conclusions that depends on assumptions not tested by implementation is correspondingly lowered in strength. The record of maintaining the status quo and of non-action is likewise evaluated by the positions and time it actually covers and by the materials that are absent (§12.9, §16.6), and gains no advantage merely because a record already exists. This does not entail that the options actually perform the same; differences must come from evidence and cannot be produced in advance by the setup of the comparison. For each option, state at least the description of the option, which forecast it cites, normative premises, people affected, rights floors, expected path, the worst outcome that is still acceptable, cross-circle spillovers, distribution of costs and benefits, value of information, risk of lock-in, reversibility, resource costs, implementer, authorization, stopping, restoration, and remedy.

| Dimension of Comparison | Question | What Cannot Substitute |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Target and path | Which path is the option intended to change? | An abstract promise to “make things better” |
| Protection floor | Who might suffer unacceptable harm? | Average benefit |
| Distribution | Who benefits, who pays, and when? | The aggregate net value |
| Cross-circle spillovers | Does local improvement externalize costs? | Metrics from the primary circle |
| Value of information | Can the option distinguish mechanisms or paths? | The dramatic character of the action itself |
| Reversibility and lock-in | If it goes wrong, can it be stopped, reversed, or remedied? | Verbal promises |
| Permissions | Who may decide, execute, and appeal? | A model’s suggestion or a job title |
| No action | What path will unfold if nothing is done? | An assumption of zero cost |

If options cannot be compared on a single scale, retain the outcomes on multiple dimensions and disclose the conflicts. Do not force them into a sum. Conflicts among value premises should be handled by qualified subjects and procedures. The model should fully show where conflicts arise and what their consequences are. It may offer a preference and reasons for deliberation under openly stated normative premises. It cannot make a binding final decision in place of a qualified subject.

The value of information can be written as a formal object with stated conditions. Let a denote the action, θ the state, Z the information, and U the utility accepted in advance. Then `EVSI=E_Z[max_a E(U|Z)]−max_a E(U)`. EVSI is nonnegative when the information Z can be obtained free of charge and can be ignored once obtained, and when the action set and objective remain unchanged. Actual investigation also has costs in time, privacy, and resources. It may miss a time window or change the available actions. Its net value should therefore be counted separately. Two clues may change the action only if both are obtained. The value of understanding can exist independently and need not all be converted into this quantity for decision-making. 〔Studies 07.08, formal statement of conditions〕

### 12.10.1 From Identifiable Answers to Feasible Choices

A question can have a sufficient answer while action remains infeasible. There can also be a commonly acceptable action before all states have been identified. For each state z compatible with the available material, let `A_ok(z)` denote the actions acceptable under the disclosed rights floors, resources, and valid permissions. In a finite, single-round deterministic choice, if the intersection `∩ A_ok(z)` is nonempty, the common options in it can be compared directly without first distinguishing all states. This gives one positive condition under which bounded action is possible while unknowns remain. Its formal statement is given in §4.18.3. If the intersection is empty, “there is a solution for every state” is insufficient to establish that the right one can be chosen now. In that case, check whether obtaining more evidence, waiting, narrowing the task, or taking a protective action with independent grounds could change the conditions.

The intersection concerns only the credible states listed and the explicit constraints. It does not guarantee that unknown states will never arise. Risk probabilities, costs, or normative tolerance can support other choice rules, but they must be stated explicitly. The worst-case criterion must not be concealed as the only rational one. Permissible randomized or sequential strategies must also be analyzed separately for their respective objectives. The single-round condition above does not rule them out.

### 12.10.2 Joint Feasibility of Multiple Options

When several actions are feasible individually, also check whether implementing them at the same time would draw on the same capacity, budget, staff, and stopping channels. If two units of service must both be completed in the current period and it has capacity for only one unit, each is feasible on its own but they are infeasible together. Added capacity next period cannot recover a deadline already missed in this period. Adding capacity in the same period or adjusting the deadline with adequate grounds and approval can yield a new feasible option. It must not be used to rewrite the old task as completed.

Joint comparison should therefore account for resource use, task dependencies, and key deadlines together so different departments do not commit the same resource twice. Parallel work shortens waiting only when conditions allow. Where investigation, authorization, implementation, and taking effect depend on one another in sequence, they must still follow that order. Treating completion of the first node as proof that the last affected person is already protected misjudges both timing and coverage.

## 12.11 Action Ceilings and Trials to Obtain Information

Evidence, reversibility, permissions, and protection together determine the action ceiling. When evidence is weak, risk high, action irreversible, or permissions insufficient, an appropriate output may be to observe first, narrow the action, improve the information, protect people affected, initiate an appeal, or take no action for now.

A trial to obtain information still carries responsibility, however small the action. It must specify the trial object, people affected, minimum scope, reversibility, stopping, data uses, and remedy. Those in low-power positions must not be used as material for model calibration. Participation must not be described as voluntary where there is no genuine ability to exit.

| Combination of Conditions | Example of the Permitted Ceiling |
| --- | --- |
| Weak evidence, low harm, reversibility, and clear authorization | Small-scale observation or exploratory action |
| Moderate evidence, manageable harm, and the prior state can be restored | Phased action with stringent stopping conditions |
| Strong evidence but insufficient permissions | Submit to the authorized subject and do not execute independently |
| Strong evidence, but the action is irreversible and protection requirements are unmet | Suspend and complete the procedures and protections |
| Urgent safety threat | Take only the minimum protective action under external emergency authorization, and review it as soon as possible |

## 12.12 Outcome Write-Back and Model Learning

Outcome write-back for foresight and choices can only add to the record. It does not overwrite existing records. What is written back includes the time the outcome was observed, the source, the actual outcome, which path it matches, calibration metrics, comparison with the simple baseline, unexpected effects, review at affected positions, model updates, downgraded assertions, retired variables or paths, and the next review.

Action outcomes must not be evaluated only against the main target. Also check side effects, cross-circle spillovers, cost distribution, appeals, people unable to exit, and long-term clocks. One success does not establish that a mechanism holds universally. One failure may be due to a deviation in execution. Use the registration and arrangements set down in advance to distinguish evidence about the mechanism from deviations in execution. Explanations about execution must not be used arbitrarily to rescue the model.

## 12.13 A Complete Example of Foresight and Choice

Continue with the public departure from a job (§10.11, §11.11). A conditional forecast could set the target as “whether the team’s voluntary turnover rate over the next three months exceeds the threshold set down at registration.” The threshold is set down at registration with reference to the historical baseline and the baseline for similar teams, for example one and a half times the higher of the two; the definition of the turnover rate, the data source, and who compiles the figures are stated along with it, as is the margin between the turnover rate and the threshold within which the result is recorded as “unresolved.” The input cutoff is one week after the public statement. The simple baseline uses historical departure rates and trends in working hours. The multi-circle model adds team trust, management’s response, bridging by the professional community, family care, and platform exposure. Possible paths include public attention fading while internal problems persist, institutional adjustments followed by gradual repair, and external bridging that triggers departures in succession.

Early signals include actual changes in working hours, handling of appeals, statements by members, hiring, and outside opportunities. Contrary signals include a policy being announced without execution, or public quiet accompanied by increasing silence internally. After three months, compare the multi-circle model with the simple baseline. Do not declare success by picking an intermediate signal that happened to match.

Bounded choice should compare at least maintaining the status quo, responding only through public relations, immediately adjusting resources, starting with a reversible pilot for working hours and appeals, delaying major reorganization to gather information, allowing team members to transfer, and taking no structural action for now while strengthening protection and observation. Each option requires checking permissions, people unable to exit, the distribution of costs, reputational effects across circles and effects on families, stopping, and remedy. The model can show which options are more likely to change the path under which conditions. The final choice still depends on normative premises, lawful authorization, and procedures for the people affected. Under these conditions, the model should also state its current analytical recommendation, why other options were not selected, the costs, and the conditions for revising the judgment. A recommendation does not change the status of execution permission that has yet to be obtained.

## 12.14 When to Choose Not to Act

Taking no action can be prudent or evasive. Taking no action for now or limiting activity to protective observation can be warranted when the object and facts are unclear, an action is irreversible and evidence insufficient, permissions are missing, or the protection floor is unmet. It can also be warranted when the proposed action is expected to shift costs to people unable to exit, neither the simple baseline nor the complex model can distinguish the paths, or external intervention could interrupt an ongoing recovery.

Taking no action requires stricter review when harm is ongoing, inaction reinforces entrenched advantages, the responsible subject has a clear statutory duty or commitment, or people in low-power positions cannot exit on their own. The same applies when delay would create irreversible lock-in or when “waiting for more evidence” is used to defer indefinitely. Even without the main action, minimum protection, disclosure, appeal channels, or temporary uptake may be needed.

## 12.15 Where This Part Stops

The conditional foresight layer may publish judgments with a target, horizon, baseline, signals, calibration, and write-back. When norms, protection, and authorization are all clear, the bounded choice layer can compare action, delay, exploration, exit, and no action, and provide a conditional, withdrawable choice record. Even when execution has not been authorized, an analytical recommendation can still be completed within what the evidence and explicit normative premises allow. It must fully explain the options, opposing arguments, distributional consequences, and conditions for revising the judgment. Its status for real-world adoption must be stated separately.

These layers cannot guarantee the future, eliminate conflicts of value, replace law, professional norms, participation by people affected, or real-world authorization, or turn model accuracy into a qualification to rule. Any use that exceeds these boundaries should be blocked by the gates of Part 13 and handed over to Part 16 for governance, suspension, or retirement.

## 12.16 Format for Publication to Readers

When publishing externally, deliver the full analysis by default. Open with the current judgment and its scope, then develop the conditions, evidence, and uncertainty in full. The main text should retain the items that apply to the current kind of output, including the current cutoff, target and horizon, scope of objects and circles, simple baseline, all substantive path comparisons already performed, the conditions for each path to hold, early and contrary signals, strength of expression, suspension, and the next review. Substantive analysis must not be omitted on the grounds that it does not change the main conclusion, belongs to a secondary branch, or is not a decisive reason. Conditions must not be hidden in footnotes, and “the model thinks” must not stand in for evidential responsibility. Shorten the visible answer only when the user explicitly asks for a brief reply or specifies a shorter length, while retaining the full analysis. If the analysis exceeds the capacity of one delivery, deliver it section by section and provide the complete file, stating what has yet to be delivered. Summaries, links to attachments, and coverage markers cannot substitute for the argument in the main text.

An analysis of bounded choice should state explicitly that it has entered the normative layer. It should list the value premises, deciding subject, affected positions identified and the limits of identification, protection floor, available options, distributional consequences of action and no action, authorization status, action ceiling, stopping, restoration, and remedy in full. The current analytical recommendation may come first, followed by the complete reasons for accepting and ruling out each option, costs, objections, and conditions for revising the judgment. If authorization has yet to be obtained, state clearly that the recommendation is for deliberation and that execution in reality has yet to be authorized. An imperative must not be used to make a recommendation look like a decision that can be executed. Lack of execution permission must not reduce an analytical choice with adequate grounds to a list of questions.

| Publication Status | Permitted Wording | What Must Be Avoided |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Explanation only | “Current evidence supports mechanism A and leaves B open.” | “Therefore, the next step must occur.” |
| Projection only | “If X continues and Y occurs, path P receives support.” | “The model’s prediction of P is settled.” |
| Registered forecast | “Within horizon T, P currently takes priority over Q. See contrary signal S.” | Hiding the baseline, horizon, or failure conditions |
| Normative checks not yet passed | “An analytical recommendation can be made under explicit premises. Real-world execution still requires normative premises, the protection floor, itemized authorization, and operational procedures.” | “Authorization has yet to be obtained, but execution can begin immediately.” |
| Externally authorized | “The authorization record permits the subject to execute within the ceiling and stop under the stated conditions.” | Attributing authorization to the model |

Interpretation after publication is also subject to governance. If readers mistake conditional foresight for a certain prophecy, a candidate personality hypothesis for a fact, or an option comparison for an order, the publisher should correct the misunderstanding without exploiting it to increase the publication’s impact. Append any update as a new version and keep the original title, probabilities, horizon, and failure record traceable.

[^tn-circle-13]: Translator's note: Circles may be parallel, nested, overlapping, or bridged.

<a id="part_13"></a>

# Part 13 Judgment Procedures and Tools

This Part explains how to convert the objects, propositions, scales, mechanisms, actors, multi-circle joint states, and requirements for dynamic projection defined in the preceding twelve Parts into limited judgments that can be observed, questioned, reviewed, and withdrawn. It adds no facts about the world. Filling in a table completely does not establish a fact. Before the tool workflow begins, the candidate object must already have been defined by the seven elements of a structural object (§3.1), and its position on the nine scale axes (§5.2) must have been stated. If the object, boundary, scale, time window, identity criterion, or intended use changes, existing judgments must not simply be carried over.

The tool workflow has two levels. The seven gates (§13.3) are the only main workflow. The five gates and thirteen steps (§13.4) are the layer that elaborates a diagnosis[^tn-diagnosis-14]. The seven gates determine whether a judgment can proceed to the next level. In complex cases the five gates and thirteen steps spell out the material that must be submitted. They do not issue a separate “pass” that competes with the seven gates or produce a second set of workflow results.

The most important boundary is this: the tool layer confers no authorization. Even when the workflow, evidence, and strong-judgment kit (§13.5) are all complete, the outputs are limited to descriptions, candidate mechanisms, comparative judgments, strong-judgment candidates, or requirements for action. Real-world action must still go separately through the normative choice record (§14.7), the ten bridging components required by the conclusion rule “Normative Bridging” (§4.14.1), one and the same valid itemized authorization, and the four-step operational procedure (§14.6). A tool output cannot substitute for any of them.

The workflow below governs judgments formed according to the structure of this framework, and the handoff of those judgments. Reading, checking against the original text, and clarifying a low-impact question can use concise records suited to the task. Not having gone through the whole tool workflow is no basis for declaring that established facts in the domain do not exist. Formal diagnosis, foresight, or high-impact use must meet all of the corresponding conditions. Renaming an output cannot reduce the responsibilities it carries.

## 13.1 Four Conversions

There are four conversions on the way from structural variables to requirements for action. The four conversions do not swap terms from the theory for labels of real-world situations. With each conversion, the responsibility for recording increases. If any step does not pass, the outputs that depend on it stop before that step. The formal completeness of a later step cannot make up for the failure. Other independent judgments are reviewed separately on their own grounds and intended uses.

| Conversion | Required Result | Where to Stop If It Does Not Pass |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structural variables to observable signals | A record of signals that specifies the object, scale, observation position, time window, measurement method, and missing-data status | A conceptual mapping or a gap in the material |
| Signals to strength of evidence | An evidence record that separates sources, observations, comparison conditions, coverage, counterexamples, alternative explanations, and uncertainty | Ungraded material or a hypothesis to test |
| Strength of evidence to level of judgment | A judgment that defines its proposition clearly and states limits of applicability, contrary conditions, falsification conditions, and withdrawal conditions | A candidate explanation or an observational assessment |
| Level of judgment to requirements and ceiling for action | A list of affected positions, the protection floor, prohibited actions, stopping, appeal, and restoration, stating which of the normative premises, itemized authorization, operational procedures, and the conclusion rule “Normative Bridging” (§4.14.1) are still missing | Description, a need for more evidence, or a requirement to take no action |

Each of the four conversions guards against one error. The first, from structural variables to observable signals, prevents a narrative about structure from being treated as an observed fact. The second, from signals to strength of evidence, prevents citations, materials, or declarations of position from being treated directly as evidence.
