The third, from strength of evidence to level of judgment, prevents correlation, analogy, or one narrative of how a mechanism works from being elevated to a conclusion. The fourth, from level of judgment to requirements and ceiling for action, prevents a leap from a factual judgment to action. Passing all four conversions leaves authorization status unchanged.

If any conversion does not pass, the later conversions that depend on it can only be recorded as “not carried out.” The propositions, comparative judgments, strong-judgment candidates, and requirements for action that they support must also be stopped or downgraded. Downstream conclusions that arise from the same gap must not regain their original ceiling through renaming, splitting, or opening another branch. A later “not carried out” only preserves this chain of failure. Even a complete strong-judgment kit cannot repair the break. A judgment may retain its original standing if it does not depend on the failed step, has independent grounds, and its use meets its own requirements. If the gap affects the overall source status, a shared factual premise, the object boundary, or lawful conditions for use of the entire task, stop or downgrade all dependent outputs together. If a check required for high-impact adoption does not pass, the same judgment must not retain its original use merely by being called an ordinary opinion.

## 13.2 Using the Eleven Basic Structural Concepts and the Eleven Human Variables

The eleven human variables of Part 7 (§7.3) apply to the human structured world. The eleven basic structural concepts of Part 3 (§3.5) are general. The tool layer can use both sets side by side in the same case. Matching numbers, equal counts, or similar questions are not taken to establish one-to-one equivalence.

When using them, state at least which basic structural concept or which human variable is used, the effective object, its position on the nine scale axes, the selected support route, the evidence for this case, alternative explanations, missing-data status, the judgment ceiling, and the action ceiling. Three of the six human-domain clauses (§7.1) are empirical hypotheses: “Meaning and Coordination,” “Power, Mediation, and Reflexivity,” and “Historical Trace Carriers.” Each may enter the specified routes only through a specific test of its own (§4.2). The four empirical questions can support empirical claims only through formal tests (§4.1) pre-registered before the results appear. The detailed descriptions of the concepts and variables (for the human variables, see Appendix A) can raise questions, but filling in every item cannot establish facts about the object.

## 13.3 The Seven Gates as the Only Main Workflow

The seven gates are taken one by one for each specific proposition, in the order of its dependencies. If a gate does not pass, the later gates that depend on it can only be recorded as “not carried out,” and the corresponding judgments and requirements for action stop or are downgraded. A later “not carried out” cannot raise again the ceiling already lowered by the gate that did not pass. Nor can one acknowledge that the object or evidence did not pass a gate while letting the related later procedures claim to have passed. A judgment that does not depend on the failed step must still undergo its own independent review of evidence and intended use. Another proposition’s passing must not be used to conceal this proposition’s failure. Once the overall source status, a shared factual premise, the object boundary, or the lawful conditions for use of the task cease to hold, all outputs that depend on them stop together. When the object, the evidence relied on, affected positions, or intended use changes substantially, start again from the earliest gate affected.

| Gate | Core Question | Output Ceiling If It Does Not Pass |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Effective Object Gate | Do the object, boundary, position on the nine scale axes, time window, and identity criterion support the current judgment? | Redefine the object, record the scale as “unknown,” or review the object conversion |
| Evidence Traceability Gate | Are sources, materials, observations, evidence, counterexamples, cases, and judgments distinct and traceable? | Organization of materials, candidate questions, or hypotheses to test |
| Affected Positions Gate | Which positions will see their circumstances change through direct, indirect, second-order, cross-domain, or intertemporal effects? | Supplement the accounting of impacts. Suspend strong judgments and high-impact uses |
| Power and Anti-Retaliation Gate | Can people in low-power positions safely add evidence, rebut claims, refuse, stop, and appeal? | Draw no adverse inference from silence. Lower the levels of publication and judgment |
| Mediation and Reflexivity Gate | Do metrics, platforms, AI, public evaluation, or the act of diagnosis change the evidence and the object? | High reflexivity remains unresolved. Restate the judgment as a conditional state transition |
| Strong-Judgment Procedure Gate | Has the complete strong-judgment kit been submitted for the proposition whose intended use and foreseeable impacts trigger the strong-judgment procedure? Public dissemination requires closer scrutiny. It does not by itself elevate all analyses to strong judgments | Stop the relevant strong judgments and high-impact uses. Review separately any comparative judgment that stands independently and meets the requirements for its use |
| Action Ceiling Gate | What is the most that may be required? Which actions are prohibited, and when are stopping, appeal, and restoration called for? | Description, gaps in evidence, no action, or continued deliberation |

Passing all seven gates indicates only that the records required at each gate have no gaps. It does not establish that the conclusion is true. Empirical propositions are still judged by their own definitions and the evidence of specific tests. Normative objectives still require explicit normative premises. Real-world action still requires normative choice, the conclusion rule “Normative Bridging” (§4.14.1), itemized authorization, and operational procedures (§14.6). The “Action Ceiling Gate” in particular can only record whether the external normative and authorization layers are in place. The tool workflow cannot write the result as “authorized” on its own.

The “Strong-Judgment Procedure Gate” has a specific applicability rule. Ordinary outputs at the “lightweight description” and “standard judgment” levels (§13.6) may record this gate as “not applicable,” but the record must state why the strong-judgment procedure is not triggered on this occasion. Recording it this way does not block the “Action Ceiling Gate.” Once this gate is recorded as “passed,” the same record must include the complete results of the strong-judgment kit (§13.5), with every item passed. Writing only the word “checked,” or leaving the reason blank, cannot substitute for these eight results.

The scope of identification for the “Affected Positions Gate” is determined under §14.4.1. Positions that section requires to be listed in full must be listed in full; for other positions, the record must state how far they were traced and why tracing stopped. For explanation and diagnosis tasks without a comparison of options, the test is whether further tracing could change the conclusion or its level, the scope of use, or protective arrangements.

## 13.4 The Five Gates and Thirteen Steps for Elaborating a Diagnosis

Go through the five gates and thirteen steps when the object is complex, responsibility is heavy, reflexivity is high, or the seven gates (§13.3) call for more detailed evidence. The five gates are local checks within this elaboration. They do not produce a second set of main workflow results.

| Elaboration Gate | Material That Must Be Developed | Corresponding Main Gates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Object Gate | Object, boundary, scale, and time window | Effective Object Gate |
| Evidence Gate | Cost of signals, sources, weights, and review | Evidence Traceability Gate |
| Scale Gate | Position on the nine scale axes, objects and evidence within each scale, and changes in scale | Effective Object Gate and Evidence Traceability Gate |
| Responsibility Gate | Effects on rights and resources, contrary conditions, repair windows, appeals, and review | Affected Positions Gate, Power and Anti-Retaliation Gate, and Strong-Judgment Procedure Gate |
| Observation Gate | Baseline before observation, reactions during observation, reactions after publication, and a ceiling on recursion | Mediation and Reflexivity Gate |

The thirteen steps, in order from the real-world question to write-back, form a chain of work that can be checked.

| Step | Minimum Deliverable |
| --- | --- |
| Start With the Question | A real-world question in language outside the framework, the requester, and the intended use |
| Identify the Object and Boundary | Effective object, subsystems, higher-level environment, and external channels |
| Separate Signal Types | Separate columns for facts, behavior, resources, feedback, narratives, feelings, conjecture, and noise |
| Record Participation in Observation | Whether those observed are aware of it, observer power, impacts of publication, and candidate responses |
| Identify the Dominant Constraint | Candidate constraints, the selected constraint, evidence for selection, and competing constraints |
| Record the State and Window | For an applicable object, which of the seven state prototypes (§8.3) it corresponds to, its position within that state, parallel subsystems, and contrary conditions. If inapplicable, state why and retain the domain’s own states and windows |
| Examine the Core Structure | Anchor, uptake layer, transmission chain, boundary, and feedback write-back |
| Identify Key Variables for Protection | Variables to protect, paths to harm, resources, redundancy, and paths for repair or return flows |
| Record Uptake and Repayment | Cost bearers, recipients of return flows, rights to stop, long-term overextension, and shifting of harms |
| Identify Hidden Risks and Boundary Types | Maintenance debt, mismatches between fast and slow processes, metric substitution, distorted summaries, and candidate object conversions |
| Propose Candidate Mechanisms | Competing mechanisms that the material permits and that could change the judgment, the evidence each requires, evidence that weakens them, and rules for eliminating them. If no plausible competing explanation exists, state the scope of the search and the failure conditions. Do not invent mechanisms to meet a quota |
| Anticipate Branches | Triggers, early signals, contrary conditions, repair windows, and minimum requirements for action |
| Produce the Output and Write Back | Output in ordinary language, conditions that trigger revision, scope of the record, review, withdrawal, and restoration |

Several of these steps have limits of their own. When the “Record the State and Window” step uses the seven state prototypes, it can use them only for human intentional collectives to which they apply. The prototypes must not be forced onto objects to which they do not apply, and they must not be treated as levels of maturity or as fate. When the “Identify Key Variables for Protection” step finds an important variable for protection, it can only propose a need for protection on that basis. When the “Record Uptake and Repayment” step finds uptake or overextension, this cannot generate a duty to make sacrifices or establish full responsibility. Candidate mechanisms proposed in the “Propose Candidate Mechanisms” step must not bypass the conditions for causal claims (§2.4). The branches given in the “Anticipate Branches” step do not describe a certain future. If the “Produce the Output and Write Back” step lacks review and withdrawal, the judgment must not be entered into organizational records, eligibility, allocation, or public memory.

## 13.5 The Strong-Judgment Kit

Whether a judgment is a strong judgment is determined by its uses and foreseeable impacts. Tone, length, and confidence of expression do not determine the category. A judgment enters the strong-judgment procedure if it is intended or reasonably foreseeable for use in real-world action or decisions about eligibility, rights, or resource allocation. The same applies if it has a material impact on a specific subject’s reputation and place in public memory, or if it is embedded in automated, organizational, or institutional decisions. Check the actual use of intermediate scores, recommendations, or material screening when they affect these decisions downstream.

Public dissemination is one factor that raises the requirements for scrutiny. It should be assessed in light of the object evaluated, factual allegations, identifiability, reach, and consequences. Publication alone is insufficient to raise every analytical output to a strong judgment. Ordinary work can reach definite conclusions when evaluating arguments, explaining mechanisms, or articulating normative views, provided the uses and impacts above are absent and the evidence and review meet the task’s requirements. Calling an output commentary, research, or a draft does not exempt it if it actually meets the strong-judgment conditions.

Only a judgment handled at the “strong-judgment candidate” level (§13.6), with all seven gates (§13.3) passed and each of the following eight items passed individually, may be recorded as a strong-judgment candidate. It still confers no authorization to act in reality.

| Component | Required Question |
| --- | --- |
| Contrary conditions | What circumstances would weaken, reverse, or lead to withdrawal of the judgment? |
| Repair window | Where is the window, what supports it, and when does it cease to hold? |
| Evidence requirements | What evidence supports the judgment, what evidence is missing, and what evidence weighs against it? |
| Access to appeal | Who can file an appeal, who is responsible, what is the time limit, and can the outcome change? |
| Anti-retaliation protection | Which activities are protected, how is protection monitored, and how can retaliation be reported independently and remedied? |
| Right to add evidence | How can evidence be added, how can existing records be corrected, and how are downstream records corrected in turn? |
| Trigger for external review | When is review triggered, who reviews independently, and can the reviewers see the materials and stop the result from taking effect? |
| Restoration and write-back | Which state is restored, who carries out the repair, which version of the record governs, and how are all records brought into agreement? |

If any of the eight items is missing, the judgment does not pass the “Strong-Judgment Procedure Gate” (§13.3). It must not become a strong-judgment candidate or retain its original high-impact use. It may be recorded only as an internal hypothesis, an open assertion, or a candidate mechanism within the limits of its materials and actual use. A comparative judgment at the “standard judgment” level may remain if it does not depend on the missing item, has independent grounds, and does not trigger a strong-judgment use. Failure of a common premise still blocks all judgments that depend on it. Renaming or splitting must not be used to evade that limit. Access to appeal does not count as an effective appeal if it cannot change a record or action. Being external in name does not establish independence. A statement, an apology, or the release of a new version does not amount to actual restoration and repair.

## 13.6 Diagnostic Levels

Diagnosis has three levels, called for short “lightweight description,” “standard judgment,” and “strong-judgment candidate.”

| Level | When It Applies | Output Ceiling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lightweight description and exploratory questions | Low complexity, low impact, reversibility, and limited information | Description, questions, and the next observation |
| Standard reviewable judgment | A structural comparison is needed, but the judgment will not be used for action carrying high responsibility | A comparative judgment within stated limits or a candidate mechanism |
| Strong-judgment candidate carrying high responsibility | Judgments with substantively high impact or embedded in automated, organizational, or institutional decisions. Public dissemination is reviewed in light of the object, factual allegations, identifiability, and consequences | A strong-judgment candidate after the seven gates and the strong-judgment kit pass |

A higher level adds responsibility for recording and does not make a judgment “closer to the truth.” The level must be downgraded if evidence coverage declines, the object undergoes conversion, reflexivity becomes uncontrolled, or appeals or anti-retaliation protection fail. Urgency does not permit omitting the object, protection, or stopping conditions. When waiting is costly, the tool may only propose, separately from the applicable authorization, the narrowest requirement for action that can be withdrawn and monitored.

## 13.7 Six Formal Tools

There are six formal tools. Each has its own purpose and its own limits.

| Tool | Purpose and Limits |
| --- | --- |
| Source–Evidence Ledger | Keep sources, materials, observations, evidence, counterexamples, coverage, and uncertainty separate. It does not prove a proposition |
| Open Assertion Record | Leave a provisional judgment that can be questioned, falsified, or withdrawn, to serve as a target. Do not use it for action carrying high responsibility |
| Proposition Validation Form | State the proposition type, evidence, counterevidence, falsification conditions, impacts, and ceilings item by item |
| Forecast Registration | Set down in advance the prediction, window, triggers, early signals, contrary signals, and which propositions the result is to be written back to |
| Counterexample and Scale Stress Test | Use boundary cases, adversarial explanations, and changes in scale to locate failures and narrow the scope |
| AI Output Boundaries | Require a statement of sources, missing material, the responsible human, uncertainty, prohibited uses, and review and withdrawal |

The Source–Evidence Ledger must not turn “has a source” into “is supported.” An open assertion cannot substitute for proposition validation. A failed prediction must be written back to the relevant proposition. An internal stress test is only a wind tunnel and does not supply external empirical support. The tools may cite one another’s records, but must not form a circle in which they vouch for one another.

Automatic checking is suited to a few tasks: checking items that can take values only from fixed options, checking whether references correspond to real material, checking whether versions and statuses agree from place to place, and checking whether calculations can be reproduced. It cannot replace assessment of materials, testimony from people affected, causal identification, or choices about values. Work that can be done mechanically should be left to programs so that readers can examine the actual grounds for judgments. The complete record of the process and clear prose can be kept separately, provided each can be found from the other.

## 13.8 Limits on the Use of AI

AI can organize materials, check the items in a record, compare different versions, propose candidate questions, list alternative explanations, and find inconsistencies in formatting. Where the evidence and normative premises allow, AI should also compare mechanisms, form refutable judgments, recommend options, and draft complete institutional arrangements, plans, and commentary.

AI must not invent sources, treat information recalled from training as current evidence, express consent on someone’s behalf, interpret silence as consent, take the place of a deciding subject or authorizing authority, or hide uncertainty. It must not make high-risk real-world decisions independently.

AI outputs must state what materials were used, what is missing, which content is observation, which is inference, and which is analogy, who is responsible for the final judgment, how the output may be used, and when it is to be reviewed or withdrawn. Where disclosure of identity, retaliation risk, or justified opacity is involved, omissions made for protection must remain distinguishable from “no evidence.”

Responsibility for AI use should also reflect the actual division of work among those who provide materials, decide objectives and permissions, maintain systems, carry out actions, and review results. Facilities and procedures that perform technical steps do not become subjects capable of bearing moral or legal responsibility merely because they output recommendations or execute instructions. Organizations legally capable of bearing a specified responsibility must be assessed separately according to their institutional status and the matter at issue. Greater automation does not put all responsibility on the person who clicks last. Reviewers must have sufficient materials, time, capability, and authority to stop actions in practice. The organization must also provide the resources needed for these conditions.

## 13.9 Workflow Records and What Failure Means

Each pass through the tool workflow must leave a workflow record. The items of this record are fixed, and users must not add items of their own. It states the following: the records of the object and scale; the diagnostic level used (§13.6); the result of each of the four conversions (§13.1); the result of each of the seven gates (§13.3); whether the five gates and thirteen steps (§13.4) were gone through; whether the strong-judgment kit (§13.5) was triggered; evidence; alternative explanations; uncertainty; the category of output; the judgment ceiling and the action ceiling; the handoff to the normative layer; appeal; restoration; and status.

The action ceiling has only three levels: “description only,” “diagnosis only,” and “requirements only.” Which categories of output may appear at each level is fixed. At no level can the output authorize or execute anything. Users must not claim “already authorized” in free text or expand the permitted categories on their own. A requirement for action only sets out the conditions that the external choice and authorization procedures need. It is not an executable command.

A handoff to the normative layer must point to external records that can be checked: the normative choice record (§14.7), the record of the check under the conclusion rule “Normative Bridging” (§4.14.1), and the authorization record. Where these records are not yet in place, this must be stated plainly. Pointing to them must make clear the object, action, scope, and time, and what the verification actually rests on. Vague labels, claims of having passed, or a record that circles back to cite itself cannot establish permission. The specific format of references is determined by the tools and practices actually adopted. This does not change one boundary: the tool must not issue authorization itself.

The results must remain distinguishable. “Passed” means that the records required for that item met the requirement. “Failed” means that the step was carried out but did not meet it. “Not carried out” means that the step was not done because an earlier gate did not pass or because of a limit of scope. “Unknown,” “not applicable,” “unobservable,” and “withheld for protection” remain four distinct missing-data states (§2.9). “Failed” must not be rewritten as “not applicable.” Content withheld for protection must not be rewritten as “does not exist.”

The workflow record itself never has the effect of an authorization. Even when there are records to point to for the external normative choice, the check under “Normative Bridging,” itemized authorization, and operational procedures, the workflow record only checks them and hands off to them. It cannot create an authorization of its own. All reviewed outputs must retain an accessible route of appeal and actual routes of withdrawal and correction. A tool conclusion that cannot be withdrawn must not be put to a high-impact use that is difficult to reverse.

## 13.10 The Nine Gates for Multi-Circle Projection

The seven gates (§13.3) are the only main workflow for explanation and diagnosis. When a task explicitly calls for dynamic projection, conditional foresight, or bounded choice, elaborate that workflow with the nine gates. The nine gates must not bypass the seven gates’ requirements for the object, evidence, affected positions, power, reflexivity, the strong-judgment procedure, and the action ceiling.

| Gate | Core Check | Output If It Does Not Pass |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Facts as They Stand | Event type, source, time, evidence cutoff, and disputes | List of factual questions |
| Joint Object | Actors, circles, relations, membership, and the identity criterion | Candidate groupings or a return to a single focus |
| Two Channels and Clocks | Material conditions and experience–meaning conditions relevant to the task, clocks, and unknowns. Irrelevant items are recorded as “not applicable” once the reason is stated | Retain the state snapshot. Suspend propagation that depends on missing conditions and review independent paths separately |
| Propagation Through Mechanisms | Channels, thresholds, delay, feedback, and cascades | Candidate mechanisms and observations that can distinguish them |
| Branching Paths | Conditions, parent and child nodes, and early and contrary signals | Parallel paths without forced ordering |
| Forecast Registration | Target, horizon, simple baseline, calibration, and write-back | Scenario projection only |
| Normative Choice | Normative premises, the protection floor, affected people, options, and no action | Suspend recommendations blocked by the gap. Retain evaluations that stand independently, conditional recommendations under explicit premises, and requirements for more evidence. This confers no permission to execute |
| Authorization and Execution | Itemized authorization, operational procedures, responsibility, stopping, restoration, and remedy | External handoff without execution |
| Outcome Write-Back | Results, comparison with the baseline, deviations, downgrades, and retirement | Retain the record of failure and start a new version |

The tool can propose candidate circles at the “Joint Object” gate and variable candidates at the “Branching Paths” gate, but every candidate always remains only a candidate. If the “Forecast Registration” gate does not pass, outputs must not use forecast language such as “will happen” or “expected to prove accurate.” If the “Normative Choice” or the “Authorization and Execution” gate does not pass, outputs must not give executable instructions. The “Outcome Write-Back” gate does not permit overwriting the original record.

## 13.11 Limits on AI in Dynamic Runs

AI can organize materials, check original passages that can be located, find which items are missing from a record, propose and compare competing paths, check whether definitions and arrangements are consistent, and calculate metrics registered in advance. Under explicit normative premises it can also form well-grounded local judgments and recommendations and draft complete texts.

AI cannot certify a real-world event solely on the basis of content it has generated, its own statements, or internal procedures. It cannot diagnose personality, disclose information on behalf of those concerned, use its own classifications to decide circle boundaries that bind others, treat simulations as facts, settle disputed value premises for others, or issue authorization.

Whether external material supports a particular fact must be judged separately according to the material’s status, method, counterexamples, and intended use. Faithfulness to a source does not automatically establish that what it says about the world is true. For a variable automatically proposed by AI, the system must record that it is only a candidate proposed by a model, and state the minimal test and prohibited uses. It must not be upgraded before the corresponding external evidence is available.

### 13.11.1 Checking AI Materials and the Chain of Tool Actions

When checking a generated answer, examine separately whether the source exists, whether the citation details are correct, whether the original passage supports the sentence, and whether the fact asserted in the sentence has adequate grounds. A source’s silence on the matter does not establish that the sentence is wrong. Accurately restating a mistaken source does not establish the facts. Where local knowledge, oral accounts, or protected materials have no public webpage, retain appropriate means of verification and limits on public disclosure. They must not be treated as nonexistent on that basis alone.

Retrieval augmentation can improve access to materials and performance on a task. Consistency or uncertainty checks can also detect certain errors. Their effectiveness remains limited by retrieval coverage, shared sources, and the types of error. An error repeated reliably can appear consistent. Several models repeating the same inaccurate material do not supply several independent pieces of evidence. A formal checker can confirm a derivation under stated premises, but cannot establish that those premises hold in reality.

For automated action, record the recommendation, tool request, application execution, external state, and consequences separately. The model writing “stopped” does not establish that the executor received a stop instruction. An interface showing “deleted” does not establish that downstream copies are gone. A person changing a recommendation does not establish that the change took effect before an irreversible action. Permissions for actual protection and correction must be exercisable in the corresponding system.

### 13.11.2 Task Endpoints and a Verifiable Execution Chain

How far a series of tool operations is to be verified is determined by the user’s request or by the task an institution sets. If the request is only for a draft, delivery can be complete when the draft has been saved correctly, can be opened, and its content meets the requirements. If the task requires changing an external record, the tool returning “success” is not enough. The change must still be confirmed by the state of the corresponding external object. If the task requires actual remedy, it must further be verified that the resources, rights, or services actually reach those concerned. Actual completion of a narrower endpoint need not wait for every consequence in people’s lives. A success message returned by the interface cannot substitute for completion of a broader endpoint.

| Stage | Minimum Object of Verification | Typical Break |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Form the recommendation | Objective, materials, object to be changed, and permitted scope | Treating generated text as already adopted |
| Make the tool request | Specific action, parameters, the current version of the object, and permissions | Sending a correct recommendation to the wrong object |
| Execute in the application | Whether the request was received, executed, or rejected, and how repeated requests are handled | A request arrives but is queued, fails, or is executed repeatedly |
| Check external state | Whether the target and dependent objects changed as intended | A local marker changes while actual execution still reads the old state |
| Check the task outcome | The specified benefit or protection endpoint and remaining problems | A corrected record takes effect, but the missed opportunity is not restored |

When several tools operate at the same time, first distinguish three cases: operations that can read independently, operations that can modify independently, and operations that write to the same object. Changes to shared state must preserve their order, state which version of the object the change presupposes, or settle how conflicts are handled. Before an irreversible action, verify again that permissions and stopping conditions are still valid. A request timing out means its outcome is unknown. Do not assume it was not executed and repeat it. Check the request identifier or object state first, then decide whether to retry. These are responsibilities for execution. They do not require every application to use the same log format.

Stopping has its own completion conditions. Record separately the issuing of a stop instruction, acknowledgment by the executor, termination of actions already in progress, and remedy of consequences that have already occurred. If only the first two steps are confirmed, report that scope accurately. If winding down safely requires a limited action under a separate responsibility, continue it on its own grounds. Stopping the main task must not mean abandoning the necessary continuation. When repair fails, keep a record of the object for which repair failed and of the real-world consequences. A new, normal output must not overwrite them.

[^tn-diagnosis-14]: Translator's note: Diagnosis here denotes a nonclinical assessment within the framework.

# Part 14 Normative Choice

The preceding structural grammar, four empirical questions, scale transformations, mechanisms of operation, and human variables address “how objects exist, operate, and change, and what grounds we have for explaining them in these ways.” This Part asks a different question. Among several possible directions, who may choose, on what grounds, whom does the choice bind, and how do we stop and repair if it fails?

The two kinds of question must be kept separate. An explanation can be highly reliable and still be insufficient to confer authority to act. A goal can receive wide support and still breach rights floors, shift costs to low-power positions, or exceed the decision maker’s jurisdiction. Normative choice is therefore not a passage appended to diagnosis. It is a separate layer of conditions between explanation and real-world action.

The requirements in this Part belong to three levels, each with a different scope.

The first level consists of principles of argument. They state what a normative judgment must distinguish: facts and what ought to be; the value premises used, and the conflicts among them; beneficiaries and those who bear the costs; and, where options are chosen, the options, no action among them. Analytical recommendations for deliberation are bound by them as well.

The second level consists of substantive safeguards. They state what real-world adoption must actually have: first, valid authorization covering the action; second, the substance of the protections referred to by the ten items of the protection floor (§14.8), including identification of affected positions and low-power positions, safe submission and anti-retaliation, genuine refusal and exit, accessible appeal and independent review, adding evidence and correcting records, restoration and remedy, and action ceilings and expiry.

The third level is the record format. It states how this framework records the above for its own “authorized” status (§14.7), for example by pointing to the no-action option with a unique identifier and by binding exactly ten items of the protection floor. Other practices that carry equivalent responsibilities for protection, tracing, and review may adopt different formats. Whether they are equivalent must be confirmed by independent review, not claimed by the party that adopts the practice.

The test of whether a requirement belongs to the record format is this: if deleting it would change who is protected, who bears the costs, who has the right to decide, who can stop, or who can correct errors, it does not belong to the record format.

## 14.1 Facts Do Not Entail What Ought to Be Done

Factual propositions describe “what is.” Normative premises state “what is worth pursuing, protecting, or prohibiting.” Claims that “a structure is stable,” “an option is more efficient,” “the system retains a certain type,” or “a risk is rising” cannot directly entail “therefore this should be done.” Facts have a defined role in choice. They determine whether an option is possible, what its consequences might be, and the extent of risk and uncertainty. They do not choose values or create authorization on their own.

Any process that moves from explanation or diagnosis to real-world action must therefore go through the four-step operational procedure (§14.6), one step after another. The first step, “Fixing the Facts and Evidence,” fixes in advance the facts, evidence, scale, and uncertainty to be used. The second step, “Stating the Normative Premises and Conflicts,” states the normative premises actually adopted this time (§14.3), conflicts of value, beneficiaries, and those who bear the costs. The third step, “Reviewing Authorization and Comparing Options,” compares options including no action and reviews the scope of authorization, authorization, jurisdiction, validity period, and conflicts of interest. A separate normative choice record then fixes the decision. Only at the fourth step, “Bounded Execution and Correction,” can the approved option be turned into bounded execution that is reversible, monitorable, stoppable, open to appeal and restoration, and ends on expiry.

The severity of a diagnosis provides no direct route to action. High model confidence provides no route to broader permission. Stronger evidence can raise the ceiling for descriptive judgments, but cannot raise the action ceiling by itself.

Among the twelve conclusion rules, the conclusion rule “Normative Bridging” (§4.14.1) checks whether the bridge from description to real-world choice is valid, but it does not choose values. It checks only whether the descriptive conclusion, current evidence, explicit normative premises, conflicts of value, the protection floor, the scope of authorization, options, no action, the four-step operational procedure, the action ceiling, and conditions for correction all meet their requirements at the same time. Least harm and proportionality (§14.4) must be explicitly selected, explained, and reviewed in the specific choice record. They cannot be left implicit in the rule “Normative Bridging.”

## 14.2 Three Distinct Processes of Selection and Choice

Selection and choice cover at least three structurally distinct processes: systemic selection, decision-making by a subject, and collective governance. Conflating them personifies natural or distributed processes, expands personal preferences into public power, or reduces public procedures to the will of those with power.

Systemic selection has no unified deciding subject. It refers to variation or differences producing different outcomes through environments, feedback, competition, replication, and retention mechanisms. Examples include natural selection, differential retention in markets, and content spreading as a result of algorithmic rewards. An analysis of systemic selection needs to state the unit of selection, environment, retention mechanism, time window, and stochastic null model (for the null model, see §3.1). One may say that a form is retained, replicated, or eliminated. One must not say that the system “considers it better.” Retention by itself does not establish normative justification, nor do survival, stability, popularity, or efficiency. The action ceiling for systemic selection is a description of the selection process. Its choice record cannot enter the “authorized” status (§14.7), and its options cannot include an external-action option.

Decision-making by a subject is constrained. The deciding subject must be identifiable and can decide only within their own permissions, genuine options, territory, and validity period. An apparent “choice” must not be recorded as free consent if it arises from coercion, lock-in through defaults, deprivation of information, insufficient capability, unsafe refusal, or blocked exit. Failure to exit does not amount to consent. Entering a process does not amount to continuing consent. One subject’s choice does not automatically bind others.

Collective governance is governance authorized through a procedure. It addresses common affairs. The fact that they are common does not establish that the majority can represent everyone or that the scope of impact equals the scope of jurisdiction. A governance decision must make it possible to trace its boundaries, how the agenda was formed, who has authority to represent, which positions can participate, how dissent is preserved, how minorities are protected, how conflicts of interest are handled, who executes and reviews it, and when authorization expires. Numbers, loudness, efficiency, claims to represent, and legal form cannot by themselves substitute for bounded public authorization.

The three types have strict boundaries. Systemic selection cannot acquire intent or normative justification by borrowing the language that describes subjects. Decision-making by a subject cannot decide for others beyond the subject’s own permissions. Collective governance cannot bypass procedure and present governance as an enlarged version of personal choice.

## 14.3 The Five Normative Premises: Stating in Each Choice Which Are Adopted (N1–N5)

The five normative premises do not operate automatically as background assumptions. Each choice record must publicly list which of them are actually adopted for this choice and say whether each serves as an objective, a constraint, or a veto condition. A normative premise that has not been stated must not appear silently in the conclusion.

These five are normative premises that this framework itself openly commits to (see §16.14). They serve mainly to constrain and to veto, and may also be used as objectives as the preceding paragraph provides. The positive objectives a choice pursues, for example reducing a certain harm, expanding a certain opportunity, or sharing a certain burden fairly, mostly lie outside these five; this framework does not select these objectives for the user, nor does it rank multiple legitimate objectives. They are put forward separately by the subjects who propose and adopt an option and are stated in the same way: the content, the proposer, whether it is used as an objective, a constraint, or a veto condition, the reasons relied on, and whom a choice made under it benefits and who bears its costs. A premise outside the five does not qualify merely because it has been stated: it must not override the protection floor, nor the constraints among the five adopted for this choice; whether the proposer and the adopter are entitled to do so, and whether the procedure of adoption qualifies, are reviewed under §14.5 and §14.6; where it conflicts with other premises, it is handled under the conflict record of this section; where it is itself disputed, the analysis sets out side by side the judgments under the different premises and does not select one on behalf of the entitled subjects (§14.9.1). For any of the five not adopted for this choice, the reason must be stated; one of the five that is relevant to this choice must not be left unadopted on the ground that it would constrain or veto the selected option or another premise.

The first premise, “Explanation Does Not Confer Authority to Act,” vetoes any direct move from facts to action. On its own, this premise can yield only no action, a need for more evidence, or continued deliberation. It cannot generate an affirmative proposal.

The second premise, “Protection Must Not Be Downgraded,” requires scale elevation and action to maintain or strengthen existing protections at low-power positions. If the infrastructure that protection needs is missing, it is the action that is narrowed, not the protection.

The third premise, “High-Impact Judgments Must Be Correctable,” requires genuine access to appeal, independent review, stopping, withdrawal, restoration, remedy, and write-back to the authoritative version.

The fourth premise, “Love and Undertaking Must Not Be Conscripted,” prohibits invoking love, responsibility, care, or the persistence of a system to demand unilateral, unlimited sacrifice without an option to exit.

Bounded responsibility under the fourth premise precludes demands made in the name of love, care, or system persistence for unilateral, unlimited sacrifice without an option to exit. It does not cancel bounded commitments, obligations of support, contractual duties, or remedial responsibilities that have independent grounds, nor does it cancel public burdens that are shared under valid rules and have a definite scope and duration; whether such burdens are justified is still argued separately under this part’s requirements on authorization, distribution, and proportionality (§14.4, §14.6). Ending or transferring a responsibility should specify who will actually take over for dependents, for how long, and with what remaining risks. This requirement must not be used to force those harmed to remain exposed to harm. Capability, causal contribution, benefit, fault, and duties of remedy should be justified separately. 〔Studies 06.06, 09.02, 10.07, 21.06, 23.01–23.07〕

The fifth premise, “Persistence and Systemic Selection Do Not Establish Normative Justification,” limits stability, efficiency, coherence, and outcomes of systemic selection to evidence about consequences. They must not substitute for a judgment of normative justification.

Normative premises in combination can conflict. For example, quickly limiting losses can conflict with full participation. Expanding public benefits can entail risks to the rights of those in minority positions. A short reversible trial can conflict with a long-term goal of stability. Conflicts cannot be smoothed out with a total score. Each conflict must be recorded separately and be traceable, with a list of the conflicting premises, the affected positions, the objections, the decision rule, and the current status. An unresolved substantive conflict can lead to suspension, a narrower trial, or retention of no action. Deleting objections cannot “resolve” it. When every feasible option (including suspension and no action) leaves unmet legitimate claims or irreversible losses, see §14.9.1.

The rights floor consists of the items of the protection floor actually in force for the current choice (for the ten items of the protection floor, see §14.8). It sets a boundary each option must pass first. It must not be treated as a preference freely exchangeable for efficiency. The rights floor and the normative premises have distinct roles. The normative premises state the grounds for choice, and the protection floor states the conditions of protection that no grounds can override.

## 14.4 Generating Options, Consequences Across Scales, and Distribution

Choice begins by generating a set of comparable options. It does not consist of finding reasons for a preselected option. Each option needs a fixed identity, and the following are fixed for it in advance: the kind of option it is, its action type, target object, territory, validity period, reversibility, expected impacts, and distributional impacts. When an option’s action, object, territory, or validity period changes, it should be put forward again as a new version or a new option. The same option must not be quietly reshaped after review.

Each set of options must contain one and only one no-action option, and it must be possible to say clearly which one it is. The no-action option is the baseline path in which the proposed new action under consideration is not carried out. Events can still occur. Existing maintenance, statutory duties, actions already under way, and the conditions for their continuation must be recorded separately. Choosing no action does not remove existing obligations. The resources and arrangements needed to actively maintain the status quo are compared as a separate option. Use the same time window to account for natural changes, accumulating risks, opportunity costs, and distributional consequences on the baseline path. Whether intervention is necessary can be judged only if no action is included. Removing it often amounts to assuming in advance that “something must be done.”

Systemic selection has another kind of option, the system variant, which compares different outcomes under different environments or retention mechanisms. It does not let the system decide. The options for decision-making by a subject and for collective governance may include external-action options, but on entering the “authorized” status one of those external-action options must be fixed. After that, the record kept outside the choice record of the selected action (that is, the action actually to be carried out) must match this option item by item: the same option, the same subject, the same object, the same action, the same territory, and the same validity period.

Consequences must be stated across scales. For every option, use at least the nine scale axes (§5.2) to specify the aggregation level, spatial extent, time span, organizational level, causal level, observation resolution, scope of influence, network topology scope, and scope of authorization where consequences occur. An immediate local benefit cannot represent long-term system benefits. An average improvement cannot cover a local exclusion zone. Stability at a higher level cannot make up for actual losses suffered by subjects at a lower level.

The distribution ledger must record benefits, costs, risks, impacts on rights, and shifts in burdens at each position, and must state whether the power position of each position is low, medium, high, or unknown. The list of affected positions includes the positions that §14.4.1 requires to be listed in full, as well as positions affected indirectly, at second order, across domains, and across generations that are identified under that section. Among them, the positions where it is harder to speak, exit, provide evidence, or shift costs must also be marked specifically as low-power positions. Every option must state who benefits, who bears the costs, who has decision-making authority, who is unable to refuse, whether costs shift from positions with more power to those with less, and whether unobservable positions are being mistaken for absent ones.

Least harm and proportionality are two explicit principles of choice, namely the principle of least harm and the principle of proportionality. The record for each of the two must specify which principle is used and which version of it, the selected option, all options compared, evaluation dimensions, adequate reasons, the evidence relied on, the reviewer, the time of review, and the status. The principle of least harm must be applied to the current choice. It must explain which harms can be avoided across all feasible options and the no-action option, and why the selected option is the narrowest. The principle of proportionality must also be applied to the current choice. It checks suitability, necessity, benefits and the costs imposed on rights, intensity, scope, and duration separately. When an existing arrangement or intervention is argued to be necessary, the dependence, capability gaps, or risks that it has itself created cannot alone serve as evidence of its necessity. To say that a dependence, capability gap, or risk was created by the arrangement requires materials that show it (§2.4, §7.6.1), and it must be separated from needs that existed before the arrangement appeared or exist apart from it: the original needs that the arrangement meets do not count as dependence it has created. The argument for necessity must additionally compare with the case in which the arrangement is absent and proportionate support and transition are provided; this envisaged case is written out under §12.10 as equally close to reality, and its ideal operation is not compared with the arrangement’s actual performance. This does not entail that the arrangement may be removed immediately; the steps of removal and alternative uptake remain under §14.8 and §15.2.3. Neither principle is a synonym for a “good objective.” Neither can be reduced to a slogan that cannot be reviewed or to the bare name of a principle.

When the two principles are applied to the current choice, the evidence relied on must be traceable within the evidence actually used this time. The reviewer must be distinct from the deciding subject and must be a specific person who bears responsibility for independent review. Review must not come later than the option’s entry into the “authorized” status. Only the current version of a principle can be used. Expiry, the validity of the ten items of the protection floor, and the timing of further review must all cover the validity period of the selected option. An expired review record cannot be used to keep the “authorized” status in place.

### 14.4.1 The Scope and Limits of the Responsibility to Identify

Impacts that are indirect, second-order, cross-domain, or intergenerational have no natural endpoint, so identifying them is a responsibility proportionate to risk. Directly affected positions, low-power positions that are known or have been pointed out by others, and positions that application modules require to be listed separately must all be listed in full; the proportionate standard below does not apply to them. For other positions, identification traces outward along the channels already stated and the nine scale axes. The more severe, irreversible, widespread, or likely to accumulate the possible harm is, and the lower the power position of those possibly affected, the farther the tracing should go. Tracing may stop when continuing it can no longer reasonably change the judgment, the comparison of options, or the protective arrangements. Channels not yet stated that others point out must be added to the tracing, or reasons for not adopting them must be stated. This limit is recorded together with the channels already searched, the positions consulted, and what remains unknown, so that others can challenge it.

Unknowns are handled in two ways. The first kind is an unknown for which there are reasonable grounds to think it may reveal a failure of the protection floor, or that is sufficient to change the comparison of options (including least harm, proportionality, and distribution). Such an unknown blocks the part of adoption it affects until evidence is added, the option is narrowed, or protection with separate grounds is in place. All other unknowns are the second kind. They are recorded as they are, with conditions set for observation and renewed identification. Positions identified only after the fact enjoy the same appeal, correction, and remedy and need not first prove that they could have been foreseen.

The limit of identification, the division between direct and indirect, and the kind to which an unknown is assigned cannot be decided solely by a party that benefits from a narrower limit. Their grounds are published in advance and open to appeal, and they are referred to independent review in high-impact cases or when there is a conflict of interest. The same responsibility applies to no action and to maintaining the status quo. Those harmed under the status quo are not exempt from identification because the harm has long existed. The proportionate standard applies only to identifying indirect and more distant positions. It does not reduce the protection that identified positions receive under the ten items of the protection floor, nor can it postpone protection against known harm on the grounds that identification cannot be exhaustive.

## 14.5 Coercion, Defaults, Agendas, Representation, and Minority Protection

Before a subject says “yes,” check the conditions under which they can say “no.” Both decision-making by a subject and collective governance must check the conditions of coercion and choice item by item and keep a record of the check. It examines whether direct or indirect coercion exists, whether the default locks in the result through inertia, complexity, or penalties, whether information is understandable and symmetric, whether the subject has decision-making capability, whether refusal is safe, and whether exit is genuinely feasible. Each check must give a status, rationale, and the evidence relied on. A status of “unknown” does not count as passing. An item recorded as “not applicable” must also state why it genuinely does not apply. If the item “decision-making capability” does not pass, or the conditions needed for participation are insufficient, this shows that the “yes” given on this occasion cannot be treated as free consent, and it requires stating what support and what adjustments in arrangements are needed, who provides them, and when the matter is reviewed again (§16.12, §16.16); the refusal and objections of the person concerned do not lose their force on that account and are still handled in the corresponding procedure under §16.13. Such a shortfall does not by itself constitute a reason to cancel the standing of the person concerned to participate and to raise claims, nor a reason to postpone that standing repeatedly or indefinitely. The basis for when the conditions count as met must be published in advance and be open to appeal; where the party that provides the conditions for forming the capability is the same party that judges whether the standard is met, the matter is referred to independent review. This qualification does not cancel bounded representation and requirements of professional qualification that have independent grounds, nor does it automatically generate new voting rights or membership (§14.10).

Default design is not a neutral background condition. Who sets the default, how much switching costs, and how silence is interpreted can all change the distribution of choices. Coercion also takes forms beyond commands. Tying access to essential resources to compliance, retaliation through relationships, identity exposure, withholding information, unaffordable exit costs, or moralizing care responsibilities can turn formal options into a single path.

The evidential weight of consent varies with conditions. Not exiting does not by itself amount to continuing consent. If an initial choice also changed the conditions of later choices, for example through interrupted skills, housing or services tied to relationships, debt, or dependence on care, “continuing to stay” provides weaker evidence. Two things should be checked separately: the conditions under which consent was originally given, and the conditions under which refusal, negotiation, and exit are still possible now. This does not cancel bounded commitments and obligations of support that have independent grounds; their ending and transfer are handled under the normative premise “Love and Undertaking Must Not Be Conscripted” (§14.3). Nor does it require every future choice to remain open forever. The refusal, stopping, and exit referred to by the protection-floor items “Genuinely Effective Refusal and Stopping” and “Genuine Exit and Alternative Uptake” (§14.8), however, are not closed by past consent. If materials show that consent, approval, or satisfaction after the fact was shaped precisely by the arrangement of education, defaults, rewards and penalties, or information that is under evaluation (§7.3.8), it cannot alone establish that the arrangement is harmless or justified; it must also be checked whether the persons concerned can access contrary materials, can raise objections, and can make a substantive comparison among options. This does not cancel the standing of the persons concerned to judge: the analyst must point out the constrained conditions item by item and must not, on the strength of the analyst’s own judgment of their interests, rewrite their consent or objection wholesale as “having been deceived”; nor does it entail that all education, custom, or persuasion is manipulation.

Collective governance must also check its governance procedure item by item and keep a record of the check. Agenda formation checks who can raise questions, who can exclude options, and when emergency procedures end. Representation checks the source and scope of authorization, whether it can be withdrawn, and who is unrepresented. Participation checks safety, accessibility, information, and actual capability to influence decisions. Minority protection checks rights that majority decisions cannot cancel, local exclusion zones, and conditions for suspension. The conflict-of-interest check asks whether the people who decide, execute, evaluate, and benefit are the same. Accountability for execution checks whether responsible parties can be reviewed, stopped, and replaced.

Responding to specific views and allowing rules to change are different capabilities. Whether it is feasible to veto a proposal, propose an alternative, amend agenda rules, or replace those who hear a matter or make the final decision must be stated separately. When responses are possible only within a set topic while the agenda and the final decision cannot be challenged, record truthfully that “the rule layer cannot be changed.” Do not record this as an absence of feedback, nor as adequate capacity for correction already being in place. Recording it in this way does not substitute for the conditions for correction. In high-impact cases or when there is a conflict of interest, if the final decision cannot be challenged and there is no external independent review, neither the normative premise “High-Impact Judgments Must Be Correctable” (§14.3) nor the protection-floor item “External Independent Review” (§14.8) counts as satisfied. What evidence or dispute over rights is sufficient to trigger review at the rule layer should be published in advance.

Formal participation does not amount to genuine participation. A public meeting, a complaint channel, or a majority vote cannot by itself establish that people in low-power positions can safely express views and influence the decision. Each objection must be preserved separately and be traceable, together with its claim, the position it comes from, evidence, reasons for how it was handled, deadline for response, and safe submission channel. Within the framework, substantive objections capable of changing key facts, rights floors, option feasibility, or valid permissions must be addressed before entering the “authorized” status. Suspend the affected part if the reasons raised have not received a response suited to them. Whether an objection is decisive in this way is judged by criteria published in advance and open to appeal, and the question is referred to independent review when there is a conflict of interest. Objections must not be excluded because few people raise them, because a majority deems them “unimportant,” or because they are inconvenient to handle. When differences in values persist after a reasoned response, preserve the minority view under an explicit decision rule that meets the requirements. Passing does not require fabricating unanimity.

Within the framework, “authorized” is an internal status that marks the scope of use the framework endorses for itself. It does not substitute for legal validity under real-world institutions, official powers, or consent of those concerned. The procedures above cannot override matters that applicable law or the protection floor makes nonwaivable. A procedure record cannot supply a legitimate decision rule where none exists. Emergencies require separately specified temporary authority, the narrowest scope, expiry, and subsequent review. “Objections have been answered” does not confer emergency power. Three situations should be recorded separately: the existence of opposition, reasons for opposition that remain unaddressed, and failure of protection conditions. 〔Studies 14.06, 19.02, 21.04, 25.02〕

## 14.6 Scope of Authorization, the Four-Step Operational Procedure, and Bounded Authorization (J Axis, O1–O4)

The scope of authorization specifies who may decide, on what source of authority, for which object and action, and within which territory and validity period. Authorization must hold item by item. One and the same valid authorization must cover the deciding subject, target object, single action, territory, and entire validity period at once; this is called itemized authorization. One authorization covering the subject and another covering the action cannot be combined into a single authorization. An increase in the scope of observation, scope of influence, or technical capability cannot be taken to expand jurisdiction.

The choice record must fix the source, scope, and validity period of authorization. Each option’s territory must equal that scope, and its validity period must fall within that period. To proceed to external action, the choice record, the selected option, the record of the selected action, and that itemized authorization must match item by item. The existence of a source of authorization does not establish legal validity. Legal validity does not establish normative justification. These must be stated separately in the third step of the four-step operational procedure, “Reviewing Authorization and Comparing Options.”

The four-step operational procedure is not an optional appendix. The first step, “Fixing the Facts and Evidence,” prevents facts, thresholds, and evidence levels from being changed after seeing the options. The second step, “Stating the Normative Premises and Conflicts,” keeps value premises, those who bear the costs, and conflicts visible. The third step, “Reviewing Authorization and Comparing Options,” prevents omission of no action, conflicts of interest, and the limits of authorization. The fourth step, “Bounded Execution and Correction,” prevents a bounded decision from expanding during execution into an indefinite, irreversible action for which no one is responsible. If any step is missing, the choice record can go no further than the “under review” or “suspended” status (§14.7).

Entering the “authorized” status also requires the following. The normative premises adopted are all stated on record and can be found, and they do not consist only of “Explanation Does Not Confer Authority to Act” (§14.3). Conflicts of value and objections have been recorded. Each of the ten items of the protection floor passes. Affected positions and low-power positions have been listed and identified under §14.4.1, and the limit of identification has been recorded. The selected option is a feasible external-action option. Least harm and proportionality have been explicitly selected (§14.4). A valid itemized authorization covers this action. The records of the four steps of the operational procedure correspond to one another and follow on from one another. Stopping, appeal, independent review, restoration, remedy, and lapse on expiry are all actually capable of changing the status.

Itemized authorization specifies sufficient coverage for a particular action. It does not deny that actual institutions consist of multiple actions, each with its own authority. Intake, adjudication, preservation measures, service of process, and enforcement may be carried out in succession by different subjects under the law. Check each action’s own authorization and prerequisites separately, then explain how the preceding result serves as valid input to the next step. Errors in both directions need to be avoided. Several authorizations, each missing a piece, cannot be combined to create authority for the same action. Nor does the fact that no one person holds all permissions invalidate an entire lawful procedure with multiple steps.

Personal consent, private appointment, public authority, and an organization’s legally established standing to make a request can also be valid separately. When a public action is lawful without a private appointment, that does not establish personal consent or permit expansion into other matters. The framework’s internal issuance status determines only the scope of use it is willing to certify. The legal effect of external procedures, normative disputes, and actual effects of protection must still be assessed separately on their respective evidence.

## 14.7 Status, Action Ceilings, and the Correction Loop

A choice record has only seven statuses: draft, under review, authorized, suspended, stopped, restored, and closed. Every change of status must append to the record the previous status, the time, the responsible party, and the grounds. It must not overwrite the existing history.

The “draft” status permits organizing materials and comparing options within existing valid permissions. It grants no new authority for real-world intervention.

“Under review” means that the first three steps of the four-step operational procedure (§14.6), normative conflicts, protection, or authorization are still under review. A need for preservation measures may be raised at this stage, but actual protection, freezing of resources, collection of further evidence, or reversible trials still require applicable, independently valid authorization. Actions under existing statutory duties or emergency powers are recorded within their own scope. They acquire no additional permissions from the “under review” status.

Only decision-making by a subject and collective governance can enter the “authorized” status, and the action ceiling covers only the specific option selected and authorized.

Enter the “suspended” status when a key fact, protection, authorization, procedure, or monitoring condition ceases to hold, and stop the part of implementation affected by that failure. The “under review” or “suspended” status by itself does not authorize freezing resources, restricting access, collecting information, or continuing intervention. Action needed to avoid immediate harm requires a separately valid duty or authorization, a specified scope, and conditions for stopping and review.

Enter the “stopped” status when a condition for stopping is triggered, authorization is withdrawn, the validity period expires, or a prohibited action is taken. Terminate the affected actions under the applicable stopping procedures, and verify safe wind-down and any remedial duties that remain independently valid. Do not wait for new theoretical grounds.

Enter the “restored” status after the recovery set in advance has been completed and verifiable remedy and write-back to the authoritative version have been initiated.

The “closed” status can be entered only when outstanding harm, appeals, remedies, and responsibilities for records have been settled or formally handed off. Any later new action requires a new record.

For each action, its maximum level, prohibited actions, conditions that trigger stopping, and the responsible party with authority to stop it must be stated in advance. The final action ceiling is the narrowest intersection of the following: the descriptive ceiling, normative principles, the protection floor, the selected option, that itemized authorization, the trial scope set by the fourth step, “Bounded Execution and Correction,” reversibility, and expiry. Tightening any item tightens the overall ceiling. A failure or unknown in any item cannot be offset by “high scores” elsewhere.

Appeal must be accessible, have a time limit, and be capable of changing a record or an action. It must lead to external independent review in high-impact cases or when there is a conflict of interest. Anti-retaliation mechanisms protect submitting evidence, raising objections, refusal, stopping, appeal, and exit. Restoration goes beyond withdrawing an order. It includes returning to an acceptable state, correction of authoritative records, synchronization of downstream versions, remedy of real harm, and tracking of residual harm. Every authorization has an expiry time and lapses automatically at expiry. Continued execution must go through authorization again rather than being renewed by default.

Correction has four distinct endpoints. Views are heard safely. Relevant evidence is understood. An authority with jurisdiction actually changes the erroneous decision. Restored resources and rights reach the people concerned. An earlier step can have independent value without closing a later one. A higher rate of overturned decisions is not automatically better. One should check whether substantiated errors can be corrected, who could not enter the process, and what actually reaches people after correction. A record of restoration cannot erase harm that occurred, opportunities that were missed, or costs incurred by others. 〔Studies 21.04, 21.08, 28.04〕

## 14.8 The Ten Items of the Protection Floor and How They Connect to the Choice Record (PF-1–PF-10)

The ten items of the protection floor always remain one complete whole. Scale elevation, object aggregation, option comparison, and convenience of execution do not reduce it. A choice record must account for each of the ten items in turn, with none missing and none repeated. Each item states its applicability status, rationale, evidence, mechanism, responsible party, and conditions that trigger stopping, together with the arrangements for appeal, review, restoration, remedy, and expiry. The rights floor that the record states must be exactly the same as the items among the ten that are currently “in force.” A general statement that “protection has been considered” is insufficient.

The mechanism on which each protection relies must be a mechanism actually stated in the same record, namely one of safe submission, anti-retaliation, appeal, independent review, restoration, remedy, tracking of residual harm, or write-back to the authoritative version. The responsible party for the protection must match the owner of that mechanism. A mechanism that has a name but no content, a mechanism that cannot be found in the record, and independence that is merely claimed do not count as protection. Items of protection specific to humans may be recorded as “not applicable” only if the enclosing object and the downstream use together establish that the impacts are exclusively nonhuman. If the enclosing context involves effects on humans, sentient subjects, mixed objects, rights, or resources, rewriting the scope of impact as “nonhuman only” does not lower the protection floor.

The ten items, in order, are as follows.

Item one: Listing Affected Positions and Low-Power Positions. The affected positions and low-power positions listed and identified under §14.4.1 are entered in the options and the distribution ledger.

Item two: Low-Exposure Channels for Submission. It provides anonymous submission, submission through a representative, or low-exposure submission, so that a high-risk channel requiring a real name is not the only route.

Item three: Genuinely Effective Refusal and Stopping. Refusal and stopping are genuinely effective within the process. Past consent does not amount to permanent consent.

Item four: Effective Appeal. It provides appeal with a time limit and the ability to change the outcome.

Item five: Anti-Retaliation. It protects submitting evidence, raising objections, refusal, stopping, appeal, and exit against retaliation.

Item six: Adding Evidence and Correcting Records. It allows evidence to be added, disputes to be marked, source records to be corrected, and downstream versions to be synchronized.

Item seven: External Independent Review. It provides external independent review when impacts are high, conflicts of interest exist, or internal correction fails.

Item eight: Actual Capability for Withdrawal, Restoration, and Repair. Withdrawal, restoration, repair, and write-back to the authoritative version all need to exist as actual capabilities.

Item nine: Genuine Exit and Alternative Uptake. It provides genuine exit and transfer. Where exit is impossible, it provides representation and alternative arrangements to take over.

Item ten: Action Ceiling and Expiry. It fixes in advance the action ceiling, prohibited actions, conditions that trigger stopping, the responsible party, and the time of review.

The “independence” named in the seventh item is judged by the actual relation between the reviewer and the decision under review and is checked against verifiable records; it is not confirmed by the party under review or by the reviewer (§16.4, §16.8, §16.20). A reviewer who took part in the original decision, or whose appointment, remuneration, appraisal, or promotion is controlled by the party that made the original decision or by the same chain of power, does not count as independent. Where the reviewer has a further relation of funding, status, or commercial interest with the party that made the original decision, where the materials used in the review come only from the party under review, where the conclusions of the review are returned only to the party under review, or where the reviewer relies on materials and methods from the same source as the original decision, these circumstances must be stated, together with the extent to which the review is unaffected by them.

When the objects affected are humans, sentient subjects, mixed objects, or unknown objects, all ten items of the protection floor must be “in force.” Any item that is “pending,” “failed,” or “not applicable” blocks entry into the “authorized” status. Mechanisms specific to humans may be recorded as “not applicable,” with reasons, only when the evidence limits the object and downstream use to purely nonhuman processes. The tenth item, “Action Ceiling and Expiry,” and the requirements that real-world action must meet for the scope of authorization, responsibility, stopping, review, restoration, and expiry, however, always apply. When the use changes, it must be reviewed again. The earlier “not applicable” cannot carry over.

When the objects affected are sentient subjects other than humans, the items among the ten that depend on the object’s own exercise, namely submission, refusal, appeal, and exit, are not on that account recorded as “not applicable,” and they must not be recorded as “in force” where no actual mechanism exists; neither the “exclusively nonhuman” impacts nor the “purely nonhuman processes” mentioned above include sentient subjects. Where a representative exercises these items on their behalf, the representative must be independent of the actor and of the benefiting party (“independent” as judged under the explanation of the seventh item above), must take the interests of these subjects as the matter represented, and must be able actually to stop or change the action; the items are recorded according to the matters and the force that the representative actually covers, and the part not covered is recorded as “failed.” Where there is no such representative, these items are truthfully recorded as “failed”: the action does not obtain this framework’s “authorized” status, though an analytical recommendation for deliberation can still be formed within the lowered judgment ceiling (§5.8); the decision in reality is made by a subject with the corresponding duties and authority, under its own authority and bearing responsibility for it, the protections that can still be preserved continue to apply, and the recommendation must state the narrowest scope, an expiry time, and subsequent review (§14.9.1). Whether an object is sentient is judged by the evidence of the relevant domain; this book sets no separate standard.
